mission.target: Τοπωνύμια πειρατικών και κουρσάρικων ορμητηρίων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο
mission.purpose: Εντόπισε και τεκμηρίωσε ιστορικά τοπωνύμια που συνδέονται με πειρατικά ή κουρσάρικα ορμητήρια, αγκυροβόλια, κρησφύγετα, φυσικά λιμάνια, όρμους, νησίδες, σπηλιές και βάσεις επιχειρήσεων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο κατά τον 17ο αιώνα. Δώσε προτεραιότητα σε πρωτογενείς πηγές, σύγχρονους περιηγητές, ναυτικούς χάρτες, portolans, αρχειακά τεκμήρια, προξενική αλληλογραφία και διοικητικές αναφορές. Για κάθε τοπωνύμιο κατέγραψε: ιστορική μορφή ονόματος, σύγχρονη ταύτιση αν είναι ασφαλής, γεωγραφική θέση, είδος χρήσης ως πειρατικό/κουρσάρικο ορμητήριο, ποιος το χρησιμοποιούσε, χρονολογία ή εύρος χρονολογιών, ακριβή πηγή και παραπομπή, απόσπασμα όπου είναι διαθέσιμο, και βαθμό βεβαιότητας. Ξεχώρισε αυστηρά τεκμηριωμένο γεγονός, πιθανή ταύτιση και υπόθεση. Μην θεωρείς ένα τοπωνύμιο πειρατικό μόνο από νεότερη παράδοση ή ονομασία. Αναζήτησε επίσης ονομασίες τύπου Porto dei Corsari, Porto dei Ladri, Pirate Bay, Corsair harbour και αντίστοιχες ελληνικές, ιταλικές, γαλλικές, ισπανικές και οθωμανικές μορφές, αλλά αντιμετώπισέ τες μόνο ως όρους ανάκτησης μέχρι να επιβεβαιωθούν από πηγή. Νέα πραγματική εκτέλεση μετά τη διόρθωση της μηχανής. Για κάθε τοπωνύμιο καταγράψτε ακριβές απόσπασμα, πηγή, σελίδα/φύλλο/αρχειακή αναφορά, χρονολογία, χρήστες και είδος χρήσης. Η επιδρομή δεν αποδεικνύει ορμητήριο. Σύγχρονη ταύτιση και συντεταγμένες μένουν άγνωστες χωρίς τεκμήριο. Διακρίνετε πρωτογενή πηγή, δευτερογενή μελέτη, ερμηνεία και υπόθεση. Καμία αυτόματη επαλήθευση. Καταγράψτε πρόσβαση ανά connector και πραγματικά βήματα μοντέλου.

discoveries.title: Τα «βρεσίματα» και τα «τζακίσματα» στο Αιγαίο: μέ αφορμή ένα περιστατικό του 17ου αιώνα
creator: Δημήτρης Δημητρόπουλος
discoveries.context_excerpt: Με αφορμή ένα περιστατικό πειρατείας που συνέβη στο Αιγαίο τον 17ο αιώνα -και διασώζεται στην τοπική βιβλιογραφία- διερευνάται το ζήτημα των υπολειμμάτων (εμπορευμάτων, εργαλείων, πρώτων υλών) που εκβάλλουν στις ακτές των νησιών από τυχόν ναυαγισμένα πλοία. Τα ιδιότυπα αυτά αγαθά, όπως και τα πλοία που έχουν ναυαγήσει ή έχουν μείνει ακυβέρνητα και προσαράζουν στις ακτές έχουν σημαντική οικονομική αξία και για το λόγο αυτό υπάρχουν ειδικές προβλέψεις για τα δικαιώματα επ’ αυτών στο εθιμικό δίκαιο και στην καθημερινή πρακτική των χριστιανικών κοινοτήτων.

request.target: Τοπωνύμια πειρατικών και κουρσάρικων ορμητηρίων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο
request.purpose: Εντόπισε και τεκμηρίωσε ιστορικά τοπωνύμια που συνδέονται με πειρατικά ή κουρσάρικα ορμητήρια, αγκυροβόλια, κρησφύγετα, φυσικά λιμάνια, όρμους, νησίδες, σπηλιές και βάσεις επιχειρήσεων στην Ανατολική Μεσόγειο κατά τον 17ο αιώνα. Δώσε προτεραιότητα σε πρωτογενείς πηγές, σύγχρονους περιηγητές, ναυτικούς χάρτες, portolans, αρχειακά τεκμήρια, προξενική αλληλογραφία και διοικητικές αναφορές. Για κάθε τοπωνύμιο κατέγραψε: ιστορική μορφή ονόματος, σύγχρονη ταύτιση αν είναι ασφαλής, γεωγραφική θέση, είδος χρήσης ως πειρατικό/κουρσάρικο ορμητήριο, ποιος το χρησιμοποιούσε, χρονολογία ή εύρος χρονολογιών, ακριβή πηγή και παραπομπή, απόσπασμα όπου είναι διαθέσιμο, και βαθμό βεβαιότητας. Ξεχώρισε αυστηρά τεκμηριωμένο γεγονός, πιθανή ταύτιση και υπόθεση. Μην θεωρείς ένα τοπωνύμιο πειρατικό μόνο από νεότερη παράδοση ή ονομασία. Αναζήτησε επίσης ονομασίες τύπου Porto dei Corsari, Porto dei Ladri, Pirate Bay, Corsair harbour και αντίστοιχες ελληνικές, ιταλικές, γαλλικές, ισπανικές και οθωμανικές μορφές, αλλά αντιμετώπισέ τες μόνο ως όρους ανάκτησης μέχρι να επιβεβαιωθούν από πηγή. Νέα πραγματική εκτέλεση μετά τη διόρθωση της μηχανής. Για κάθε τοπωνύμιο καταγράψτε ακριβές απόσπασμα, πηγή, σελίδα/φύλλο/αρχειακή αναφορά, χρονολογία, χρήστες και είδος χρήσης. Η επιδρομή δεν αποδεικνύει ορμητήριο. Σύγχρονη ταύτιση και συντεταγμένες μένουν άγνωστες χωρίς τεκμήριο. Διακρίνετε πρωτογενή πηγή, δευτερογενή μελέτη, ερμηνεία και υπόθεση. Καμία αυτόματη επαλήθευση. Καταγράψτε πρόσβαση ανά connector και πραγματικά βήματα μοντέλου.

Résumé : À travers les portraits de onze aventuriers des mers dix hommes et une femme , Laure-Hélène
      Gouffran nous fait pénétrer dans le monde en convulsion de la Méditerranée occidentale
      à la fin du Moyen Âge. Ancrés dans les fonds d archives, les récits de vie qu elle
      propose dessinent les figures mouvantes et en clair-obscur d individus au destin étonnant.
      Depuis la cité de Marseille comme port d attache et point de vue sur le large, on
      se mettra dans le sillage de corsaires aux profils variés, brigands seigneuriaux du
      château de Brégançon, mercenaires castillans ou encore marchands marseillais pirates
      à l occasion. C est aussi une profonde et vaste réflexion sur l histoire des prédations
      maritimes qui est ici mise en route ; une exploration pionnière ouvrant indéniablement
      sur des horizons nouveaux. [source éditeur]

      sous son autorisation.Leurs actions régulières et en course, sous le pavillon rouge
      à croix blanche, furent si multiples et si couronnées de succès que les musulmans
      surnommèrent ces marins Les Scorpions de la mer.En effet, en dehors des campagnes
      officielles, qu'elles soient systématiques comme lors des « caravanes », ou en expédition
      militaire ponctuelle comme l'attaque d'Alger, toute une flottille de bâtiments très
      divers, de la galère à la barcasse, se livrait, sous armement privé, à la course.
      Ces expéditions, connues sous le nom de « corsaires », étaient destinées à engranger
      des profits, officiellement destinés à soutenir le premier type d'opération.Mais ces
      chasses relevaient de processus plus compliqués qu'à première vue, et leurs buts étaient-ils
      si clairs ?   [source éditeur]

Résumé : Loin des légendes et des fantasmes, la première véritable histoire de la piraterie.
      Barbe-Noire est sans doute le plus illustre, Anne Bonny la plus féminine et Jack Sparrow
      le plus attirant (et surtout le moins réel !), mais que sait-on véritablement des
      pirates, corsaires et flibustiers ? S'il est certain que les pilleurs des mers ont
      régné sur les Caraïbes au XVIIIe siècle, on ne peut toutefois pas résumer leur histoire
      à ce truisme. En effet, dès l'Antiquité, le monde maritime est conçu comme un espace
      où il n'y a aucune règle si ce n'est celle de la loi du plus fort. Dans la mer Méditerranée,
      les marines crétoise, phénicienne et grecque sont donc confrontées à des pirates qui
      usent de force et de ruse pour parvenir à leurs fins. Mais une forme de collaboration
      s'installe progressivement entre les bandits des mers et le pouvoir politique : les
      premiers écoulent facilement leur butin dans les ports et sur les marchés, tandis
      que les seconds se procurent des marchandises inédites à bon prix. Ainsi se développe
      la piraterie. Puis, dès le Moyen Âge, apparaissent la course et les corsaires, ces
      fameux " pirates d'État " autorisés à piller et attaquer les bateaux ennemis. À partir
      du XVIe siècle et des grandes découvertes, on rencontre le flibustier – savant mélange
      entre le pirate et le corsaire – qui sévit essentiellement dans le bassin caribéen.
      Dans cette grande synthèse complète et inédite, Alain Blondy retrace avec maestria
      leur histoire. Au gré des incursions terrestres, des razzias, des attaques de navires
      et des prises de butin, l'auteur nous fait voyager, à travers les siècles (Xe siècle
      av. J.-C. – XIXe siècle) et les peuples (Vikings, Chinois, Ottomans...), de la Méditerranée
      à l'Océan Pacifique en passant par les mers du Nord. [source éditeur]

ABSTRACT
Occasioned by the death of Creveliers oﬀ Astypalaia:
The island’s role in the raids by Catholic corsairs during the 17th century
Giorgos Koutzakiotis

Between shortly before midnight of the 24th and early morning of the 25th of September 1679, the life of
French corsair Hugues Creveliers, leader of the most important corsair company active in the Aegean sea
in the 1670s, came to an inglorious end oﬀ the coast of Astypalaia, due to the blowing up of his ship by a
member of his crew. The present study takes a closer look at the details of the event and attempts to
portray the role that Astypalaia played in the raids of Catholic privateers against the Ottomans during the
seventeenth century; raids which had become a regular occurrence because of the protracted Venetian-
Ottoman wars. The privileged geographical location of the island made it an ideal base for the corsairs to
launch their attacks against commercial ships following the routes between Alexandria and Constantinople.
At the same time, Astypalaia was an excellent hideout for corsairs, not only because they could ﬁnd provi-
sions there (such as bread, wine, etc.) and stock up with drinking water, but also because the island provided
plenty of safe anchorages. The names of Astypalaia’s havens in French and Italian portolan texts, along with
other information of the time (testimonies about corsair contracts written on the island and marriages
between privateers and local Greek women), attest not only the strong relationship that the corsairs built
with Astypalaia, but also the degree of appropriation of the place by them. In the last part of this study we
examine the role of the bay of Vathy in the corsair raids, since this is most likely where the explosion
of Creveliers’ ship took place. This particular bay has similar traits to other anchorages in the Cycladic
islands where we know that corsairs repaired their ships, since they had built small forts or batteries at the
narrow entrances to these lairs so that no enemy ship could approach. In-situ research conducted by the
author on the south side of the narrow straits of Vathy bay led to the discovery of similar built structures
which seem to be relevant to the frequent corsair presence there.

B. J. Slot a formulé l’hypothèse que les carazzi étaient déterminés sur la base
des taxes ottomanes ou, peut-être, sur la base des taxes que les Vénitiens avaient
imposées aux îles de l’Égée au cours de la guerre de Crète, car aucun témoi-
gnage ne nous est parvenu qu’ils aient établi un nouvel enregistrement. Le même
historien, étudiant les données des sommes annuelles que les Vénitiens avaient
perçues finalement de chaque île des Cyclades entre 1684 et 1693, a constaté des
fluctuations dans les sommes, mais aussi des interruptions dans le versement des
taxes. Il a considéré qu’elles étaient dues à l’inefficacité des percepteurs d’impôt
plutôt qu’aux réactions des habitants, qui auraient pu craindre l’éventualité de
représailles ottomanes. En outre, il a remarqué que les Cyclades avaient versé
normalement leurs taxes en 1687, 1689, 1690, 1692, années au cours desquelles
la flotte vénitienne avait lancé de grandes attaques contre les Ottomans.9
    Certaines de ces questions sont élucidées par un document vénitien qui décrit
les changements principaux survenus jusqu’en 1694 dans le mode de taxation
de l’Archipel. Avant tout, ce texte nous informe que le montant des carazzi était
défini par le capitan generale et qu’il avait fluctué en raison de l’impuissance des
insulaires à répondre à l’exigence fiscale des Vénitiens car les habitants, «outre
qu’ils étaient pauvres», étaient «soumis à des violences et à des saignements par
les Turcs et les corsaires chrétiens, voire même par quelques navires pirates de
La Canée, de Rhodes et d’Eubée, qui empêch[ai]ent le commerce entre les îles».10
Plus précisément, il est rapporté que la somme totale des taxes avait augmenté
sous le capitan generale Domenico Mocenigo (1690–1692) et qu’elle avait di-
minué de presque la moitié sous le doge Francesco Morosini, lorsqu’il avait as-
suré de nouveau le commandement de la flotte (1692–1694). Néanmoins, dans la
plupart des îles, cette diminution n’était pas très importante: par exemple, Milos
devait verser 7000 réaux au lieu de 10000. En tout état de cause, en 1694, les
Vénitiens n’avaient pas réussi à collecter la somme totale des taxes déjà dimi-
nuées, en dépit des menaces de punition et, en général, des pressions exercées sur

les habitants,11 dont nous parlerons plus loin.
    Il est probable que les carazzi avaient aussi augmenté au cours du précédent
exercice de Morosini, lorsqu’il était capitan generale (1684–1690), puisqu’on
conserve deux documents d’élection d’émissaires de la commune de Mykonos
qui lui sont adressés, afin de «le prier de faire un geste de pitié vers le grand poids
supplémentaire dont [les] accablait le carasi», et «de le prier d’être charitable et
de [les] cautionner pour qu’ils paient suivant l’ancien libretto».12 Quant à l’«an-
cien libretto» rapporté dans le document, c’était probablement le registre conte-
nant les reçus des versements de la taxe qui attestait du régime en vigueur pendant
la guerre de Crète, puisque l’historien contemporain des événements Alessandro
Locatelli écrit formellement que les carazzi avaient été imposés dans les îles, en
juillet 1684, de la même façon que lors de la précédente guerre.13 Par ailleurs,
une lettre de Morosini adressée aux habitants de Symi témoigne directement du
fait que les Vénitiens étaient revenus dans l’Égée non seulement avec les mêmes
exigences, mais qu’ils avaient aussi usé de leurs vieux arguments pour assurer le
versement ordinaire des taxes par les insulaires: «si vous acceptez l’obligation de
donner ce que vous donniez au temps de la guerre passée du Regno de Crète, je
vous protègerai des corsaires».14
   Cet ordre d’imposition renouvelée des carazzi dans l’Archipel était appliqué
par deux escadres de la flotte vénitienne placées sous le commandement du capi-
tan estraordinario delle navi Alessandro Molin et du capitan ordinario delle navi
Daniele Dolfin.15 Le fait que «[le capitan delle nave] collectait les carazzi dans

    Mais qui était donc ce Français Diode? Il s’agissait du négociant marseillais,
Jean Dieudé, fils de Jean Dieudé et de Batronne Arnaud.25 Du Journal de l’am-
bassadeur Girardin, on peut déduire quelques éléments de sa vie. Après le milieu

nance du sultan. Le ministre Colbert allait ainsi donner à Dieudé la permission

1000 écus.

avait été chargé après 1690 de la collecte des carazzi sur toutes les îles de l’Égée
(et pas seulement des Cyclades) car il pouvait plus aisément assurer le transfert de
l’argent et des denrées remises en guise de paiement, les protégeant des attaques
de la flotte ottomane, ainsi que des Barbaresques et des corsaires chrétiens.
    Grâce à sa longue présence commerciale dans l’Archipel, Dieudé avait indu-
bitablement à sa disposition le réseau français des propriétaires de navires et des
capitaines, qui s’activaient avec une grande liberté de mouvement dans la zone
de guerre, puisque la France poursuivait sa politique de neutralité.34 Néanmoins,
les autorités françaises ne demeurèrent pas sans rien faire face à ces agissements
de leur ressortissant, même si leur réaction se fit attendre. Le 24 novembre 1694,
le gouvernement français approuvait les ordres donnés par l’ambassadeur de
Constantinople au consul de Milos concernant le désengagement des Français
de cette activité, qui indubitablement aurait pu ébranler les relations franco-ot-
tomanes. Plus précisément, François Goujon devait, d’une part, interdire le noli-
sement par Dieudé de bâtiments français destinés à la collecte des taxes; d’autre
part, désarmer tous les navires français qu’utilisait déjà le percepteur à cet effet et
renvoyer leurs équipages en France, puisque leurs capitaines ne disposaient pas
du congé de l’amiral.35 Ajoutons que ces bateaux-ci naviguaient sous pavillon
français, puisque leurs capitaines s’étaient procurés des passeports auprès des

   An Introduction to the Archaeology of Piracy

This study serves as the introduction to the volume The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity and aims to survey
­scholarship on ancient piracy, while primarily assessing the possibilities and limitations of an archaeological approach to
 the ­phenomenon. The paper is structured in two main parts. The first part offers a concise overview of research on ancient
 piracy from the late 19th century to the present and addresses a series of key issues, including the definition of piracy
 and the fluidity of its boundaries, the range and forms of pirate activity, the social and ethnic heterogeneity of pirates,
 the complex relationship between piracy and trade, the varied responses of official authorities and social perceptions of
 piracy in the ancient world. The second part focuses on the archaeology of piracy. It begins by outlining the history of
 ­archaeological research in this field and the methodological challenges posed by the difficulty of linking pirate activity to
  specific archaeological evidence. It then introduces the A.P.Pir.A. project, which sought to develop a framework for the
  meaningful integration of piracy into archaeological discourse through the study of the phenomenon in the Greek seas
  from the Final Neolithic to the Roman period (ca. 4000 BCE – 330 CE). The paper further explores the ways in which
  piracy can be approached archaeologically by drawing on different categories of material evidence, such as settlements,
  ­fortifications, funerary assemblages and iconography, in direct dialog with the individual contributions to the volume. It
   concludes with reflections on future directions of research, emphasizing that, despite inherent methodological ­challenges,
   piracy can be documented through material culture. From this perspective, archaeology is shown to contribute not only
   to the identification of piracy as a historical phenomenon but also to a deeper understanding of its social and economic
   impact in the ancient world.

“Pirates always used to harass those who sailed the sea, even as brigands did those who dwelt on land. There was
never a time when these practices were unknown, nor will they ever cease probably so long as human nature
remains the same” (Cass. Dio 36.20.1, trans. E. Cary, London and New York, 1914). The accuracy of Cassius
Dio’s remark is borne out even today: despite the existence of powerful state and transnational organizations
with the technological capacity to eradicate piracy altogether, pirate activity persists unabated in critical sea-
lanes throughout the globe. The present volume addresses aspects of the earliest phases in the long history of
piracy, with a particular emphasis on assessing the potential of an archaeological approach to the phenomenon.
   This introductory chapter outlines the emerging field of the archaeology of piracy. It first provides a concise
survey of the numerous studies on piracy in antiquity, from the late 19th century to the present. Attention is
then drawn to specific issues that are essential to the scholarly investigation of piracy, both ancient and more re-
cent. This is followed by an overview of the development of the archaeology of piracy, tracing its trajectory from

PIRACY IN ANTIQUITY: A CENTURY AND A HALF OF SCHOLARSHIP

Research on piracy in antiquity dates back roughly a century and a half to Jules M. Sestier’s pioneering study
La piraterie dans l’antiquité (1880). Most early works (e.g., Sestier 1880; Ormerod 1922, 1923, 1924a, 1924b;
­Ziebarth 1929) attempted to present broad historical overviews of ancient piracy based on Greek and Latin
 ­textual information. Others, such as Ellen C. Semple (1916) and John A. Davison (1930), analyzed ancient
  piracy along more specific lines: Semple examined the geographical and economic conditions that fostered
  ­Mediterranean piracy, while Davison briefly considered Cicero’s role in the promulgation of the Lex Gabinia,
   the law that granted Pompey extraordinary and unprecedented powers to suppress piracy in 67 BCE. He treated
   it more as a vehicle of Roman Republican politics than as piracy per se. This pioneering phase of research was
   characterized more by comprehensive treatment of the source tradition than by critical methods of analysis;
   the works tend to furnish narrative descriptions, often echoing ancient authors’ moralizing tones and treating
   ­“piracy” as a transhistorical phenomenon that warranted little explanation. Ormerod’s synthesis (Ormerod
    1942a) at least attempted to identify typologies of maritime predation and regional patterning, whereas Semple’s
    geographical lens foreshadowed later attention to the environmental and economic constraints on piracy.
     A second phase of research, extending from the 1960s to the end of the 20th century, comprises more
s­ ynthetic treatments, such as the studies by Yvon Garlan (1978, 1987), Benedetto Bravo (1980) and William
 K. Pritchett (1991), as well as the studies by David Tandy (1997) and Alastair H. Jackson (1973, 1995, 2000)
 on ­pirates in Early Iron Age (EIA) and Archaic Greece, respectively. The bulk of scholarly attention, however,
 tended to focus on the Hellenistic and Roman periods (e.g., Dell 1967; Maróti 1968, 1970; Hassall et al. 1974;
 Ward 1975, 1977; Lintott 1976; Crawford 1977; Brulé 1978, 1999; Clavel-Lévêque 1978; Sumner 1978; Mattingly
 1980; ­Ducrey 1983; Gabbert 1986; Marasco 1987; Braund 1993; Tramonti 1994a, 1994b, 1995; Herz 1995; Ferone
 1997; Ager 1998; Günther 1999; Perlman 1999). Here the analysis becomes more analytical, with scholars in-
 terrogating legal categories, state responses and the political economy of violence. Micro-regional case studies,
 such as piracy in Crete, Cyclades and Cilicia (e.g., Brulé 1978; Ducrey 1983; Marasco 1987; P   ­ erlman 1999),
 likewise began to replace trans-Mediterranean narratives.
    A milestone in the treatment of ancient piracy occurred with the publication of Philip de Souza’s Piracy in the
Graeco-Roman World (1999), the first systematically argued and critically documented synthesis to map p     ­ iracy
from the Archaic period through Late Antiquity. De Souza integrated literary and epigraphic evidence with
historiographical reassessment, to reframe “piracy” less as a fixed social phenomenon than as a p ­ ropagandistic

The study of ancient piracy has now advanced beyond its treatment as a timeless scourge or a minor footnote
in naval history. The field increasingly understands piracy as a historically contingent and context-dependent
repertoire of practices, shaped by shifting political economies, security regimes and cultural perceptions. This
reframing has freed scholarship from uncritical reliance on ancient authors’ moralizing narratives, simplistic
stereotypes and prejudices, allowing instead for more nuanced analyses of how communities, poleis and empires
constructed, negotiated and instrumentalized the label of piracy.

cannot be said for the term piracy (on the language of ancient piracy see, for instance, MacDonald 1984; Ferone
1997, 43–67; 2008; de Souza 1999, 2–13; Pianezzola 2004). The earliest known occurrence of the word appears
in a mid-3rd century BCE inscription from Rhamnous in Attica (SEG XXIV 154, line 22; de Souza 1999, 3–4;
for a translation and comprehensive analysis see https://www.atticinscriptions.com/inscription/AIO/823). This
does not imply, however, that the practice of piracy did not exist prior to that time. For example, both Homer
and Thucydides describe individuals who, in modern terminology, would be characterized as pirates, even
though the term they employ is robbers (ληϊστῆρες, e.g., Hom. Od. 3.73, 17.425, or λῃσταὶ, e.g., Thuc. 1.8.1, 6.4.5;
for piracy in the Homeric epics see Samaras and Gounelas forthcoming, with further references). In several
instances, even this term is omitted and the pirate nature of the behavior has to be inferred from the context.
     Not long after its first attestation, the term pirate acquired a distinctly negative connotation. Almost
­invariably the pirate is portrayed as the “other” – the outsider, the foreigner, the villain. Rarely does an indi-
 vidual define himself as a pirate, while conversely there are numerous instances in which third parties apply
 the term selectively, depending on their relationship with the person in question. A striking example is Nabis,
 king of Sparta in the late 3rd and early 2nd century BCE. While ancient authors such as Polybius (13.8.2) and
 Livy (34.32.18, 34.36.3) describe him as a pirate, the demos of Delos in an honorary decree proclaims him a
 proxenos and benefactor (IG XI.4 716, lines 9–10; for further discussions on Nabis see Mendels 1979; Karafotias
 1998; Brulé 1999; see also Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume). This discrepancy is not unique. Similar
 dynamics appear in other contexts, such as in the varying depictions of Cilician seafarers, who are alternately
 presented as pirates, allies or even clients, depending on the political alignment of the sources (see Dawson and
 Rauh, this volume). Such examples demonstrate how piracy, far from being a fixed category, is part of a con-
 tested vocabulary of power, legitimacy and control of mobility.
    The selective application of the label pirate underscores its fundamentally relational and perspectival nature:
in ancient written sources (and in later ones as well) it operates less as an objective descriptor and more as a
rhetorical and ideological tool. Thus, any scholarly engagement with ancient piracy must not only catalog in-
stances of the term’s usage, but also interrogate the sociopolitical stakes embedded in those usages. Acts should
be evaluated as piracy (or not) according to clearly defined parameters, rather than merely based on whether
ancient observers classified them as such.

  ­ ethodological challenges in the study of the phenomenon. One such challenge arises from the inconsistent

­filibusters, buccaneers and corsairs are employed without sufficient attention to their semantic distinctions

definitions are provided but vary widely, as each scholar attempts to create a unique working framework, often
out of dissatisfaction with existing ones. For instance, Henry A. Ormerod (1924a, 60) cites the English legal
definition of piracy as an act of robbery and violence at sea, which, if committed on land, would constitute a
felony because it lacks the authorization of a sovereign state. Philip de Souza (1999, 1) describes pirates more
concisely as “armed robbers whose activities normally involve the use of ships”. Such inconsistency highlights
the conceptual and methodological challenges involved in the study of ancient piracy. If the phenomenon is
difficult to define, it logically follows that placing it in its proper historical context is equally challenging.
    During the initial stages of the A.P.Pir.A. project (see below), it became clear that while existing definitions
address key aspects of piracy, none could fully encompass the complexity and variability of the phenomenon.
One of the first steps of the project, therefore, was to adopt a working definition – one that is informed by earlier
scholarship, but one that is also tailored to the specific aims of the investigation. According to this definition, an
act qualifies as piracy when it fulfills the two following criteria: as is widely acknowledged in the literature (e.g.,
de Souza 1999, 1–2; Bradford 2007, xi; Skowronek 2016, 4), piracy must constitute an act of robbery inherently
linked to the maritime sphere, regardless of whether ships are directly employed; in addition, the primary
­motive of piracy must be private economic gain (Samaras 2015, 191; see also Knapp 2018, 36).
     This definitional framework proves useful in addressing two major conceptual challenges for the study of
piracy. The first concerns the nature of a pirate’s relationship to the sea. Contemporary perceptions –heavily
influenced by literary and cinematic representations– associate pirates inextricably with ships and seafaring
life. Historically, however, this connection was not universal. While pirates frequently utilized ships to launch
attacks against other vessels or to conduct coastal raids, there are documented instances in which they operated
without ships. Practices such as the looting of shipwrecks –a common occurrence in antiquity, particularly in
regions prone to maritime accidents (e.g., Strabo 5.4.2; 7.6.1; Arr. Peripl. M. Eux. 37; Tsetskhladze 2000–2001,
13; see also Rougé 1966; Mataix Ferrándiz 2022)– and, even more strikingly, the deliberate orchestration of
shipwrecks for the purpose of plunder, constitute a peculiar form of “land-based” piracy (see more in Samaras
and Gounelas forthcoming).
      The second major issue addressed by the proposed definition is the distinction between piracy and ­warfare.
Numerous recorded instances concerned raids that transpired during military conflicts, however much they re-
semble piracy in both their tactical execution and their underlying motivation. The difficulty in distinguishing
between these two forms of organized violence (piracy and warfare) has already been noted by several scholars
(e.g., Wachsmann 1998, 317–21; de Souza 1999, 31–6; Emanuel 2021, 24–9). As previously argued (Samaras
2015, 189–91), the fundamental difference lies in the nature of the action: war, even when e­ conomically mo-
tivated, is essentially political in character, whereas piracy belongs to the economic realm and lacks any clear
­political agenda. This conceptual distinction is by no means modern. Fernand Braudel (1973, 867) ­characterized
 piracy as “a means of making a living,” noting, in his discussion of the Algerian corsairs, that “if the corsairs
 came home empty-handed there would be famine in Algiers”. Much earlier, Aristotle had similarly identified
 raiding (ληστρικὸς βίος) as one of the fundamental modes of subsistence, alongside pastoralism, fishing, hunting
 and agriculture (Pol. 1256a–b; see also Xen. Cav. 8.8). Of course, this differentiation between piracy and war
 exists primarily at a theoretical level. In reality, the boundaries between the two are often blurred. Neverthe-
 less, the distinction remains analytically useful, as it emphasizes that regardless of the ideological or political
 ­justifications that were sometimes attached to it, piracy was, first and foremost, an economic pursuit.

From opportunistic acts to pirate fleets: the spectrum of ancient piracy
Piracy in antiquity can be categorized according to several distinct forms, depending on both the nature of
the operation and the profile of its targets. These include direct attacks by one ship against another in open
waters; raids launched from multiple ships against unprotected coastal or near-coastal targets, such as isolated
farmsteads, rural shrines or pastoral groups; full-scale assaults on larger settlements or even urban centers;
and the plundering of shipwrecks – whether resulting from natural causes or deliberately orchestrated by local
inhabitants along treacherous coastlines. Some of these activities, particularly shipwrecking and opportunistic
raiding, occurred in a gray area between piracy, salvage and subsistence predation, especially in economically
marginal regions (see below).
    Beyond this typology, it is important to consider the range and degrees of organization within pirate activity.
At the most rudimentary level, piracy could consist of isolated and opportunistic acts, such as a merchant vessel
abducting a lone shepherd or fishermen appropriating cargo from a wreck. Such events were neither system-
atic nor premeditated, but rather ad hoc responses to immediate prospects of gain. At a more complex level,
however, piracy could assume forms of semi-permanent, structured organizations. Ancient literary sources
describing the Cilician pirates of the late Hellenistic period (ca. 139–67 BCE) attest to the existence of pirate
flotillas, fortified bases and long-range operations targeting major maritime routes and wealthy sites, including
prominent sanctuaries (e.g., Strabo 14.5.2; App. Mith. 14.92–93; Plut. Pomp. 24.2–5; see more in Dawson and
Rauh, this volume). Earlier examples include the Cretan and Aitolian poleis of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE,
which are portrayed as having incorporated piracy into their formal diplomatic and economic practices (on
Cretan and Aitolian piracy, see Brulé 1978; de Souza 1999, 70–6, 80–4; Perlman 1999; on “state” piracy by
Phalasarna and its colony Aigilia, see Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume). These examples challenge
simplistic dichotomies between statehood and criminality and invite a more dynamic understanding of ancient
piracy as a phenomenon operating across multiscalar social, economic and political environments.

Who were the pirates? The social and ethnic heterogeneity of pirate crews
The conventional portrayal of a pirate as a marginal and socially deviant figure –rejected by or alienated from
the norms of settled society– is problematized by both archaeological and historical evidence from antiquity and
subsequent periods. Rather than existing entirely outside the social fabric of settled communities, pirates fre-
quently lived within them, resided in ordinary dwellings and participated to varying degrees in local economic
and social life. From a socio-economic perspective it seems clear that piracy was not necessarily a p       ­ henomenon
restricted to a particular social stratum. Individuals from across the social spectrum could engage in pirate
­activity, either directly or indirectly. The participation of elites –whether aristocratic landowners, military leaders
 or hinterland warlords– should not be regarded as exceptional. On the contrary, access to ships, crews and ex-
 tensive political or military contacts often made it easier for members of higher social orders to initiate and to
 sustain maritime raiding. A characteristic example is Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos in the third quarter of the
 6th century BCE, whose naval power and pirate activity are explicitly noted by Herodotus (3.39.3–4). Polycrates
 not only used piracy to amass wealth, but he also used it to project power across the eastern ­Aegean and beyond,
 thus illustrating how piracy could be incorporated by elite figures into broader strategies of state-building and
 regional dominance. Similar dynamics are evident with the late H       ­ ellenistic Cilician pirate n
                                                                                                     ­ etworks mentioned
 above, where pirate bands, according to several ancient authors (e.g., Strabo 14.5.2; App. Mith. 14.92), operated
 under the protection or with the complicity of local rulers and by drawing support from otherwise peaceful
 coastal populations. These pirates established semi-permanent bases throughout the ­Mediterranean and main-

Dawson and Rauh, this volume).
      Conversely, individuals from lower social strata also participated in piracy, though typically through
­different avenues. Many served as crew members or engaged in raiding on a temporary or ad hoc basis, having
 been drawn into pirate activity through economic hardship, displacement resulting from conflict or the c­ ollapse
 of traditional subsistence lifeways. For example, one plausible scenario –previously proposed by the present
 author (Samaras 2015, 193)– is that, following the disintegration of the Mycenaean palatial system in the
 ­Postpalatial Aegean, “the unemployed mercenaries of the Palatial period” continued to deploy their martial
  ­expertise ­independently, turning to, among other activities, piracy as a means of survival and wealth acquisition.
    An important aspect of pirate identity –potentially relevant for archaeological interpretation– is the social
and ethnic heterogeneity of pirate crews. Although direct evidence is often limited, textual sources attest to
the fact that these groups often comprised individuals from diverse geographic origins and socio-economic
backgrounds, reflecting the translocal, interwoven nature of seaborne raiding parties and the flexible structures
that supported them. For example, Appian reports that the Cilician pirate fleets of the late Hellenistic period
comprised not merely Cilicians, but also “men of Syrian, Cyprian, Pamphylian, and Pontic origin and those of
almost all the Eastern nations” (Mith. 14.92, trans. H. White, New York, 1899). It is safe to assume, therefore,
that the collective designation Cilicians most probably referred to pirate bands whose origins were ethnically
heterogeneous.
    The social origin of individuals engaged in piracy also most likely shaped the motivation of those who
­ ursued such activity. For people originating from marginal, resource-scarce environments –such as arid is-
p
lands, mountainous coasts or depopulated rural zones– piracy plausibly represents one of the only available
means of subsistence or economic advancement. In contexts of pronounced social inequality, where wealth and
status were as a rule inherited and beyond the reach of impoverished elements, piracy offered an alternative
route to power, prestige and sometimes even to formal authority. For those of elite status, piracy served dif-
ferent, though complementary, functions: it enabled the accumulation of wealth, the demonstration of martial
skill and the reinforcement or expansion of social influence. In this regard, piracy functioned not only as an
economic activity but as a socio-political mechanism embedded within local and regional dynamics of power,
status and survival.

Piracy and trade: rethinking an apparent paradox
Very often, scholars or commentators assert that interruptions in maritime trade during a given period were
likely attributable to piracy or, conversely, that periods of flourishing commercial activity demonstrated an
absence of piracy. Underlying such views is the self-evident assumption that piracy worked as a disincen-
tive to maritime trade. However, the historical reality is far more complex. Longitudinal studies of piracy
clearly demonstrate that maritime trade not only persisted but often thrived during periods of intense pirate
­activity. This apparent paradox challenges linear models of economic disruption and invites a more nuanced
 ­interpretation of the historical relationship between piracy and trade.
    Vincent Gabrielsen, a scholar who has studied the significant upsurge in piracy during the Hellenistic p ­ eriod,
emphasizes that commercial centers prospered during this upsurge throughout the Aegean (Gabrielsen 2001,
220–23; 2013, 147–53; see also Gabrielsen 2003, which focuses in particular on the relationship between piracy
and a distinct form of commercial activity, namely, the slave-trade). His analysis discredits the simplistic duality
of trade versus piracy and instead proposes a model of functional coexistence, wherein pirate enterprise was
structurally integrated into broader patterns of economic exchange. As Fernand Braudel has observed (1973,
887), this positive correlation between piracy and trade is not unique to antiquity, but extends into more recent
periods as well. The reasons for this seem clear: maritime trade provided the necessary structural conditions
–the targets, the sea-lanes and the maritime markets– for piracy to thrive and to prevail. Typically, following

a successful pirate venture pirates would engage in forms of exchange to realize the value of their plunder,
for example, to exchange whatever goods they had plundered for those they actually needed. Contrary to the
­romanticized portrayals in literature and film, pirates did not hoard treasure in caves or bury it beneath the
 sand. Rather, they raided ships and settlements, seized portable goods and subsequently entered the ­commercial

 Souza 1999, 56), “piracy itself could be considered as a form of trade”. As such, it was extremely commonplace
 for some individuals to alternate between piracy and mercantile activity, depending on the circumstances and
 the calculated prospects of financial gain. This fluidity between roles reflects not merely opportunism, but a
 socio-economic continuum within which violence, commerce and illegality frequently overlapped.

a Phoenician merchant decides to sell the “son of Castor” into slavery (Od. 14.287–298). The scenario is then
repeated by a group of Thesprotian traders (Od. 14.334–359). Likewise, Eumaeus recounts that he himself was
­abducted by Phoenician merchants after they had stayed in his homeland “for a whole year [...] and traded for

 so much narrative ­embellishments as they are culturally grounded reflections of a world in which the bound-
 aries between trade and raiding were permeable, and where seafaring groups could assume multiple identities
 depending on ­context and objectives.

Official responses to piracy: suppression, toleration and collaboration
Another issue that merits critical attention is the relationship between legitimate authority and piracy – a
­relationship that ranges from overt hostility to open collaboration. While the antagonistic stance of states or
 local powers toward piracy may appear natural or even inevitable, it must be emphasized that this hostility was
 by no means hypothetical. Throughout antiquity, a number of political and military authorities actively ­pursued
 large-scale campaigns to suppress piracy. Occasionally, ancient literary sources attributed the eradication of sea-
 borne piracy to a particular figure, such as Minos (Thuc. 1.4.1, 1.8.1–2) or Jason (Plut. Thes. 19.4). Historical fig-
 ures, like Themistocles (Nep. Them. 2.1–4) and Cimon (Plut. Cim. 8.5), were likewise credited with clearing the
seas of pirates. Naval powers, including Corinth (Thuc. 1.13.5), Athens (Aristid. Or. 13.113), Rhodes (Diod. Sic.
 20.81.3; Strabo 14.2.5; Aristid. Or. 44.570), and Rome (Cic. Leg. Man. 33; Strabo 14.3.3; App. B Civ. 2.1.1; Mith.
14.95), earned widespread reputations for policing the seas and keeping them safe from pirates. Nevertheless,
despite these confident assertions by ancient sources, the actual effectiveness of anti-­piracy operations appears
to have been limited, especially with regard to any long-term impact. Even in the case of the most renowned
anti-piracy campaign, that of Pompey in 67 BCE, modern scholars (e.g., de Souza 1999, 179–85; Tröster 2009,
esp. 28–31; Lampinen 2022, 52–3) have significantly questioned ancient testimony that Pompey eradicated
piracy once and for all (e.g., Cic. Leg. Man. 33; App. B Civ. 2.1.1; Mith. 14.95; Flor. 3.6.13–15; Oros. 6.4.1).
Such assertions appear to have been shaped or amplified by Roman political propaganda intended to glorify
Pompey’s extraordinary efficiency and military competence as a commander. Scholars have expressed similar
concerns regarding the success of Rhodian anti-piracy efforts, the actual effectiveness and long-term conse-
quences of which appear to warrant closer scrutiny, despite the assertions of ancient sources (see K    ­ almpourtzi,
this volume).
    Alongside these repressive strategies, there is substantial evidence of cooperation and complicity between
official powers and pirate actors. Pirates frequently depended on the collaboration of or toleration by authori-
ties, frequently by offering a share in their stolen gain in exchange for strategic advantages. These might include
access to safe harbors during storms or while attempting to evade pursuit, as well as access to marketplaces,
where they could dispose of their plunder and procure essential supplies. Conversely, political and military
leaders often collaborated openly with pirates by actively recruiting their naval expertise, local knowledge and
combat skills to further strategic goals or to undermine rivals.

THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF PIRACY: FROM MARGINAL NOTES TO EMERGING
FIELD

Until the early 21st century, archaeological investigations linked to piracy remained sparse and largely ­incidental.
Since the 2000s, however, scholarly interest in the archaeology of piracy has increased significantly, with a
growing number of studies exploring the phenomenon through material remains. Among the most systematic
contributions are the edited volumes by Russell Skowronek and Charles Ewen (2006, 2016, 2023), Jean Soulat
(2019) and Lynn Brenda Harris and Valerie Ann Johnson (2022), which collectively represent key milestones
in the development of the field (see also Hartnett and Dawdy 2013). Unsurprisingly, these works concentrate
on the so-called “Golden Age of Piracy” (late 17th to early 18th century), focusing primarily on the Caribbean
Sea and, to a lesser extent, the Indian Ocean. In contrast, the Eastern Mediterranean, and particularly the

Greek seas, has yet to see comparable systematic archaeological engagement, despite evidence of sustained
pirate and privateer activity throughout the early modern period (e.g., Krantonelli 1985, 1991, 1998; Harlaftis
et al. 2016). Recent studies by George Koutzakiotis (2023, this volume) demonstrate the potential of integrating
­archaeological research with the rich documentary evidence of the period, revealing promising avenues for the
 study of piracy in this region.
    A similar paucity of archaeological studies is evident for piracy in classical antiquity. A pioneering example
linking specific archaeological finds to the phenomenon of piracy was advanced by Antonios Keramopoullos
(1923, 42–3), who argued that the seventeen shackled individuals uncovered during Konstantinos Kourouniotis
and Stratis Pelekidis’ excavations at Phaleron were probably pirates executed for their deeds (see also Bosnakis
2020, 159–69). Otherwise, references to piracy in the archaeological literature have been few and, when they do
appear, they are typically brief and interpreted from a victims’ perspective. Some have pointed to the numerous
Late Classical and Hellenistic towers situated on islands and along the eastern Mediterranean mainland coast,
to suggest that these functioned as bastions to protect coastal communities and private landowners from pirate
raids (e.g., Ormerod 1924a, 41–3; 1924b, 31–2; Young 1956, 132–33; Osborne 1986, 173–74; Pritchett 1991,
352–58; Seifried and Parkinson 2014, 310). Likewise, the intense piracy that plagued the Aegean in the first half
of the 1st century BCE has led many scholars to attribute the contemporaneous evidence of violent d     ­ estruction
at Delos to pirate raids that are reported to have occurred there in 88 and 69 BCE (e.g., Mattingly 1980; Rauh
1993, 68; Hatzidakis 1997, 293, 307; Siebert 2001, 93; Rotroff 2014). Vassilis Lambrinoudakis (1981, 161; 1987–
1988, 299) has suggested that a destruction layer dated to the early 1st century BCE at the sanctuary of Apollo
Maleatas in Epidaurus is likewise attributable to a pirate assault.
    In addition to studies that rely on archaeological data to address the likely impact of piracy on the wider
public, some researchers have attempted to utilize archaeological remains to identify the likely habitats and
operational bases of pirates themselves. Probably the most systematic archaeological research of ancient ­piracy
to date is the Rough Cilicia Archaeological Survey Project, directed by Nicholas Rauh (1997, 2003, 2004, 2019;
see also Rauh et al. 2000, 2009, 2013, Kaye and Rauh 2020, Hoff et al. 2024, as well as Dawson and Rauh, this
volume), which, from 1996 to 2014, attempted to identify the settlements and hideouts of the notorious ­Cilician
pirates along the coast of modern day Gazipasha, Turkey (for the Cilician pirates see also Avidov 2008; Zoroğlu
2009; Tomaschitz 2013). Beginning in the mid-1980s, Elpida Hadjidaki (2001, 2015, 2020) has been directing the
systematic excavation of ancient Phalasarna, a polis in western Crete closely associated with ­Hellenistic piracy.
Since 2000, Aris Tsaravopoulos (2015, 2023; see also Johnston et al. 2012; Kozatsas et al. 2014; T­ saravopoulos
and Kroustalis, this volume) has been excavating the site of Antikythera, a colony of Phalasarna, that is likewise
presumed to have functioned as a pirate base. Meanwhile, Adonis Kyrou (1990, 137–41; 1996–1997; see also
Lolos 2006) has persuasively argued that the fortified hill of Choriza on the island of Hydra served as a base
for Samian pirates, who were active around 530 BCE. Yet another category of remains plausibly linked to pi-
racy, those of ancient shipsheds, straddles the boundary between terrestrial and underwater archaeology (Baika
2007–2008; Blackman et al. 2013, 238–41; see also Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume on the shipshed
at Antikythera).

Hartnett and Dawdy 2013, 40; Rauh 2019, 49). The problem stems primarily from the fact that the material re-
mains of pirates are often indistinguishable from those of wider, “law-abiding”, society. For example, structures
and ships employed by pirates frequently resembled those employed by the general public, in the same manner
that the destruction inflicted on an ancient settlement by a pirate raid might resemble that of a military assault.
What seems crucial is that archaeologists assess the question within an interpretive framework, one that con-
siders piracy as a fluid, dynamic phenomenon with the potential to shape local and regional economies and, at
times, to catalyze political and social transformations in any given era. This interpretive framework is precisely
what the A.P.Pir.A. project has intended to create.

Scope and objectives
Hosted by the Department of History and Archaeology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, the
A.P.Pir.A. project transpired between January 2021 and June 2024, with funding from the H  ­ ellenic F

for Research and Innovation. The research team consisted of seven archaeologists, led by the present author
as principal investigator, alongside Nadia Giagkoudaki, Orestis Goulakos, Panagiotis Gounelas, Alexandra
­Malliou, Konstantinos Pantzouris and Dimitris N. Sakkas. Throughout the duration of the project, this small
 group of early-career researchers attempted to construct a spatially diachronic approach to the archaeology of
 piracy. Our aim was to develop a framework through which piracy could be meaningfully integrated into the
 archaeological discourse, a framework sufficiently broad to incorporate evidence of piracy across the breadth
 of the eastern Mediterranean Sea and across a timeframe extending from the Final Neolithic to the Roman era
 (ca. 4000 BCE – 330 CE).

Methodology and research implementation
The project unfolded in four distinct stages. The initial phase focused on piracy in classical antiquity, specifically
from the Archaic to the Roman period. This decision has the obvious advantage of drawing on the information
provided by literary sources about piracy to allow for more comprehensive analysis. Textual references pro-
vide the added value of furnishing detailed information about piracy that can be cross-referenced against the
­extensive archaeological record of the same era.
    To facilitate systematic documentation and analysis, the team developed a digital database using the open-
source online platform Heurist. Design by the author of this paper, the database is intended to record, manage
and analyze material drawn from a wide range of ancient Greek and Latin sources (e.g., historical narratives,
oratory and inscriptions) that contain either explicit or implicit allusions to pirate activity in the Greek maritime
world during the period in question. The entries –compiled primarily by A.P.Pir.A. research team members
Orestis Goulakos and Konstantinos Pantzouris– amount to nearly 500 records and have yielded tremendous
insights into the historical evolution of piracy in classical antiquity, the operational strategies of pirates and
the manner in which they were perceived by their contemporaries. This database constitutes a comprehensive
repository that will facilitate the systematic study of ancient piracy through textual evidence.
     For example, the analysis of the statistical data derived from the database reveals that, while piracy ­appears
to have been a continually recurring phenomenon throughout classical antiquity, the Hellenistic period (323–27
BCE) stands out as a peak moment of pirate activity, particularly in the eastern Mediterranean basin. These
­findings validate two fundamental conclusions: first, that piracy constituted an endemic feature of the maritime
 landscape of classical antiquity; and second, that sustained efforts to suppress piracy by naval powers, such as
 Athens, Rhodes and Rome, achieved limited and temporary success at best (on this issue see de Souza 1999,
 38–41, 48–53, 83–4, 161–78, 184, 204–10; Lampinen 2022, 52–3; also, on Rhodes and Rome’s campaigns against
 piracy, see respectively Kalmpourtzi, and Dawson and Rauh, this volume).
     Following the study of the written sources, a systematic correlation was undertaken between the
a­ rchaeological evidence and the data extracted from the database. This process facilitated the formulation of
 specific archaeological criteria and attributes derived from the material record that may under certain condi-
 tions be applicable to the phenomenon of piracy. For example, a list of representative features emerged that
 appear to characterize an archaeologically identifiable pirate base, that is, a settlement where a portion of the
 population, however large or small, engaged occasionally or habitually in piracy. The scale of such bases ranges
 widely from small encampments to full-fledged cities. Importantly, the material remains of these sites often
 do not diverge significantly from those of conventional settlements, thereby making their identification all the

more challenging. Nevertheless, pirate bases do tend to display fundamental recurring traits that assist with
their recognition. These can be grouped into four broad thematic categories:
    1. Chronological context
    •    Evidence that a given site was occupied during a period when piracy is known to have been prevalent
         in the vicinity. Establishing the habitational time frame of a settlement within the context of known
         piratical disturbances seems prerequisite to drawing a connection between the two.
    2. Spatial and geomorphological characteristics
    •    Site selection: Pirate bases are frequently situated in coastal areas that offer concealment or limited
         visibility from the sea and/or mainland. These sites exploit natural topographical advantages, yet are
         strategically positioned in proximity to important maritime routes.
    •    Suitability for pirate operations: Pirate suitability is typically linked to topographical features, such
         as bays, coves or natural harbors, that facilitate ambushes, provide shelter and enable eavesdropping
         on passing sea traffic. In certain instances, the suitability of a location is further corroborated by the
         chronological reuse of the exact same site or an adjacent location as pirate bases, most likely because
         the physical and strategic advantages of the site lent themselves to recurring use by pirates over time.
    •    Anomalous sites and finds: Some sites are situated in locations that appear, at first glance, wholly
         ­unsuitable for permanent habitation or harbor development (e.g., barren terrain, lack of accessible an-
          chorages). When settings such as these reveal the presence of “unanticipated” valuable, high-status
          ­artifacts, the likelihood that they served an atypical or illicit function becomes archaeologically relevant.
    3. Functional and structural features
    •    Short-lived occupation: Particularly in the case of small settlements, the archaeological record may point
         to a temporally limited or episodic occupation, often interpreted as opportunistic or purpose-built,
         rather than part of a long-term habitation pattern.
    •    Fortification systems: In addition to natural defenses, some sites exhibit evidence of artificial
         ­reinforcement through constructed for

e assemblages of finds and features at such sites often indicate a strong
         ­connection between the inhabitants’ economic or subsistence strategies and the sea. This may be
          ­reflected in the presence of maritime artifacts, infrastructure or iconographic motifs.
    •    Martial character: The presence of weaponry, martial iconography or other artifacts associated with the
         use of violence may point to a community familiar with or habituated to armed conflict. While such
         indicators are not exclusive to piracy, their co-occurrence with other characteristics described above
         strengthens the argument for pirate occupation.
    It should be emphasized that the presence of one or even several of these traits does not by itself confirm the
identification of a given site as a pirate base. Nor is the combination of all these features required to justify such
an interpretation. Obviously, the greater the number and consistency of such indicators at a given site, the more
compelling the need to include pirate activity within a range of archaeological interpretations. For instance,
the application of the above criteria, in conjunction with the analysis of literary sources on ancient piracy, led
Konstantinos Pantzouris to propose that the fortified site at Kastraki on Agathonisi may not have served solely
as a defensive outpost safeguarding Miletus and its maritime trade against the pirates, who were particularly
active in the region during the Hellenistic period. Rather, the site itself may have participated in pirate activity
–likely targeting non-Milesian interests– thereby functioning both as a protective and a predatory node within
the complex maritime landscape of the time (see Pantzouris, this volume).
    The establishment of archaeological criteria for the identification of piracy enabled the team to proceed to
the second phase of the project, namely the investigation of piracy during periods, when archaeological data

Research outcomes and archaeological challenges
As a concise evaluation of the research results of the A.P.Pir.A. project, the findings can be described as highly
encouraging. The project successfully identified specific sites that either conceivably served as pirate bases or
were assaulted by pirate raids and it recognized potential components of pirate activity across various catego-
ries of artifacts (e.g., pottery, rock-engravings, seals). Furthermore, the research demonstrated that during the
extensive time frame under consideration, the levels of pirate activity in the Greek seas varied significantly,
ranging from isolated incidents of piracy to sustained periods of piracy capable of influencing the outcome of
political events. Periods of heightened pirate activity, identified with varying degrees of certainty, include the
EBA II (ca. 2700–2200 BCE), the Postpalatial period (ca. 1200–1050 BCE), the Geometric period (ca. 900–700
BCE), the Archaic period (ca. 700–480 BCE) and the Hellenistic period (ca. 323–67 BCE). Notably, these phases
often coincide with episodes of political disintegration, economic disturbance or weakened public authority –
highlighting the interplay between piracy and wider societal transformations.
       Perhaps even more significantly, the project contributed to a deeper understanding of the fundamental
­challenges that confront the archaeology of piracy. As mentioned above, pirates rarely left behind material
 ­evidence of their activities, and when they did, such traces were often indistinguishable from those of con-
  temporary “law-abiding” communities. The A.P.Pir.A. project underscores the limitations of traditional
  ­archaeological paradigms, which have too often underestimated the archaeological signature of piracy or dis-
   missed it as ­archaeologically “invisible” or marginal. In addition, the project revealed two key findings that
   suggest that an archaeological approach to piracy is indeed feasible, despite the methodological challenges: (1)
   Despite regional and chronological variations, piracy exhibited distinct diachronic features, not only in terms
   of operational practices and areas of activity but also in terms of the perceptions of piracy that prevailed in
   public consciousness; (2) Pirate activity does leave a strong archaeological signature, which is detectable when
   subjected to innovative, interdisciplinary and critically reflexive methodologies. Only through such approaches
   can the archaeology of piracy move beyond the perception of an elusive or marginal phenomenon and establish
   itself as a productive field of inquiry, capable of offering new insights into the dynamics of maritime violence
   and its impact on ancient societies.

TRACING ANCIENT PIRATES IN THE ARCHAEOLOGICAL RECORD

Identifying ancient pirate bases
The results of the A.P.Pir.A. project, together with the studies presented in this volume, underline both the
­challenges and the prospects of developing an archaeology of piracy. Despite methodological and interpretive
 difficulties, archaeological research has proven capable of identifying sites that may have functioned as pirate
 bases across different regions and periods. Well-known examples include Choriza on Hydra, ­Phalasarna in
 western Crete and Antikythera (see above; also Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis, this volume). Furthermore, some
 of the contributions to this volume point to potential pirate involvement at other sites of classical ­antiquity
 (particularly during the Hellenistic period), such as Kastraki on Agathonisi (Pantzouris) and the islet of
 ­Antidragonera, close to Kythera (Markakis).
    Crucially, the field is no longer confined to historical periods with textual evidence but now extends to
prehistoric and proto-historical contexts. Sites such as Strophilas on Andros and Vathy on Astypalaia indicate
possible pirate activity already in the Late Neolithic and Early Helladic I periods (Giagkoudaki). The likeli-
hood appears even greater at certain Early Cycladic settlements (Angelopoulou; Giagkoudaki), with the site
of Kastri on Syros standing out alongside those of Panormos on Naxos, Kynthos on Delos and Markiani on
Amorgos. In the LBA, and particularly in its final stages, several sites in Cyprus (e.g., Pyla-Kokkinokremos,
Maa-­Palaiokastro) and Crete (e.g., Pseira, Mochlos, Kastri at Palaikastro, Elias to Nisi, Kalo Chorafi, Korakia
on Dia, Kastrokephala) likely served, at least in part, as pirate bases (Driessen; Vokotopoulos). Comparable
patterns persist through the transition to the EIA and across the period itself, as evidenced by Meganisi in the
Inner Ionian Archipelago (Vikatou and Staikou) and by a series of coastal and island sites in the Aegean that are
discussed by Panagiotis Gounelas.
    The systematic reconsideration of such sites as potential pirate bases will contribute to the identification
of the structural and spatial characteristics of early pirate settlements and to the elucidation of their material
culture. This perspective is particularly valuable at locations where pirate activity appears to have been more
than episodic, constituting instead a communal way of life, as has been suggested with the examples of Pyla-­
Kokkinokremos in Cyprus and Meganisi in the Inner Ionian Archipelago (Driessen; Vikatou and Staikou).

Topography and persistent pirate activity
Several studies in this volume emphasize the importance of coastal topography to the location of recurring
pirate disorders. Contributions by Adam Dawson and Nicholas Rauh on Cilicia, George Koutsouflakis on the
Phournoi archipelago, Nirefs Markakis on Kythera, and Olympia Vikatou and Vivian Staikou on the C      ­ entral Io-
nian Sea collectively demonstrate that regions with nonlinear coastlines, that is, those characterized by ­islands,
inlets and coves offering concealment, narrow sea passages that forced merchant vessels to travel at reduced
speed and alongside predictable sailing routes, as well as heavily trafficked maritime corridors rich in commer-
cial targets, experienced recurring patterns of piracy. Within this framework, the area associated with the noto-
rious Liburnian pirates, discussed by Filip Budić, though far less studied than Cilicia, the Aegean or the Ionian,
emerges as a particularly promising field of research, combining topographical suitability with a well-attested
pirate tradition.

Fortifications and defensive strategies
Another critical yet ambivalent component in the archaeology of piracy highlighted in several ­contributions
to this volume is the presence of fortifications. While, as Jan Driessen emphasizes, pirates occasionally
erected their own defenses, they more typically appropriated existing structures. The tendency to associate
well-­constructed fortifications with organized polities does not preclude their use by pirates, as the sites of
­Phalasarna, ­Antikythera and those in Cilicia demonstrate (Tsaravopoulos and Kroustalis; Dawson and Rauh).

Rather, the remains of fortified sites (especially smaller bastions nestled along remote coastlines) underline
the multiplicity of functions that defenses could assume, functioning sometimes as bulwarks against piracy
and at other times as strongholds for pirate bands themselves, as argued by Konstantinos Pantzouris for the
fortified site of Kastraki on A
                              ­ gathonisi. In fact, through his recent archival and field research about the occu-
pation of particular A­ egean islands by pirates and corsairs of the 17th century, George Koutzakiotis (2023, this
volume) corroborates Driessen’s view that pirates themselves typically resorted to makeshift, hastily constructed
structures (see also Dawson and Rauh, this volume on the survival of Hellenistic fortifications employing a
­“vernacular” masonry technique in coastal Rough Cilicia and their potential link to piracy).

Beyond stereotypes: wealth, prosperity and pirate settlements
It is equally essential to challenge entrenched stereotypes that restrict our understanding of piracy and restrain
its archaeological study, such as the assumption that pirate settlements were invariably small, impoverished and
littoral. As Jan Driessen observes, “the size and prosperity of a coastal settlement do not exclude its role as a po-
tential pirate’s nest”. Indeed, the presence of exotica and wealth, normally interpreted as evidence of prosperity
resulting from commercial exchanges, may, in fact, reflect pirate occupation. This seems particularly plausible at
modest coastal settlements, such as Mochlos and Petras in eastern Crete. The presence of luxury goods at these
sites suggest that they functioned as pirate hideouts or as safe havens, where pirates could obtain provisions and
exchange plunder for foodstuffs.
    Adam Dawson and Nicholas Rauh’s study of the Cilician pirates further clarifies potential modes of o  ­ peration
through the selection of “occluded sites” by ancient pirate bands. These scholars demonstrate how pirates situ-
ated in coastal centers along vulnerable sea-lanes maintained visual contact with seaborne targets indirectly by
communicating with lookouts situated at occluded satellite sites in the highland interior. Strategically positioned
to observe maritime traffic while remaining invisible from the sea, the inland lookouts potentially delivered
early-warning signals to pirate bands waiting along the coast. This pattern, substantiated through systematic
surface survey and GIS analysis, is valuable not only for reconstructing evidence of ancient pirate practices, but
also for demonstrating the need to incorporate the investigation of interior sites into the archaeology of piracy.

Funerary contexts and mortuary display
A similar interpretative approach applies to funerary contexts. Jan Driessen suggests that the presence of exotica
and valuable artifacts, especially when combined with weaponry, in burials such as the Griffin Warrior’s tomb
at Pylos or the rich grave excavated by Nikolaos Platon on Skopelos might be attributable to successful pirate
raids. Panagiotis Gounelas has similarly argued that certain EIA burials, such as Tomb 79 at Lefkandi, may
represent instances where wealth, possibly acquired in part through piracy, was manifested through mortuary
display. More broadly, in periods of demonstrable or particularly intense levels of pirate activity and in regions
topographically suited to such practices, the combination of exotica, prestige goods and weaponry in burial
assemblages should at least raise the possibility that the interred person had engaged in piracy.

Piracy in visual arts
Piracy’s cultural impact also resonates in the visual arts, despite the tendency of ancient artistic production to
focus on elites and to underrepresent the everyday activities of social inferiors. The unnerving impact of pirate
activity on the public consciousness all but insured its occasional depiction. Several well-known works ranging
from the Flotilla Fresco at Akrotiri, the Siege Rhyton from Mycenae (Driessen; Sakas) and the depiction of
Ramses III’s naval battle against the Sea Peoples in the Medinet Habu relief in Egypt (Ladas) to the Middle
Geometric krater 31.11.2 in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Gounelas) and the Late Archaic cup B436 in the
British Museum (Manakidou), have all been interpreted as representations of piracy.

     In any event, it should be emphasized that visual sources, much like textual ones, tend to frame piracy
through narratives of success. Regardless of whether the artwork depicts victories over pirates or successful
­pirate raids, specific historical events or broader reflections of maritime supremacy, such representations are
 consistently articulated from the victor’s perspective. Even mythological scenes –most notably the popular
 story of Dionysus’ attempted abduction by Tyrrhenian pirates, examined in detail by Stamatis Fritzilas in this
 volume– reflect contemporary familiarity with piracy and similar historical realities potentially embedded in
 myths.

The maritime sphere and underwater archaeology
  Turning to the pirates’ main sphere of activity –the sea– it seems that, for the moment, its contribution to
  the ­archaeology of piracy remains limited. Scholars broadly agree that in both prehistoric times and ­classical
­antiquity ships employed for piracy –whether systematic or opportunistic– did not differ substantially from
 contemporary vessels (see Giagkoudaki on the EBA; Tsonakas on the LBA; Nakas on the Classical and
 ­Hellenistic periods). A constant requirement of pirate ships in all eras was speed, maneuverability and stealth-
  iness; ­nevertheless, it must always be borne in mind that even the humblest craft could be employed for pirate
  purposes.
    Underwater archaeology faces long-recognized difficulties in linking finds directly to piracy (see above), a
point also emphasized by George Koutsouflakis in his study of the Phournoi archipelago in the eastern Aegean.
Nevertheless, the Kyrenia shipwreck and recent studies on it provide reasons for optimism that careful excava-
tion and systematic study of shipwrecks will illuminate future pirate contexts, as has already been shown with
early modern examples (e.g., de Bry 2006; Lizé 2006; de Bry and Roling 2016; Soulat et al. 2023; see also Page
and Ewen 2016). To this evidence may now be added shipwreck no. 23 that sank off the modern settlement
of Bali in Phournoi. The wreck is dated to the early 19th century and was apparently scuttled after capture
and plunder (Koutsouflakis). Furthermore, as the same scholar rightly concludes, combining terrestrial and
­underwater data holds the potential to reconstruct patterns of pirate activity in regions of particular interest.

Future directions and concluding remarks
The archaeology of piracy in antiquity is progressing with increasing methodical rigor and organization,
­providing fresh avenues for future research. This view is fully confirmed by George Koutzakiotis’ contribution,
 which effectively “closes the curtain” on this volume by examining piracy and the corso in the Aegean during
 early modern times, a period more accessible archaeologically than is antiquity. Two main categories of mate-
 rial culture relevant to piracy have been identified: (1) remains directly linked to pirate activity and the need
 to secure ships, loot and personnel; and (2) everyday objects and artifacts. For the first category, geographical
 context is decisive: such finds occur in locations otherwise inexplicable or uniquely suitable for piracy. For the
 second, although direct association is difficult to prove, Koutzakiotis reminds us that pirates were embedded in
 the societies of their time, sharing the same essential needs as their contemporaries.

In general, considering the factors outlined above (such as the importance of topography and the p    ­ ositive
correlation between piracy and maritime trade), promising contexts for investigating ancient piracy include
­regions that display a combination of favorable geomorphology, a pirate tradition and periods of robust mari-
 time trade. The fact that such examples are numerous in Greek seas and across the wider Mediterranean does
 not diminish the phenomenon, but rather highlights its potential scope and dispersal. When such conditions
 ­correspond with additional indicators, like coastal fortifications, “hidden” or “inconvenient” settlements,
  weapons in ships or burials, or martial imagery displayed in maritime settings, piracy should at least be in-
  cluded among the interpretative possibilities. Furthermore, case studies such as those of Adam Dawson and
  Nicholas Rauh on Cilicia and Nirefs Markakis on Kythera demonstrate the potential of GIS analyses to the study
  of ancient piracy. Finally, Jan Driessen’s advice to “focus on time periods during which major state organizations
  were either absent or weakened” seems particularly useful and is confirmed in nearly every contribution to this
  volume. As Leonidas Vokotopoulos points out, in times of political and social instability there were always those
  who perceived turbulence not as a problem but as an opportunity.

CHARTING NEW WATERS: TOWARDS AN ARCHAEOLOGY OF PIRACY IN
ANTIQUITY

Until recently, archaeologists have largely avoided addressing piracy, owing to the methodological and
­interpretive difficulties involved. Pirates themselves often sought to conceal their activities, while the mate-
 rial culture associated with piracy rarely differed in any substantial way from that of other activities, such as
 trade or warfare. Nevertheless, piracy was an endemic feature of the ancient Mediterranean world, embedded
 in everyday life across multiple periods, and at times capable of influencing political, economic and social
 ­developments. For this reason, it is incumbent upon archaeological researchers to develop methodologies ca-
  pable of overcoming these challenges and addressing the phenomenon of piracy, thereby sharing a burden that
  has ­hitherto been borne almost exclusively by text-dependent historians. Beyond the chronological limitations
  inherent to historical research, several studies in this volume –such as Adam Dawson and Nicholas Rauh’s
  examination of Cilician piracy in the late Hellenistic period and George Koutsouflakis’s work on the Phournoi
  archipelago in the early modern era– underscore the literary hyperbole about piracy that is frequently encoun-
  tered in written sources and the consequent need for careful deconstruction. Archaeologists must, therefore,
  proceed in lock step with historians by addressing dimensions that are otherwise inaccessible to textual analysis,
  but are capable at the same time of providing an essential means of cross-reference written testimony, regardless
  of whether that testimony magnifies the scope and intensity of piracy and downplays and obscures it.
     The contributions to this volume highlight both the difficulties and the possibilities for the pursuit of the
archaeology of piracy and demonstrate that pirates left ambiguous but recognizable traces. Settlements, for-
tifications, destruction horizons, iconography and funerary assemblages may all reflect pirate activity when
subjected to appropriate contextual analysis. Case studies such as those of Aris Tsaravopoulos and Evangelos
­Kroustalis on the Antikythera shipwreck or Nirefs Markakis on Antidragonera suggest that certain sites and
 finds may in fact be best understood through the lens of piracy. The most promising directions for future re-
 search include closer integration of archaeological and textual evidence, GIS analyses, sustained attention to
 the role of slaving and ransom markets in shaping maritime economies, and greater focus on the experiences of
 victims and non-elite actors, who are all too often eclipsed in state-centered narratives.
    Above all, we must remember that seafaring identities were fluid: merchants might become pirates and
pirates could be turned into merchants or serve as naval auxiliaries. Such multiplicity, highlighted in several
contributions to this volume, underscores the complex social realities of maritime life in antiquity and suggests
that the archaeology of piracy should avoid one-dimensional approaches. Piracy should not be viewed merely
as an instrument of disruption. As Carla Antonaccio has noted (2017, 223), it could also serve as a force of

c­ onnectivity and mobility. Viewed in this light, piracy emerges not simply as criminal predation at sea but as
 a dynamic phenomenon situated at the intersection of commerce, warfare and diplomacy, embedded within
 networks of marginality, informal exchange and both resistance to and collaboration with established powers.
   We may never uncover an archaeological find that can be indisputably associated with ancient piracy. No
archaeologist realistically anticipates discovering a ship bearing a pirate flag, a buried treasure chest or a grave
with a stele explicitly identifying its occupant as a pirate. The A.P.Pir.A. project sought to transcend the treat-
ment of piracy as a marginal topic or footnote and to re-situate it within archaeological discourse as a dynamic
and multifaceted phenomenon deeply embedded in ancient societies. The contributions assembled in this
volume advance precisely this goal: they establish piracy as a legitimate subject of archaeological investigations
and invite us to begin reflecting on and engaging with the figure of the ancient pirates. In other words, the
journey into the archaeology of piracy in antiquity is still in its infancy…
