 Λῃστικός or Can We Really Talk of Pirates in the Bronze Age?

The almost honorable regard for sea raiders in Homer contrasts considerably with Thucydides’ well-known ­assertion
that Minos freed the seas from piracy, suggesting a major switch in appreciation in the ways foreign goods and slaves
were acquired in the Iron Age and how piracy affected state formation. Is Homer’s attitude closer to that of the ­situation
in the Bronze Age? Or of one phase of the Bronze Age when raiding was a general custom and a way of life? Apart from
synthesizing work by other scholars on pirates and piracy at various moments during the Aegean Bronze Age, I review
the nature and location of settlements, representations of naval warfare and raiding, as well as the p­ resence of exotica
potentially resulting from what Renfrew called “negative reciprocity” for what these can inform us on the existence of
“sea thieves”. I also discuss the sites of Pyla-Kokkinokremos and Maa-Palaiokastro on Cyprus and their potential link to
piracy or the Sea Peoples in general.

The romanticized picture of piracy presented in movies and literature, as we all know, does not agree with reality
– pirates were the scourge of the seas and still are, even if the number of pirate attacks is going down (Shane and
Magnuson 2016). While most of the Mediterranean is relatively safe nowadays, the Libyan coast has seen an
increase of pirate attacks, with ships venturing further away from the coast and threatening passing merchant
ships (Robitaille 2020). Other attacks have been noted in the Gulf of Guinea and the Straits of Singapore but, in
contrast, Somali piracy is now negligeable due to international policing in the Arabian Gulf (Soğancilar 2021;
Sandkamp et al. 2022).
     The Archaeology of Piracy in Antiquity, the topic of this volume, was already a theme of interest to scholars
during WW I (Semple 1916), but I will, for obvious reasons, focus on Bronze Age Crete. There is evidently a
problem of anachronistically attributing later connotations, since the island had a bad reputation not only in
Hellenistic and early Roman times and in the 9th and 10th centuries CE, when Arabs originally from Spain used
it as their base for pirate attacks in the Aegean (Christides 1984), but also later when, despite Venetian and later
Ottoman control, it was on the receiving end, being plagued by Barbary pirates (Davis 2017; Dimitropoulos
2022).
    Finding material traces of piracy is not an easy task neither for historical, nor for prehistoric times, since
pirates do not leave their signature in the destruction levels we encounter. To obtain some kind of starting point,
we necessarily must turn to textual evidence and later historical parallels and see if these can help us understand
the Bronze Age evidence. As to the first, one cannot avoid noticing the almost honorable regard for sea raiders
expressed in Homer, where most of the heroes commit acts of what we today would call piracy almost as a past
 · 52 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4

time, while busy laying siege at Troy (de Souza 1992). To kill time and to feed their armies, they take their boats
and grab whatever they can in the region, women especially. But Homer is also careful not to call his heroes
pirates (even if Thucydides does), while other, lesser folk and foreigners, are given the label, even if there is no
difference between their actions. Strictly speaking, however, and despite the use of the terms leistes and peirates,
one can question whether real piracy is in fact mentioned in the epics, since the term usually implies persons
who attack and rob ships at sea.
     Where the Bronze Age is concerned, we should also ask whether there was a fundamental difference ­between
what we now consider as acts of piracy and those committed by regular warriors or armies. The Mycenae silver
siege rhyton, for example, illustrates how one or more ships moored and a city was attacked (Papadopoulos
2019), and a very similar representation is preserved on a stone vase from Epidaurus, which, besides a boat
scene and a land raid, also includes a drowning person (Koehl 2006, 53, 185, 360, n. 818–19). Pirates or heroes?
If a pharaoh has his armies attacking a Levantine city, is this regular warfare, while if one city sends a ship to
pillage another city would this be piracy? The distinction is difficult to make and more a matter of appreciation.
Many scholars have tried to define piracy (e.g., Samaras 2015, this volume; Emanuel 2018) but, as far as the
­Aegean Bronze Age is concerned, Homer’s uncertainty is probably close to the truth. So, Thucydides (1.1.5) is to
 be forgiven when claiming that “no disgrace being yet attached to such an achievement, but even some glory”.
AN ARCHAEOLOGY OF PIRACY

But how can we identify pirates and piracy in the Aegean Bronze Age. Pirate expert Marcus Rediker (1987,
257–58) already recognized three essential elements that large-scale piracy needed to fulfil: (1) pirates tend
to blossom in anarchic regions that border crucial sea lanes; (2) pirates tend to exploit established maritime
­networks to prey on passing commerce, and (3) since randomly seized cargoes do not always contain foodstuffs
 essential for survival, pirates need a “nest”, that is, a nearby friendly community where they can trade their
 plundered cargoes for everyday essentials without consequence and stock up on water. This definition is quite
 revealing as it comprises several features that may be archaeologically relevant (also Rediker 2004, 2014).
     The first is that piracy thrives in anarchic regions, as it did in the late 17th century, which should imply
that when strong authorities are present, piracy would be limited. It is such a situation already alluded at by
­Thucydides when stating that King Minos suppressed piracy while installing a sea-based hegemony. Leaving
 aside whether this was just a way of introducing Athenian naval policy, there are plenty of historical parallels for
 this: the Barbary pirates were only suppressed when France took control of North Africa in the 1830s, soon after
 the First Barbary War of 1801–1805 (Martin and Weiss 2019; de Lange 2021), more or less at the same time the
 US and European nations suppressed it in the Caribbean (Wilson 2021). This criterion would hence imply that
 we should concentrate on periods without a sufficiently strong political force in the Bronze Age Aegean to look
 for pirate activities. This is not an easy task either, since a strong land-based authority does not always possess
 a navy to act in tandem. Pharaonic Egypt, for example, only invested into an oceangoing navy during the New
 Kingdom (Emanuel 2021) and there is literary evidence that Keftiou ships docked at the harbor of Peru-nefer
 (Bietak 2010). The absence of a strong authority after the fall of the Minoan and Mycenaean palaces is often
 invoked as evidently giving rise to pirate activities during the Late Bronze Age (LBA) and continuing till the
 Archaic period (esp. Hitchcock and Maeir 2018). Whether Crete or some Cretan power actually was responsible
 for suppressing pirate acts during the heydays of Minoan culture remains, therefore, a possibility. The fact that
 coastal Cretan cities do not seem to pay special attention to defensive structures could also suggest that the seas
 were safe and that no attacks were expected from that side, but I will return to this below.
   A second important criterion is the existence of crucial sea lanes through which essential trade passed ­(Arnaud
2005; 2020). Sea currents are different in summer and winter, but one assumes that most piracy would take place
during the sailing months. 4th century CE Vegetius states that sailing in the Mediterranean was ­dangerous after

September 15 and impossible after November 11 (de Souza 2016; but see Beresford 2013 for a more nuanced
view). This said, the south coast of Crete is to be avoided during summer, since the mountains give rise to what
are called katabatic squalls, a wind that carries high-density air from higher elevations down a slope under the
force of gravity (Morton 2001; Gertwagen 2016), which sometimes had hurricane force as the Apostle Paul
witnessed before reaching Kaloi Limenes (Spratt 1865, 11–12; Mourtzas and Kolaiti 2021; Curtis 2023 ; Fig.
1). ­Furthermore, as Cristoforo Buondelmonti already noticed, this coast could only be navigated by crews that
knew the topography (Pryor 2006). But even the north coast was often avoided due to the strong meltemi winds,
and, during the Crusades, ships going east would prefer to travel from the Ionian Sea close to the Peloponnese
and hence through the Cyclades and the Dodecanese, with Crete being avoided (Arnaud 2020). Trading ships
would only approach Cretan shores if they were to board one of the major coastal towns, which, in the Bronze
Age, would have been Chania, Poros or Amnissos and a few other places along the north coast that offer suffi-
cient shelter, such as Souda Bay, the Spinalonga lagoon or Siteia. The north coast of Crete was, in any case, out
of the question during winter because of the fierce winds, and still today there are days, even in summer, when
the winds are so strong that even the big ships cannot sail. But with good winds, Egypt could be reached in just
four days (Kopanias 2017, 125).
    A third criterion is the existence of a thriving maritime network, and Carl Knappett and colleagues (2008;
2011) have extensively published on this. They have concentrated on the main phases of Minoan trade and
illustrate changes caused by the disappearance of Santorini-Akrotiri. In general, the links they highlight testify
to the dynamism of interaction during the Middle (MBA) and early LBA, but the advanced LBA could do with
some more attention despite some initial attempts by Tom Tartaron (2013), Francesco Iacono (2019), and Alex
Knodell (2021).
   Lastly, pirates need a free haven, a place that offers safety but also access to food and fresh water. One may
assume that such pirate’s nests would reasonably be at some distance from these sea lanes to avoid detection.
Where do we need to look and what are we specifically looking for? Small, off-shore islands were probably
quite popular – Gavdos, for example, was known as a pirate refuge, even used by Barbarossa as his base one
time ­(Kopaka and Kossyva 1999). The islands of Dia (Vokotopoulos, this volume) and pre-Venetian Spinalonga
could be others. Pseira island with its Minoan site would in fact be a good candidate as a pirate settlement.
­Mochlos too, with its original double harbor hidden by the island itself, could well have been a settlement with a
 · 54 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4

less than favorable reputation. Sea-caves are also ideal to boat ships, sheltered from storms and views, and Crete
has many such caves that are immediately accessible from the sea. Hidden coves (e.g., Calypso or Pirate’s Cove
near Plakias, or Martsalos beach near the Ayio Farango gorge) and inlets of Crete provided ideal hiding spots
for pirates, and the further away from a major coastal settlement that had sufficient authority, the easier it was
for freebooters. Small, hidden creeks, such as those at Sissi, used to launch attacks against the Ottomans, that of
Ayios Nikolaos or Cape Sidero would have been ideal to hide before preying on passing ships.
     Why pirates do what they do is perhaps a redundant question and both Sahlins (1965) and Renfrew (1975)
have stressed how piracy is a form of negative reciprocity, an attempt to maximize personal gain from the
­transaction. Perhaps we could call it also a form of direct access, get things where you can directly, without
 paying or giving something in exchange. For the Bronze Age, we will never know whether the exotica and
 wealth in the different settlement or funerary contexts we encounter are the result of pirate activity. The eclectic
 nature of the Griffin Warrior’s assemblage at Pylos (Davis and Stocker 2022, 64, 83–4) does not rule out that
 this gentleman was occupied with less than honorable activities and the same may be true for other rich, but
 eclectic Mycenaean tombs in unexpected locations, as that on Skopelos, which, besides a marvelous long sword
 with gold foil decoration, also yielded a knife with duck’s head hilt, a spearhead, dagger and Late Helladic (LH)
 IIB Ephyraean goblets and alabastra (Platon 1949). I will come back to unusual wealth in otherwise mediocre
 archaeological contexts below.
     Apart from transmittable wealth, the epics and later historical sources inform us that people, and e­ specially
women, were sought after by pirates so that they could be sold as slaves. A study by Davis (2003; 2010) found
that, between the 16th and 19th centuries, more than a million Europeans were enslaved by Barbary pirates.
From the Linear B tablets, we learn of the presence of foreign women in the service of the palace at Pylos (Olsen
2014). Women from Knidos, Lemnos, Miletus and elsewhere were employed by the palace, usually in the ­textile
industry, and other women are explicitly called rawijaja, often translated as “captives”, hence announcing a
­passage in the Iliad where Achilles boasts of the women he captured in the area around Troy (Il. 20.193; see
 also Ergin 2007, 273). Slaves in general are mentioned in the Linear B records, but the references are relatively
 rare and slaves are always held by individuals, so I would not exaggerate official state acquisitions via piracy.
 Whether other elements, such as the terracotta spools used in textile production (Fig. 2) that show up regularly
 in Late Minoan (LM) and LH IIIA–C contexts, suggest the presence of foreign women, seems a reasonable sug-
 gestion (Driessen and Gaignerot-Driessen 2023), but we are unable to tell whether these women formed part
 of a larger population movement or whether they were captives, acquired during raids or bought in slave mar-
 kets from pirates. The oddity is that the prizes given at the Homeric funeral games –tripod basins and kraters,
 gold, horses, cattle, and women– are probably also those that were most prized by pirates. It is probably not a
 ­coincidence that Achilles brings out these prizes from his ships! (Il. 23.259; see especially Ready 2007).
     We even have less evidence when it comes to material traces of acts of piracy. That such things –attacking
and robbing ships at sea– were happening in the Bronze Age, is alluded at by the reference to Lukka pirates or
Misi in the Amarna letters (Emanuel 2020), and seems to be suggested by the scene on the north wall of the
­Flotilla Fresco of Akrotiri, Thera (Morgan 1988). This shows two main events: a seascene, usually dubbed the
 shipwreck scene, and a raid on land (Fig. 3). The first scene shows a captain with an outstretched arm and at least
 three nude people with a different hairstyle, drowning in front of his boat, and with them are floating shields
 and shepherd sticks, suggesting they may have been warriors. The nature of this scene is quite different from
 that on the opposite wall. Are these the ancestors of the Barbary pirates? Unfortunately, the scene is ­fragmentary
 so we cannot judge the nature of the ships involved nor whether the two partly preserved ships were manned
 by a crew similar to the drowning people. The second scene, the land raid, is immediately above this, so some
 connection can be assumed. Here, eight shield and spear carrying warriors with boar tusk ­helmets are heading
 inland and up the hill, where a dozen cattle are assembled, presumably to be taken away. The ­warriors are prob-
 ably the “good guys” but they are involved in what we may perhaps assume is piracy raiding. We can hypothesize
 that there is a general connection between these scenes and that a mixture of sea and land raids is hence sug-
 gested. The flotilla scene in general and the many depictions of ships in Aegean and non-­Aegean iconography

(e.g., Papadopoulos 2009; Emanuel 2021, 311–43; for ship typology, see Van de Moortel 2017) show that at least
the means and techniques of naval warfare were available, and this from an early moment onwards.
    Can we add some other archaeological indicators?
    Coastal cities with important defensive structures can evidently be interpreted in different ways: either as a
protective measure against pirates or pirates protecting themselves against potential people wanting revenge.
On Crete, however, coastal sites with defensive infrastructure are relatively rare. Ayia Photia near Siteia could
be a case in point (Middle Minoan [ΜΜ] IA; Tsipopoulou 1988) while both the sites of Petras (ΜΜ IIA; Tsi-
popoulou 2012, 55 fig. 9) and Sissi (Jusseret 2011, 173–76) were given megalithic walls at some parts of the set-
tlement. Myrtos Pyrgos also had a defensive wall, looking out towards the inland, however (MΜ IIB; Cadogan
2013).
     Although there are a few historical parallels for pirates constructing themselves serious defenses (like
­ ortuga, Bosch 2016), often they take over existing sites that may have been fortified by the first inhabitants
T
(such as Île Sainte Marie on Madagascar, a French port later occupied by pirates, or Port Royal in the Caribbean,
only turned into a fortress after the pirates had been chased). Pirates are in fact not so keen in spending much
of their time and energy into communal work. The size and prosperity of a coastal settlement do not exclude
its role as a potential pirate’s nest. Marsa Matruh, to the very west of Egypt, is sometimes called an Egyptian
trade post, sometimes a pirate’s nest (Emanuel 2016, 267). We should also not forget that Chandax –present-day
Herakleion– was the main pirate city of the Aegean during the 9th and 10th centuries CE, when it was in the
hands of Arab Moors coming from Spain till Nikephoros Phokas defeated them in 961 (Christides 1984). It was
these Moors who had protected the city with a deep ditch, hence its name El Khandak, and a rampart made of
earth mixed with goat and pig hair (Talbot and Sullivan 2005, 64). In this case, there is ample literary evidence
of course.
   Several scholars, including Hitchcock and Maeir (2014; 2018), and following Nowicki (2000; 2001), have
argued that the collapse of Aegean palace administrations during the advanced LBA opened the way for p

attacks throughout the Aegean, and, especially in Crete. Following Thucydides (1.1.7: “But the old towns, on
­account of the great prevalence of piracy, were built away from the sea.” , trans. J.M. Dent, London and New
 York, 1910), this would have provoked the a­ bandonment of coastal areas. Excavations at Sissi and Malia illus-
 trate this phenomenon during LM IIIB (Driessen and Gaignerot-Driessen 2023). In both sites, rooms were
 simply left with their objects in place – only metals were missing (Fig. 2). Were these pillaged or simply taken
 along by the original occupants when they left? Apart from piracy, the abandonment of regions can evidently
 also have other causes: natural d  ­ isasters, epidemics (malaria), environmental change (aridity) etc. (already
 Cameron 1991; Nelson and Hegmon 2001). Hence, blaming pirates should be based on an in-depth contextual
 analysis. There are, however, plenty of ­historical parallels for such a causal relation, including early Modern Italy
 that suffered from Barbary pirates (Davis 2003).
    A link between piracy and the location of settlements inland is usually inferred to explain the presence of
sites far from the coast, especially in the Cyclades, as for example the city of Xobourgo on Tenos (Kourou 2001;
Dimitropoulos 2022). Diodorus Siculus (5.6.2) also mentions that the Sicani built their settlements on strong
inland hilltops in fear of pirates. Also in East Crete, modern inland settlements such as those of Palaikastro and
Epano Zakros have been explained as forced displacement following piracy attacks by North African raiders.
Rackham and Moody (1996, 198), for example, have dubbed the far east “corsair country”, because it suffered
so frequently from pirate attacks. This would then lead to a contrasting synchronous settlement distribution
pattern with (1) perhaps only a few defendable settlements with a sizeable population left on the coast, strong
enough to face pirate attacks, (2) an occasional pirate’s nest in a more hidden location to avoid detection (as e.g.,
on Kastri hill at Palaikastro) and (3) a more general presence of smaller, inland settlements, at a safe distance
from the coast. Enduring coastal settlements such as Chania may have resisted and represent the first category
of sites. Pirate nests may have been located in the different bays east of Nisi Panteleimon, the promontory below
Vrokastro, and one of these –Elias to Nisi– was defended by a strong wall (Hayden 2001; Vokotopoulos, this
volume). Its date, however, is not entirely clear.
    Location and isolation may be important criteria to judge the nature of a settlement, but even this criterium
should be properly contextualized. The site of Kalo Chorafi, for example, excavated under the direction of
­Anastasia Tzigounaki, is located in the middle of nowhere, in a small valley in what is otherwise an extremely
 rocky coast between Herakleion and Rethymnon (Tzigounaki and Karnava 2020). The site would hence be an
 ideal candidate for a pirate lair if it wasn’t that this coastal settlement seemingly forms just one of a chain of

even Soetens (2005, 44) too has noted the similarities
between the various lookouts as shown on a Venetian map (Fig. 4) drawn by Nicola Gualdo de Priorati in 1633
and the location of peak sanctuaries (Arakadaki 1997). Could these, besides their ritual functions, also have
represented an early warning system, protecting the Cretan coasts during the heydays of Minoan civilization?
A combination of evenly spaced coastal settlements, peak sanctuaries with large vistas and beacons that could
be used in a way that tradition suggests the fall of Troy was announced would have represented a considerable
“AWACS”.
     And then there is the question of pirate attacks of coastal settlements – as I said they don’t leave their
­signature and thus it is difficult to blame pirates rather than another adversary for the destruction and pillaging
 of a settlement. A much-cited example is the Late Cycladic (LC) IIIC site of Koukounaries on Paros. Because
 of the discovery of bodies within the destruction layer, its excavator, Dimitrios Schilardi (1979; 1984), blamed
 pirates, but apparently the site was not pillaged, which would be strange in case of a pirate attack (Vlachopoulos
 2003). Each site in fact should be explored in detail: How did the destruction happen? Was it partial or ­complete?
 Pirates would, I think, rarely destroy a site entirely since it would be to their benefit if the settlement r­ ecovered
 so that it could be pillaged again. Bergen in Norway, for example, was pillaged by pirates in 1428, 1429 and 1432
 and although partly burned, enough was left to allow recovery (Stylegar et al. 2020).
    If a site was pillaged, can we identify its objects elsewhere? Or objects from one culture in another area,
without these being the result of trade? Or is there a concentration of unexplained wealth in modest coastal
settlements, like, for example, at Mochlos or even Petras? Such finds do not necessarily imply that these sites
themselves were pirate nests, but they may have provided safe havens for pirates to stock up and exchange valu-
ables for foodstuffs.
   A case in point could be the palace of Knossos, the destruction of which in LM IIIA2 remains a historical
problem. Was this the result of internal strife, an attack by a Mainland competitor, or could it have been raided
by pirates? Undefended as it is, the palace lies only an hour’s walk from the shore, a little more than 5 km. We
may also ask whether Knossos, as Athens, Rome and so many important other cities, was located inland with

such a pirate threat in mind, already in the Neolithic? Pirates tend not to venture more than between 2 and 10
km inland so as not to jeopardize an eventual retreat, although exceptions occur (Kaiser and Calafat 2014).
Whether Knossos ever was accessible by small boats through the Kairatos river from Katsambas is unlikely; thus
attackers probably came on foot. Moreover, the site was hidden from the sea by the Zafer Papoura hill (Roberts
1979), but a well-organized group could have attacked, plundered, and burned the palace in part, leaving only
Linear B tablets and pottery behind (Driessen forthcoming). Since there is only little evidence for looted mate-
rial on Crete itself in late LM IIIA2 and IIIB, this may have ended up in some other region of the Mediterranean.
In any case, Knossos palace was burnt and nothing of value was left inside, as the quotations of passages in the
first report on the excavation by Arthur Evans below suggest, a situation that considerably contrasts with the
earlier destruction of the palace at Kato Zakros or the Villa Reale at Ayia Triada:
    •    “The care with which the rooms seem to have been searched for metal objects at the time of the destruc-
         tion of the Palace no doubt accounts for the rarity of such among the finds.” (Evans 1900, 66).
    •    “The rooms of the Palace, as already noted, had evidently been ransacked for metal objects at the time
         of its destruction.” (Evans 1900, 68).
    •    “The comparative absence of clay vessels in the chambers is itself a negative indication that vases of
         precious metals were largely in use here. The search for valuables of this class, probably often renewed
         in the period immediately succeeding the destruction of the Palace, sufficiently accounts for a good
         deal of disorder visible in some of the rooms. The chests containing documents seem in most cases to
         have been broken open and the tablets thrown about on the floor. Many beautiful stone vases had been
         smashed, but these did not tempt the cupidity of a barbaric race of plunderers.” (Evans 1900, 68).
    •    “The fact that these objects in nearly all cases rested on the floor level is itself an almost conclusive proof
         that what disturbance took place occurred for the most part at the time of the destruction, perhaps even
         before the final burning of the Palace.” (Evans 1900, 69).
PYLA-KOKKINOKREMOS – A PIRATE’S NEST?

This brings me to my final point: can we explain the presence of considerable wealth, especially with varying
ethnic origins, that shows up in modest settlements, as being booty, acquired during pirate raids or as s­ ettlements
that acted as free havens for pirates? Again, Mochlos and Pseira may represent examples of such sites in view of
the rich finds made there, but here special attention is given only to the site of Pyla-Kokkinokremos on Cyprus
and the results of the new excavations (Bretschneider et al. 2023; Driessen et al. 2023). It is a site which, since its
initial excavation, has been connected to the Sea Peoples (for a discussion with references see Georgiou 2012), a
group also often assumed to have been involved in pirate activities because of the mention in Ugaritic texts that
“they lived on ships” (Hitchcock and Maeir 2014; 2018). Hitchcock and Maeir (2018) see Maa-Palaiokastro on
the west coast of Cyprus as a pirate settlement largely due to its location on a defended peninsula and the fact
that it was occupied for less than a generation. Can Pyla-Kokkinokremos also be considered as one?
    Both Maa and Pyla are short-lived settlements, suddenly abandoned, although Maa somewhat later than
Pyla, in Late Cypriot (LCyp) IIIA rather than LCyp IIC. In the case of Pyla, its now silted-up harbor was in
fact an inland lagoon and hence its ships could well have been hidden from passing boats (Brown 2013, with
references). At the same time, Pyla is close to land and sea-routes and within a day’s sailing of the rich coasts
of Lebanon and Syria. If we look at the lay-out of the Pyla settlement, there are some additional features which
render a hypothesis that it was some kind of pirate settlement feasible or attractive (Fig. 5). It is enclosed by a
perimeter wall with projecting bastions and only a few access gates on top of a 65 m hill with steep sides.
   Not only is the architecture on the site very homogenous, with all dwellings quite similar in plan, size,
and construction (at least as far as present evidence allows us to recognize), but wealthy objects were found

throughout the site, i.e., they are not limited to a few contexts only. Every house excavated comprises fine stone
vases, metal objects, outstanding decorated pots, and jewelry of all kinds. This seems to suggest a high degree
of social homogeneity between its occupants as we would perhaps expect from a pirate settlement. Since pirate

nests are often evoked as places of liberty and great egality, especially by anarchist writers, occupied by those
who don’t want to be governed (Wilson 2004; Scott 2009), Pyla’s settlement organization fits the picture. Many
of the objects –precious or not– originate from various non-Cypriot regions, such as Egypt, the Levant, the
­Aegean (Crete and Argolis), Anatolia or Sardinia. Are these simply the result of trade as Cyprus at the time –
 LCyp IIC or around 1200 BCE– has several sites that show foreign exotica, including Enkomi and Hala Sultan

 hidden wealth that is encountered as hoards (Driessen et al. 2023) likewise could suggest that these were some

 and warlike representations on kraters and rhyta (see e.g., Bretschneider et al. 2023, figures 3.53, 3.54, 4.33, 4.64,
 4.72, 5.24, 5.61, 5.66, 6.3.8) can be used as circumstantial evidence. Here especially a fragmented ship krater,

Both Maa-Palaiokastro and Pyla-Kokkinokremos belong to a period during which the Sea Peoples were
a­ ctive, and both sites have by times seen as their settlements. The Sea Peoples themselves are often seen as
 the first ­organized, major pirate coalition of the ancient Mediterranean, which, considering how they are
 ­mentioned in ancient texts, seems to correspond to what we assume pirates were doing: attacking coastal cities
  and wreaking chaos and mayhem. Jung (2009) already suggested that some European-type weaponry and other
  features ­connected to these Sea Peoples could have been brought by warriors from the Western Mediterranean,
  becoming “Pirates of the Aegean”. Were they the ones who manned the big brother of the Gurob Ship model,
  sometimes dubbed a Mycenaean pirate ship (Wachsmann 2013)?

Most of what I have mentioned in this paper remains, I am aware, highly speculative. While Bronze Age p     ­ irates
remain highly elusive, this should rather present a challenge than an obstacle and invite to more detailed con-
textual analyses. At the same time, the best guarantee for success should be to focus on time periods during
which major state organizations were either absent or weakened, as in the Early Bronze Age (e.g., Yeagley
2022; Angelopoulou, this volume; Giagkoudaki, this volume) or, as is mostly the case, the advanced LBA (e.g.,
Samaras 2015). In their book “Pieces of Eight: More Archaeology of Piracy”, Ewen and Skowronek (2016, 279)
seek to answer whether it is possible to determine piratical behavior from recovered artifacts, deciding even-
tually that “the Golden Age of Piracy [in the 17th century Caribbean] may have been too short to leave a fully
developed pirate culture that is clearly recognizable in the archaeological record”, and this despite the length of
the period. This remark should also warn us from overinterpreting our evidence.

 Investigating the Origins of Piracy in the Aegean
Trade and Maritime Raids during the Early Bronze Age

During the Early Bronze Age II, the presence of imported raw materials, artifacts and technologies reveals an active
­exchange system and widespread maritime networks in the Aegean. Overseas contacts and the accumulation of wealth
 as the result of those practices changed the dynamics of society. Opportunities for economic benefits and social promotion
 became available, intensifying competition between those involved in maritime networks. The accumulation of wealth
 in the Aegean is usually interpreted as the result of intensive trade and gift exchange. At the same time, however, some
 scholars have argued that the distribution of exotic or valuable objects and raw materials may also have been the result of
 raiding, thus dating the origins of piracy to the Early Bronze Age II period. Other scholars dispute this view, arguing that
 there are fundamental differences that distinguish trade from raiding and warfare, and there can be no question of piracy
 in such an early period, while others accept the existence of piracy but claim that, in the absence of written sources, such
 activities cannot be documented, as their archaeological signature is weak.
This paper examines the possibility of the existence of piracy in the Early Bronze Age Aegean. For this purpose, the
­differences between piracy and war are discussed, and evidence of material culture possibly related to the phenomenon of
 piracy (e.g., ship technology and iconography, material culture and its use, settlement patterns and settlement features)
 are examined. It is argued that in such early societies there were no absolute distinctions between activities like trade,
 piracy, raids and war, and that these activities cannot be approached in a modern way of thinking. The evidence in the
 material culture may be indirect, but seems to suggest that piracy could have been practiced in the Early Bronze Age
 Aegean by the same people who participated in maritime trade and other “legal” activities.

    These maritime activities provided opportunities for wealth accumulation, which could be acquired either
by trading or raiding. The quite large number of fortified settlements and the destruction layers found in some
of them, the presence of weapons in settlement or burial contexts and the iconography of the period that in-
cludes ships and daggers, have led many scholars to accept the important role of raids in the EBA Aegean (e.g.,
Agouridis 1997, 20; Broodbank 2000, 253; Sherratt 2000, 135; Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 139–42).
    On the basis of the high maritime activity of the period and the positive correlation between trade and
piracy (see Samaras, this volume), this paper discusses the possible nature of the raids in the EBA Aegean and
attempts to investigate elements that may relate to the phenomenon of piracy during that period. Initially,
different views on piracy in the Aegean during the EBA are presented and discussed. Then, the motives of
pirate activity are explored, as derived from the possible perceptions, the iconography and the archaeological
evidence. Several aspects of the material culture of the EBA Aegean, e.g., the use of some objects and their sym-
bolisms, the changes in settlement patterns and the existence of settlements with strong defensive systems, offer
indications of potential pirate activities conducted by certain island communities.
VIEWS ON PIRACY IN THE EBA AEGEAN

Wealth accumulation in the Aegean was traditionally considered to be the result of intensive trade and/or gift
­exchange (e.g., Cherry 1981, 41–68; Cosmopoulos 1991, 155–67; Halstead and O’Shea 1992), so any influences
 or innovations observed in material culture were explained as a result of peaceful exchanges, while interpre-
 tations concerning the transfer of materials, people and technical knowledge by raiding or looting were only
 ­tentative or simply absent. At the same time, relevant studies have tended to emphasize the risks of sea travel,
  which were mainly attributed to weather conditions and the small capacity of ships of this period (e.g., ­Agouridis
  1997, 2–6; Broodbank 2000, 92–6), while the dangers from human hostile activity were ­underestimated, if not
  omitted, resulting in a somewhat one-sided approach to a complex phenomenon.
    Nevertheless, a small number of scholars has occasionally supported the possibility of pirate activity in the
EBA Aegean. Renfrew (1972, 440, 763) was probably the first to date the origins of piracy in the Aegean to the
EBA II, based on Thucydides’ claims (1.4.1) about unsafe navigation before the time of Minos due to pirates and
taking into account archaeological data, such as fortified settlements and the circulation of precious metals in
the Aegean. Renfrew’s opinion was accepted by Doumas (1988, 27–9) to explain the destruction at the end of
the Early Cycladic (EC) IIA in the northeastern Aegean and Asia Minor, and the east Aegean influences on the
material culture of the EBA IIB Aegean. He argued that “refugees-pirates”, following the familiar trade routes,
settled in major trading sites of the previous period, but also established new ones at key-points. This way, he
links trade with the conflicts and destruction that took place during this period and relates them to possible
pirate incidents. More recently new arguments have been added to the debate about the changes in the Aegean
during this period, adopting somewhat different interpretation and arguing that, beyond the movements of
people actively involved in sea trade, the spread of ideas, technical knowledge and objects may also be due to
conflicts and possible pirate activities (Yeagley 2022). Also, as discussed in more detail below, longboats of the
period have been suggested to be linked to piracy (Tzovaras 2020, 17).
    On the other hand, several scholars have presented counter-arguments to the above views that either have
to do with the existence of piracy in such an early period or with the (in)ability of the research to detect this
phenomenon. For example, Agouridis (1997, 20) argues that the archaeological footprint of piracy is similar
to that of trade, so no distinction can be made between these two activities. According to de Souza (1999, 2,
15), in periods without written sources piracy cannot be documented, as it leaves no archaeological footprint.
Moreover, it should be mentioned that Broodbank (2000, 410) denies the existence of piracy in the EBA Aegean,

RAIDS IN THE AEGEAN: PIRACY OR WAR?

Despite the varying views in the debate on piracy, it seems generally accepted that maritime raids were ­conducted
in the EBA Aegean, so what should be investigated is the exact nature and purpose of these raids. Broodbank’s
objection to the recognition of these raids as pirate activities is mainly based on researchers attempting to
characterize the distant past using modern terms, perceptions and considerations. Indeed, in the EBA Aegean
there were no recognized rules equivalent to today’s maritime laws and therefore the legality or the illegality
of an action was not perceived in the same way. However, the A.P.Pir.A. project’s research about the history
of piracy reveals that pirates rarely described their activities as piracy and usually used arguments to “justify”
and “legalize” them. Also, it was very common for an action to be characterized as piracy in order to justify the
pursuit and punishment of certain people, regardless of whether they were really pirates or not and regardless
of the existence (or lack of) laws (see more in Samaras, this volume). Therefore, for a more secure approach and
understanding of the phenomenon of piracy, it seems that the characterization of an act as piracy should be
based on the examination of its objective parameters (such as, for example, means and motives) rather than on
how it was perceived and characterized by the people involved (perpetrators or victims) or whether there were
any recognized laws about maritime activity.
    Therefore, it seems necessary to investigate the nature of the maritime raids in the Aegean Sea and whether
these raids can be classified as piracy or be included in the scope of war, as it is undeniable that every war has an
economic-pillaging dimension, both in terms of motives (i.e., to boost the economy of a community or a group)
and in terms of results, as it is customary for the victors to pillage the losers. The boundaries bet

that the raids carried
out were organized and systematic and aimed at permanent results, such as the annexation of a territory or the
destruction of an economic rival. On the contrary, it is more likely that they were of small scale, carried out on
an occasional and perhaps opportunistic basis and were primarily motivated by the economic benefit of those
taking part in them. Therefore, and despite the aforementioned difficulties in distinguishing between piracy and
warfare, maritime raids in the EBA Cyclades seem to have been much closer to the characteristics of the former
than the latter.
     It should be also noted that the motive for a pirate raid may not have been only economic but also socio-po-
litical. The leaders of a community, by conducting a raid and risking themselves because of their participation
in such a dangerous action, which brought benefits to all community members, gained prestige and confirmed
and legitimized their social status within their own community. Considering the means of the period, the EBA
sea voyages were in themselves “heroic” acts, as one had to face the dangers caused by both sea and weather
conditions during travel and the resistance of the people under attack; an act could be even more “heroic”, when
the participants fought and the raiders returned with booty for the community.

intensification is unlikely to be coincidental. During this period, the need for the construction of a new light,
maneuverable and fast ship suitable for raids seems to have arisen. In diachronic perspective, speed and maneu-
verability are the essential features of all pirate ships (e.g., see Nakas, this volume about the pirate ships in the
Classical and Hellenistic periods).
MOTIVES FOR PIRACY

Since conditions and ships appropriate for pirate raids existed during the EBA, the question of the motives
for these raids inevitably arises. According to anthropological studies (e.g., Torres-Rouff and Costa Junqueira
2006, 60; Erdal and Erdal 2012, 78), social stress, resource constraints, and ecological problems (for example,
droughts and population decline), may lead to violent behavior such as raiding and looting. In the case of piracy
in the EBA Aegean, on which this paper is focused, the most obvious motive was the acquisition of valuable
objects and raw materials and as has already been mentioned, the enhanced social status of those who brought
them through such a “heroic” act. However, equally (or even more) valuable spoils may have been animals and
people, as they were necessary for the survival of a community, the former as a means of food and production,
the latter as a means of strengthening the human resource and reproduction through exogamy (Broodbank
2000, 86; Sherratt 2000, 135).
    In one of the rock-engravings from the Korphi t’Aroniou, for which it has been suggested that they date back
to the end of EC II or the beginning of EC III, an armed man leading an animal in a boat is depicted (Doumas
1965, 48–50; Fig. 1). Animals in ships are also represented in rock-engravings at Strophilas on Andros, which
date to the FN period (Televantou 2008, 47; 2009, 128; Fig. 2). These depictions are usually interpreted as the
movement of animals to smaller islands for grazing and/or breeding (Broodbank 1989, 332–33; 2000, 127–28;
see also Cherry 1985, 20), a practice still in use today in the Aegean (e.g., Chaniotis 1999, 191; Marketou 2023,
45).
     However, it should not be omitted that animals have always been included in pirate spoils and generally
bandit raids. At least in the case of the rock-engraving of Korphi t’Aroniou, the animal snatching seems to be
the most convincing interpretation (Sherratt 2000, 135), firstly because the man who leads the animal to the
ship is armed, which could be interpreted as either defensive or offensive, and secondly because the above
practice confirms martial skills and brings social prestige, especially in societies that are accustomed to robbery
and piracy. Such scenes could therefore be depicted as a reminder of heroic achievements, like later hunting
scenes. The movement of flocks for grazing and/or breeding is an undeniable practice, but it is part of everyday
­activities, which are essential and necessary for survival, but do not carry the same social prestige and therefore
 are less frequently depicted.
    Similarly, it should be considered that over time the most valuable pirate booty might have been people. The
history of piracy reveals that the most common motives for the capture of persons were in obtaining ransom for
their release and enslavement for exploitation or sale. These two motives are extremely difficult to decipher in
the ΕΒΑ Cyclades, but the possibility of the abduction of women for reproduction cannot be excluded (Sherratt

2000, 135–36).
    The population decline was one of the most serious problems faced by EC communities, which, among
other causes, could have been attributed to infertility and the unequal ratio between men and women. To
address this, the movement of people (especially women) between communities or even between islands was
crucial, as healthy descendants were ensured by exogamy. It is reasonable to assume that exogamy was generally
consensual, by mutual agreement between families or communities. However, the forcible abduction of women
also seems possible, especially given the “heroic” context in which such actions are carried out by societies that
often accept and undertake robbery and piracy. Thus, the abduction of women may have increased significantly
in times of crisis, when the population was dramatically reduced (e.g., due to a shipwreck or disease), so that
the forcible transportation of women from another region or island for procreation was one of the few available
options for community survival.
    The potentially important role of the abduction of women and animals in the ΕΒΑ Cyclades is further
strengthened by ethnographic parallels from societies with weak or absent major state organizations and high
mortality due to wars or ways of life, in which such practices were commonplace. For example, at least in the
13th century CE, in the Chaco Canyon region of the United States, raiding for women for reproductive or labor
reasons was a well-established practice, and successful warriors were associated with polygyny (Kohler and

Relationships between sea voyages, trade, and women, as well as manifestations of violence, may be
­suggested by the deliberate breakage of folded-arms female figurines in the Kavos “special deposit” on Keros

  breakage, most scholars attribute this breakage to ritual practices that took place in a funerary or religious
  context (e.g., Doumas 1972, 163; Davis 1984, 16; Renfrew 1984, 27–8; Barber 1987, 132; Sotirakopoulou 2005,
  329–30). If this is the case, the quantity of the figurines, the way they were handled, and the fact that only frag-
  ments of the abdomen, vulva and legs have been found in the depository may shed light on the way women were
  treated in religion and, by extension, in EBA society.
    The role of men and women in the ΕΒΑ society and economy, as reflected in the aforementioned aspects of
material culture, namely in the anthropomorphic figurines, the frying pans, the general presence of weapons,
and the way of using the above objects, as well as the importance and the “heroic” character of sea voyages for
island communities, suggest that exogamy and the acquisition of objects, raw materials, and animals were of
vital importance and that in order for community survival and growth everything was legitimate. In the context
of raids, therefore, woman and animal abductions were probably a common practice, and constituted a major
source of social power and prestige for the warriors-pirates who provided them to the community.

Major changes in the settlement patterns and the ways of living are usually considered to be a result of the
­emergence of new needs and demands. In this regard, the abandonment of coastal sites and the move to fortified
 sites away from the sea are often attributed to threats and invasions from the sea. Therefore, a brief synopsis of
 the settlement patterns of the EΒΑ Cyclades and the identification of such changes may be able to contribute
 to the debate on the phenomenon of piracy during this period (see Angelopoulou, this volume for a more
 ­comprehensive discussion on the EC settlement patterns).
     The EC I settlements appear to be scattered and short-lived (Broodbank 2000, 150–51, 154–56; ­Angelopoulou
2016–2017, 134). They were small settlements, based mainly on the agricultural economy, while their external
contacts were limited. The settlements of the EC IIA period were also small in size and duration, with a few
­exceptions of larger and more organized settlements, such as Ayia Irini on Kea (Caskey 1971, 368–72; B­ roodbank
 2000, 216–18; see also Wilson 1999, 2013), Dhaskalio on Keros (Boyd 2013, Renfrew 2013), and Skarkos on Ios
 (Marthari 1997, 2008a, 2018). The settlements of this period were mainly coastal or near the sea and at nodal
 points of sea routes, indicating the interest of their inhabitants in sea voyages. There seems to have been some
 concern for protection from sea raids, by choosing either defensible sites, as in the case of Dhaskalio, or sites
 at a short distance from the sea, as at Skarkos (Broodbank 2000, 212–21; Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 134–35).
      An even stronger concern for protection from the sea emerged in the following EC IIB period. Several
­settlements were now situated on defensible hilltops, and many of them were reinforced by strong fortification
 walls. For example, settlements like Kastri on Syros (Marthari 1998, 2017), Panormos on Naxos (Angelopoulou
 2014, 67–88), Kynthos on Delos (MacGillivray 1980) and Markiani on Amorgos (Marangou 2006, 81–93)
 ­indicate feelings of danger and insecurity. Kastri and Panormos were indeed destroyed and then abandoned,
  probably after a maritime raid. This change in the settlement pattern from sites near the sea to defensible sites on
  high and steep hills and with strong fortification walls, combined with the evidence of attack, destruction and
  abandonment observed in at least two settlements, are indications of the fear during this period and the violent
  raids that seem to have come from the sea.
SETTLEMENTS WITH POSSIBLE PIRATE ACTIVITY

In order to be able to recognize that a small or large part of the community of a settlement was involved (­ either
occasionally or systematically) in pirate activity, this settlement should present some or all the features identified
by the A.P.Pir.A. project: coastal and defensible sites, not easily visible but close to at least one safe harbor, nodal
point for the nearby sea routes, fortification walls, etc. (see in more detail Samaras, this volume). ­Moreover, in
settlements of this type, valuable and exotic objects are often found, the presence of which is sometimes not
adequately explained by other “legal” activities (see also Samaras 2015, 191–92).
    Settlements in naturally defensible sites, close to the sea, and with strong fortification walls have already
been witnessed in the FN period and the EBA I, as can be seen at Strophilas on Andros (Televantou 2006, 2008,
2018a) and Vathy on Astypalaia (Vlachopoulos and Angelopoulou 2019; Vlachopoulos 2021). As mentioned
above, ship rock-engravings have been found at both these sites, some of which even decorate the main gates
of the fortified settlements. It is noteworthy that in Strophilas there are over a hundred rock-engravings with
this theme, making the ship a symbol of the community and revealing its naval orientation. Several metal
objects have also been found in the same settlement, including a metal spearhead, while in Vathy there are
rock-­engravings of a unique theme with daggers, symbols of bravery and heroism indicating violent actions.
Considering that material culture is a powerful means of social display, it may be possible to accept the view that
ships transmitted messages of collective power and weapons that of individual power.

The natural defense of the site was further reinforced by the construction of a complex fortification system, in

at the site, which are prestige objects because of the raw material used in their manufacture, especially tin, which
is imported from the east. A metalworking workshop has also been found within the fortified settlement.

Also, in periods of intensive large-scale contacts and without the existence of a strong central power, as is the
case of the EBA Aegean (see also Driessen, this volume), it is almost unlikely that raids for quick and immediate
profit would not take place. More generally, most island communities were able to practice piracy, some more
and some less, and probably did so alongside other activities.

In summary, it seems quite likely that in the context of the EBA sea voyages, not only trade was practiced, but
also piracy. The frequency of this phenomenon cannot be determined, but there are other aspects that can be
understood with greater certainty. During the period under discussion, and especially in EBA II, there were
both the appropriate means (i.e., ships suitable for raiding) and strong motives, sometimes even linked to sur-
vival. At the same time, the absence of a central power created ideal conditions for piracy to flourish. Indeed,
it seems that in prehistory such acts did not carry the negative connotations that are attached to it today, as the
legality or the illegality of an action was not perceived in the same way. On the contrary, a daring and dangerous
action may have been considered an act of bravery and glory.
    Therefore, the motivation for piracy was not only driven by material factors, which would ensure survival
and/or the acquisition of wealth. Participation in risky activities, such as sea voyages and piracy, increased
the reputation and power of those who took part in them. It proved their martial and naval prowess and thus
gained the respect of the whole community. Through the possession of valuable objects and people it ensured
the ­perpetuation of future generations and the community, the warrior-pirates also demonstrated their power
and thus strengthened their social status and legitimized their authority.
     The evidence in the material culture may be indirect but, complementary to the possible perceptions of
the period, seems to suggest that piracy may have been practiced in the EBA Aegean by the same people who
­participated in maritime trade. It is very likely that the traders of the EBA were at the same time warriors, pirates
 and hunters, charged with the duty of providing their community with essential goods, animals and women,
 either through exchanges or through raids. In general, the trap of interpreting all relevant finds as the result
 of trading activities should be avoided, especially in periods with no written sources, such as the EBA. On the
 contrary, the strong possibility that a greater or lesser part of the maritime traffic of people and goods is due to
 piracy should always remain open.

 The Art of War in Prehistoric Aegean
Early Cycladic Fortified Citadels and Weapons

The development of habitation in the Cyclades during the Early Bronze Age (3rd millennium BCΕ) is little known,
as a result of the limited number of investigated Early Cycladic settlements. The proliferation of fortified sites and the
development of weaponry imply an increased interest in defense during the Early Cycladic II period (middle of the 3rd
millennium BCΕ). The establishment and the violent abandonment, following war-like conflict, of the fortified citadels at
Kastri on Syros and Korphari ton Amygdalion on Naxos (2500–2300/2200 BCΕ), are considered signs of the arrival of
new populations that marked an era of crisis and intense competition in the islands.
The aim of this paper is to evaluate the significance of both fortifications and weaponry for the evolution of the Cycladic
civilization. The war conflicts associated with the phenomenon of piracy are not a symptom of an era of cultural decline
and regression. Hostility intensified in a period of prosperity as this is reflected in settlement patterns, demography,
economy, society, and last but not least in the expanded cultural contacts in the Aegean during the Early Bronze Age. The
Early Cycladic fortified citadels are outstanding examples of collective work – a milestone in the evolution from small
farming communities to large “urban” ones.

 circulation of goods among the aforementioned areas. In addition, the architecture of some contemporary coastal settle-
 ments, and particularly the presence of fortifications together with iconographic evidence indicate other-than-peaceful
 contacts as well. From this point up to the identification of piratical activity, however, lies a considerable distance. This
 paper examines this distance through different types of archaeological evidence. After outlining the major maritime net-
 works in the Aegean of the Middle and early Late Bronze Age, the present work discusses material evidence and several
 case studies that have been interpreted as indicative for piratical activity, and which thus afford the evaluation of the
 phenomenon of piracy in the area and era under consideration.

According to the definition that was introduced and adopted by the A.P.Pir.A. project, the term piracy refers
to the seaborne robbery through some sort of ship, and also to the looting of a sunk ship even if this activity
is taking place directly from the coast, both motivated by personal profit (Samaras, this volume). This paper
is a brief review of the case studies associated with piracy in the Aegean of the Middle Bronze Age (MBA)
and the early Late Bronze Age (LBA), the Old and the New Palace period, and, also, the Final Palatial period,
in Cretan or Minoan terminology. The challenge of exploring a series of case studies with the corresponding
evidence is developed in three parts. The former roughly presents the context of maritime communications,
the major sea routes and the dominant networks in the area and era under study. The second part reviews the
actual case studies that have been interpreted as indicative for piratical activity by previous research – each one
is established on a different sort of evidence, so that they provide the opportunity not only for an up-to-date
consideration, but also for an evaluation. This is the subject of the final part, which explores in detail the best
documented case study for identifying piracy, in order to conclude with a reassessment on piracy in the MBA
and early LBA Aegean.

Attarissiya’s involvement in the raid against Alashiya is therefore considered a piratical action (Cesarano 2008,
41–5, 93) and deserves further exploration, even if its identification required the spatial expansion of the r­ esearch
area, in order to include Cyprus, and it further occurs in the expiration of the period under ­consideration.
­However, it is argued below that the main significance of the text for the assessing piracy in the early LBA
 ­Aegean lies not that much in Attarissiya’s involvement to the raid that caused the indictment of Madduwatta, as
  to that of the latter person. Moreover, that the evidence that derives from the reviewed text should be considered
  rather as analogical instead of direct.
     First of all, it is safe to argue that the accusation by the Hittite king against Madduwatta for raiding Alashiya
is established on two arguments. The former considers the claim that Alashiya was under Hittite control –
­although this was possibly not the actual case according to Beckman (et al. 2011, 99); the latter that Madduwatta
 was a client ruler and thus a vassal to the Hittite king. The very combination of these aspects renders the raid

    The difficulty of distinguishing between war and piracy has already been noted and previous considerations
on piracy in the Bronze Age Mediterranean in general and the Aegean specifically did not proven particularly
fruitful. Baruffi (1998, 10) argued that, although “coastal raiding and piracy were also significant factors during
the Bronze Age, as they have been during sporadic periods in the Mediterranean ever since. […] war and piracy
were so closely linked that it was not always clear when an enemy action was to be treated as one or the other”.
In the same vein, for the Aegean and for the periods before the composition of the Homeric poems and that of
the poems themselves, de Souza (1999, 18) argued that “piracy is so closely related to warfare in both aims and
methods that they are virtually undistinguishable” (see also de Souza 1999, 16, 21). This a

     Although the archaeological record of the MBA and the early LBA Aegean lacks such solid evidence
and in order to retrieve it we had to turn eastwards, the field of the relationships is at least promising for the
­consideration of piracy. Here too, one or more dominant powers established special relations with a series of

 discussed. It is therefore argued that the secure identification of piratical activity can be attempted through the
 reconstruction of relations among sites and, if possible, among individuals as well, while, if this consideration
 demonstrates the limitations of the archaeological record, then the sequel of the A.P.Pir.A. project might be
 developed as an interdisciplinary one.

In the previous parts of this paper and following a brief presentation of the context of maritime contacts and
networks in the MBA and early LBA Aegean, a series of case studies for piratical activity was critically discussed.
It was argued that archaeological evidence previously interpreted as indicating piratical activity in the study area
and era should be reconsidered. In the case of architecture, that the fortifications of Kolonna, even if combined
with early ship representations, are currently understood in association to the site’s outstanding role in the
Aegean of the Old Palace period, where evidently the maritime element is for the first time in the period under

consideration associated with the martial one. In the case of the iconography of the period of the New Palaces, it
was argued that, although it reproduces seaborne raiding events, the latter possibly indicate activities other than

and early LBA Aegean might similarly require the consideration and the reconstruction of relationships among

Piracy is a varied and adaptable phenomenon, which according to the circumstances appears in different forms
regarding its intensity and range, or the motives, organization and origin of those actively involved (see e.g.,
Bevan and Conolly 2013, 187–89). Geography defines the coastal zones and islandscapes best suited to pi-
racy (Hitchcock and Maeir 2018, 4–5), but does not predetermine the role(s) of their inhabitants (Bevan and
Conolly 2013, 193–95). Thus, the same regions may alternately constitute pirate nurseries or the preferential
targets of sea-raids. For example, the flourishing of the small and rocky island of Antikythera in the Hellenistic
period was largely because it became a pirate base (Bevan and Conolly 2013, 189–92). Conversely, this strate-
gically placed island witnessed successive episodes of abandonment from the 7th century CE onwards; these
coincide with periods of insecurity at seas, which suggests that the inhabitants became the victims of pirate

attacks instead of being the perpetrators of such acts (see Bevan and Conolly 2013, 192). Regarding Crete,
 in the ­Hellenistic period piracy may have contributed significantly to the economy and wider importance of
 many of its ­poleis. ­Accordingly, after the Arab conquest in the early 9th century CE, the fleets setting sail from
 Crete ­devastated the coastal regions and islands of the East Roman Empire (Christides 1981; 1984, 162–63,
 165–67, 192; ­Yannopoulos 2011, 163), so much so that it was called θεόλεστος Κρήτη (“goddamned Crete”)
 by ­Constantinus P ­ orphyrogenitus (1830, 651.15). In the 13th/12th centuries BCE, though, Crete was in the
­opposite position.
    The progressive decline of the main ports and the abandonment of the coastal areas in LM IIIB suggest that
Crete became the target of systematic attacks from the sea – a situation that apparently continued in LM IIIC.
The causes of these developments, all the more so their precocious appearance in relation to the rest of the Ae-
gean, may lie in the lack of strong polities on the island during the later part of the 13th century BCE – if not
much earlier at certain regions. The geographical position of Crete at the crossroads of the sea routes that joined
the Aegean with the central and eastern Mediterranean would have also contributed to the frequency and scale
of the depredations; if nothing else, these routes were also used by the mercenaries who offered their services to
the states of both the Aegean and the east Mediterranean – groups that would have been prone to turn to piracy
and freebooting when in need or enabled by the circumstances (Samaras 2015, 192; Jung 2018, 285–86; Maran
2022, 240–41). Having frequented Crete and being aware of its riches and internal political situation, such bands
may have chosen the island as a target of their raids and a base for further attacks – and this may have occurred
on an even larger scale in the context of the displacements caused by the 1200 BCE collapse. In this regard, if
the hypothesis of a pirate base on Dia, right in front of the port of Knossos, is indeed true, this would signify a
reality radically different from that of the “Minoan Thalassocracy” of the Neopalatial period: instead of domi-
nating the seas, the inhabitants of once mighty Knossos were under the threat of a θεόλεστος Δία.

The heyday of the Mycenaean palaces coincides with a period when international trade and overseas voyages increased,
due to the complex and centralized administrations that encouraged such actions. The Mycenaean palaces were part of an
international network linking Mediterranean elites, although there are lacunae concerning the agents who e­ ngaged in those
actions, their social identity, and the variety of seafaring activities that they could accomplish with their ­contemporary
technological means. The social background of the Mycenaean seafarer seemingly matches that of the palatial elite as the
prime agent of such actions, since the latter had the resources but also the motivation, which was the acquisition of exotic
goods, a common practice for the rulers of the Late Bronze Age. The need to obtain valuable resources may not have been
limited to peaceful means, like trade and gift exchange, but it could have involved violence, warfare, pillaging and piracy.
The main purpose of this paper is to try to approach seafarers and their affiliations, i.e., the palatial and non-palatial
agents. The difficulty in distinguishing between the last two intensifies even more when the line between warfare (which
would have been characteristic of the Mycenaean administration center) and actions related to piracy is blurred.

sectors could have overlapped (de Fidio 2001, 22–3).
    To study and understand the characteristics of the Mycenaean seafarers, we would need to utilize every piece
of evidence we have at our disposal. Detailed analyses have been conducted regarding maritime affairs by the
examination of contemporary iconography and written sources (Wachsmann 1981, 1995, 1998; Wedde 1999,
2001, 2005, 2006; Emanuel 2014, 2017, 2021), which we can utilize to investigate the people behind them. The
aim of this paper would not be to categorize certain groups rigidly as traders, mercenaries, pirates or military
personnel, but to assess the “fluidity” of their positions, as they could have been able to attain a variety of roles
(either overlapping or not mutually exclusive), depending on the circumstances and their needs.

The purpose of this paper has been to discuss some critical aspects of the identity and status of the people who
were crossing the Aegean during the LBA. Nevertheless, as shown by the discussion above, the evidence does
not point to a unique direction. On the contrary, the more we focus on these activities, the more we under-
stand that the sea was not only a place where ships sailed and goods moved through. Groups originating from
different backgrounds were able to sail the seas, each one of them bearing different agendas. The lack of total
control of the sea routes allowed those groups to accomplish various feats and assume multiple roles, potentially
interchangeably. Traders, mercenaries, warriors and pirates were able to interact with palatial and non-palatial
agents depending on the circumstances and the needs of each group.
     Detailed archaeological research and analytical studies of various categories of evidence (e.g., textual,
­iconographical) may enable us to identify certain factors, activities and networks that did affect or were affected
 by long-distance sea travel. The LBA seafarers were not necessarily representatives of their cultures, but they
 inevitably connected them through their own mobility, ideas and objects that moved with those groups.

 Seeking Timber in the Pirates’ Lairs
The New Approach to Wenamun’s Report

The Egyptians used cedar wood for the construction of both the sacred barks and the ships sailing in the ­Mediterranean
and the Red Sea. However, the lack of cedar and timber suitable for shipbuilding in general led Egypt to seek various ways
of securing the required quantity of wood. This is precisely the reason for the journey of the Egyptian priest Wenamun,
who was sent by the High Priest of Amun at Thebes to the Phoenician city of Byblos to procure the ­necessary cedar wood to
build the sacred bark of the god. During this journey, Wenamun was led into an action that could be described as piracy.
The present paper attempts to show whether the text with Wenamun’s adventures is a historical narrative, which offers
valuable information about the political, social and economic developments that took place in the eastern Mediterranean
during the end of the Late Bronze Age and the beginning of the Early Iron Age. It also attempts to identify the political,
economic and even psychological factors that contributed to Wenamun’s action of attacking a ship on the high seas and
stealing its silver. The main aim of examining this evidence is to determine whether Wenamun became, even temporarily,
a pirate.

At the end of the Late Bronze Age (LBA) in the Levant, powerful empires, such as those of the Egyptians and
Hittites, coexisted with small kingdoms, which were mostly subordinate to some of the powers of the time.
Egypt succeeded in consolidating its position in the region. The construction of Egyptian temples in Byblos
and Egyptian-style fortresses in the Levant area, as well as the installation of an Egyptian governor in Byblos,
confirm that Egypt tried in every way to secure its interests and procure the necessary supplies (Stein 2017, 17).
    This situation was maintained until the 19th Dynasty (Sherratt 2003, 49–51), but changed significantly after
the fall of the Hittite empire and the gradual weakening of Egypt in the early 12th century BCE. The new sit-
uation in the Levant is reflected in an 11th century BCE text, the story of Wenamun. The eponymous hero of
the story, whose name is transcribed as WN-Imn, traveled to Byblos to obtain the necessary timber to build the
sacred bark of Amun. This paper discusses the historicity of Wenamun’s narrative and examines the depiction
of piracy as per this text. To approach these issues, it is necessary to re-examine the text in direct relation to the
social and political conditions developed in the eastern Mediterranean during the period of its composition, i.e.,
at the beginning of the 11th century BCE.

EGYPTIAN OFFICIAL OR PIRATE?

Wenamun’s decision to rob a Tjeker ship reminds many of an act of piracy. The term piracy first appears in an
Attic inscription of the mid-3rd century BCE from Rhamnous (de Souza 1999, 3–4). However, it can be argued
that the concept of piracy predates the appearance of the term. For example, the term bandits was used by
Homer (ληϊστῆρες, e.g., Od. 3.73, 17.425) and Thucydides (λῃσταὶ, e.g., 1.8.1, 6.4.5) to refer to robbers of the
sea, i.e., pirates (LSJ, s.v. λῃστεία). In the eastern Mediterranean texts, there are several references to acts that
could be characterized as piratical (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 81–8; Sandars 1985; Derks 2016, 17–9; Hitchcock and
Maeir 2016; Kopanias 2019; contra de Souza 1999, 16–17). The Amarna letters reflect the insecurity existing at
sea and the danger faced by coastal areas, which were often attacked by groups, whose main objective was to
secure loot (EA 38; Μoran 1992, 111–12). At the same time, many inscriptions that accompany the reliefs with
the achievements of the Pharaohs point out the naval battles they fought to repel enemies attacking Egypt by
sea, with a typical example being the naval battle of Ramses III at Medinet Habu (Emanuel 2017, 63–70; Kopa-
nias 2021, 257–58; Fig. 2).
     Before proceeding with the characterization of Wenamun as a pirate or not, it is necessary to clearly d

the context within which an act can be considered as piracy. The general observation that in war armies meet
and face each other on land or sea seems rather simplistic (Emanuel 2017, 33). Shelley Wachsmann (1998,
317–21), on the other hand, considers that in war there is involvement of the participating state with its troops
and vessels, which does not happen in the case of piracy (see also Emanuel 2017, 33–5). Philip de Souza (1999,
1), referring to the piracy of Graeco-Roman times, has characterized the pirates as “armed robbers whose
­activities normally involve the use of ships”. In the story of Wenamun, there is no involvement of any state
 power. Wenamun acted alone, made a decision by himself and put it into effect immediately, without waiting
 for approval of an official state authority. In Egypt, no one knew anything about the unexpected turn of events
 that took place at Dor and then off Tyre. Wenamun neither reported anything back to his superiors, nor asked
 for their guidance about what course of action he should follow. His action was financially motivated and done
 for personal gain; he had to complete his mission and return to Egypt with the required amount of cedar.
    The question inevitably arises, whether Wenamun could be classified as a pirate. It is a fact that, based on the
modern perception of pirates, as it began to take shape in recent times, i.e., after the so-called “Golden Age of
piracy” (late 17th – early 18th century CE), pirates are described as dangerous, marginalized groups, who plied
the seas with the aim of plundering territories, killing, capturing inhabitants in order to sell them as slaves or
to receive ransom for their release. For example, such an image of pirates is captured in The Travels of Reverend
Ólafur Egilsson, a 17th-century text describing the raid of pirates from Salé and Algiers on Iceland (Hreinsson
and Nichols 2008).
   At the end of the LBA and the beginning of the Early Iron Age (EIA), however, the identity of the pirate does
not seem to correspond to the one of a marginalized person, as it emerges from history and literature of the Early
Modern and Modern periods. The environment in which the sailor, the merchant, the seafarer moves is fluid
and full of multiple and unexpected risks. This element of the variability of conditions in the marine environ-
ment influenced and ultimately shaped trade relations and exchanges (Monroe 2011, 95). In this ever-changing
