This new elite, members of which participated in the commercial networks controlled by the palaces in the
previous period, was now actively involved in trade but for their own benefit. Their involvement was achieved
either through trade (by controlling the already existing trade routes and markets) or through piracy. Therefore,
piracy should be understood as an “irregular, typically hostile, ongoing economic activity carried out for per-
sonal benefit and involving the use of ships, maritime mobility and plundering, at sea and along coastal areas”
(Knapp 2018, 36). The pirate was not necessarily an adventurer, a bandit, but could be a ship owner, a merchant
or even a government official, like Wenamun, who plundered when that was deemed necessary (Knapp 2020,
155).
     Therefore, what needs to be taken into consideration is under which circumstances a person can become a
pirate. In the Odyssey (14.191–359), the king of Ithaca, transformed into a beggar by Athena, tells Eumaeus a
fake story, as he presents himself as the son of Castor from Crete. He recounts that, just a month after his return
from the ten-year war in Troy, he sought new adventures; thus he and his companions went to Egypt for raiding.
However, this expedition did not have a positive outcome, because of a factor pointed out by the narrator
himself, which is directly related to human nature: “But my comrades, yielding to wantonness, and led on by
their own might” (Od. 14.262, trans. A. T. Murray, Cambridge, Mass., 1919). Namely, arrogance led O      ­ dysseus’
companions to raid the fields, to enslave young children and women, and to kill unsuspecting farmers and
­fishermen, until Pharaoh sent an army to confront the invaders.
     Wenamun’s transformation from the Elder of the Portal of the Temple of Amun to a pirate cannot be
­attributed to arrogance but to necessity that prompts him to such an act. The purpose of his journey was to
 secure the timber needed to build god’s great noble bark. His mission was going smoothly until he himself be-
 came the victim of a robbery. Wenamun’s decision to take a piratical action was not chosen from the beginning.
 At first, he appealed to the commander of Dor to help him find the amount that had been stolen from him,
 but Beder (or Bederi) refused to get involved, as the robbery had not been committed by any of his citizens.
 Without the help of any official authority, he decided to solve his problem by himself resorting to piracy, which
 was financially motivated and done for Wenamun’s own benefit. A possible failure would damage his prestige
 and it was highly likely he would be accused of very significant crimes. On the contrary, successful completion
 of his mission would further consolidate his position.
       For a better understanding of his act, some other factors must be taken into account. The text of
Wenamun dates to the 11th century BCE and captures the new political situation that has been formed in the
­Mediterranean. Cyprian Broodbank (2013, 394) has characterized the Mediterranean as “a

The text of Wenamun’s adventures has caused several disputes among scholars as to its historicity. There were
many who questioned the historical basis of the text, considering it to be a literary narrative with elements of
verisimilitude. However, the re-examination of the text that was attempted showed that the evidence presented
is confirmed by both the archaeological findings and the written sources from the eastern Mediterranean at the
end of the LBA and at the beginning of the EIA. The purpose of Wenamun’s journey, namely to procure cedar
from Byblos, is not a product of fiction, but seems to correspond to historical reality as Egypt did not have cedar
wood, which was necessary for shipbuilding. Also, the course followed by the Egyptian official is as expected as
the sea currents that sail in the area favor navigation. Furthermore, the mention of specific coastal cities, such
as Dor, Tyre and Byblos, confirms the historical core of the text, since they have been proven to have had a port
and port facilities and participated in the international trade network that had been formed at the beginning of
the 11th century BCE.
    At the same time, the narrative seems to reflect the political and social situation that had developed on the
shores of the Levant after the fall of the Hittite empire and the weakening of Egypt. The autonomy and power
the coastal cities in the aforementioned region had gained, affected the way that trade was as of then conducted
for Egypt, and more specifically the cedar trade. Byblos was no longer a vassal to Egypt; instead it was its ruler
who managed the cedar trade. This new reality turned Wenamun from a Priest of god Amun to a pirate in order
to complete his mission. The hero’s decision to attack and rob the Tjeker ship was a conscious action on his
part. It constituted a solution, undoubtedly unorthodox, but acceptable, which could be applied whenever the
circumstances dictated.

This paper investigates piracy in the Aegean during the Early Iron Age (late 11th–late 8th/early 7th century BCE), a
phenomenon that remains difficult to trace archaeologically due to the absence of clear diagnostic indicators. It argues
that the ­conditions emerging after the collapse of the Mycenaean palatial system, conditions that continued to shape the
ensuing ­centuries, created an exceptionally favorable environment for the development of piracy. Small, autonomous
communities o­ perated within expanding networks of maritime mobility and exchange, at a time when strong, centralized
mechanisms of ­control were largely absent. The analysis brings together five strands of evidence: maritime connectivity,
fortified island ­settlements, depictions of sea-borne conflict in Geometric pottery, warrior burials and the Homeric epics.
Considered in combination, these elements suggest that piracy was a plausible and often pronounced aspect of Aegean
seafaring during the Early Iron Age.
The paper then re-examines selected categories of evidence, from fortified sites and potential pirate havens to the ­pictorial
pottery of the 8th century BCE, highlighting particularly revealing cases such as the New York krater MMA 34.11.2
and Tomb 79 at Lefkandi. These examples underscore the fluidity of maritime roles in this period: individuals and
­communities could act simultaneously, or alternately, as traders, warriors, sailors or raiders, depending on ­circumstances
 and ­opportunity. Moreover, both Geometric iconography and the Homeric epics appear to draw on contemporary
 ­practices and lived experiences, reflecting forms of maritime violence and raiding that were far from exceptional. Overall,
  the study proposes that piracy should not be viewed as a marginal or occasional occurrence, but as a critical component
  for understanding the social and maritime dynamics of the Early Iron Age Aegean.

The principal challenge in the study of piracy in antiquity lies in developing an interpretive framework capable
of addressing the theoretical and practical problems associated with the phenomenon, while at the same time
foregrounding its significance as a substantive analytical component for understanding the past. Scholars have
long grappled with issues that pose considerable interpretive difficulties, such as the definition of piracy (e.g.,
Ormerod 1924, 60; de Souza 1999, 1; Samaras 2015, 191; Skowronek 2016, 4) or its distinction from warfare
(Samaras 2015, 191; Emanuel 2017, 33–7; 2018, 73–7). Even more demanding (and arguably more intriguing)
is the question of how piracy can be identified and meaningfully interpreted within the archaeological record.
    It is common, not only for antiquity but also for later periods, that the relationship piracy bears to other
activities, as reflected in its material traces, evokes the notion of equifinality, namely “the principle that the past
could have unfolded in a multitude of ways, each of which could have resulted in the same evidence we are

considered, despite the fact that, as will be discussed in greater detail below, the acquisition of wealth through
raiding, whether on land or at sea, was both acceptable and commonplace in the Homeric epics.
    In the case of piracy, the notion of equifinality extends to a range of issues beyond the circulation of goods.
Some of these issues enter the sphere of agency and social identity, such as, for example, the deliberate projection
of identities like those of the warrior, the seafarer or the trader. These identities are closely connected to the
figure of the pirate and may, in certain circumstances, be expressed in the funerary record.
    Regarding the EIA Aegean, which forms the focus of this paper, the well-known difficulties inherent in any
archaeological approach to piracy (see Samaras, this volume) are compounded by the particular challenges of
the period itself. These include the limited number of written sources, the generally reduced archaeological
visibility and the absence of final publications for many sites, all of which restrict the interpretive possibilities
even further. In short, piracy fails to receive adequate attention in the interpretive frameworks applied to the
archaeology of the Aegean during the early historical period, not because the phenomenon was absent, but
because clear answers to the issues outlined above, together with other questions that cannot be addressed here
in detail, remain difficult to obtain.

EARLY IRON AGE AEGEAN: AN IDEAL SETTING FOR PIRACY

Although the identification of piracy in the archaeological record remains a considerable challenge, the broader
conditions of the EIA suggest an environment in which maritime raiding would have been both feasible and
potentially widespread. The relevant data, while falling short of direct proof, collectively form a compelling
contextual basis that alleviates the inherent difficulty of demonstrating piracy beyond doubt. The discussion
that follows draws on five key spheres of evidence: maritime trade, fortified settlements, iconography, warrior
burials and the Homeric epics.

Maritime exchange and connectivity
The underlying conditions of the Aegean from the 12th century BCE onward are shaped by the political and
administrative vacuum created by the collapse of the Mycenaean palatial system. This collapse encouraged the
formation of smaller communities that operated with greater freedom of action in matters of exchange and
resource management (e.g., Eder and Lemos 2020, 136; Maran and Wright 2020, 117–18). Within this setting,
the evidence from Crete, the Dodecanese, the central and northern Aegean and Euboea indicates the existence
of trade relations and interactions among these largely self-governing communities throughout the EIA, ini-
tially within neighboring regions (e.g., Leone 2012; Mazarakis Ainian 2012a; Eder and Lemos 2020, 137–39)
and subsequently across the wider Mediterranean basin (e.g., Stampolidis 2003, 47, 51, 56, 64; Eder and Lemos
2020, 146–47).
    Despite the difficulty of identifying it archaeologically, the positive correlation between piracy and maritime
trade (Samaras 2015, 191; this volume; Hitchcock and Maeir 2016, 249–50; Emanuel 2017, 32–3, 38–9) should
not be overlooked. The ensuing movement of goods in a maritime landscape lacking strong central authority
creates numerous opportunities for predation, arising from the exploitation of vulnerable points along sea trade
routes and their nodes (see also Driessen, this volume).

Fortified settlements
Movement along the sea routes was not dangerous only for seafarers, who risked potential attacks by pirates,
but also for settlements situated on or near the coast. Maritime raids appear to have posed a significant threat
during the EIA, since in certain cases the inhabitants of Aegean islands resorted to labor-intensive responses,
such as the construction of fortifications and the choice of locations that were difficult to reach yet afforded
effective oversight of the sea or else lay far inland (Calligas 1990, 81; Snodgrass 2006, 339). Examples include
Emporio on Chios, Kephala on Skiathos, Zagora and Hypsele on Andros, Xobourgo on Tenos, Ayios Andreas
on Siphnos, Vathy Limenari on Donousa and Vrokastro on Crete (see, for example, Frederiksen 2011, 17–8,
70–3, tables 1–2; Thaler 2020, 396–98; Fig. 1).
    A comparison with mainland Greece is particularly revealing. As observed by Antony Snodgrass (2006,
333), none of the major settlements of the period seems to have possessed a fortification system. The fact that
many of these settlements, such as Athens, Lefkandi and Eretria, lie on or near the coast, could be taken as evi-
dence against the presence of piracy and in favor of safe and unhindered maritime exchange. Yet, the existence
of contemporary fortified sites on the islands weakens such an interpretation. Moreover, even in much later
periods, in which intense trade and pirate activity is firmly attested, such as the Hellenistic times, coastal settle-
ments continued to flourish (Gabrielsen 2001, 220–23).
    During the immediately preceding Postpalatial period (ca. 1200–1050 BCE), the same juxtaposition of
coastal settlements and defensible sites is observed, the latter appearing to have been chosen to guard against
seaborne threats. Several scholars have argued that the coastal sites may reflect communities engaged, among
other activities, in piracy or that the benefits of proximity to key maritime routes outweighed the potential
danger of raids (e.g., Nowicki 2000, 257–63; 2001, 29–30; 2011, 441; Wallace 2006, 636; Kramer-Hajos 2012,
815; Emanuel 2021, 285–87, 309). Nothing prevents such reasoning from being applied to the EIA as well, pro-
viding a plausible account for the coexistence of fortified island settlements and unfortified coastal ones.

(Dakoronia 1990, 1999, 2006) and, after a relatively brief hiatus, reappear in Attic funerary iconography during
the Middle Geometric period (MG, ca. 850–760 BCE; see below).
    Since no significant morphological or constructional differences can be observed in the representations
of ships between the two periods (Dakoronia 1990, 118; Eder and Lemos 2020, 137), it may be argued that
shipbuilding traditions were not entirely abandoned in the transition from the LBA to the EIA. Likewise, there
is evidence that knowledge of established sea routes was not forgotten (Stampolidis 2003, 45; Eder and Lemos
2020, 137, 147). From the perspective of both shipbuilding and seafaring, therefore, the basic conditions for
maritime travel were present from the early phases of the EIA, making the possibility of seaborne raiding and
piracy entirely plausible.
    Scholarly views on the interpretation of Attic Geometric ship scenes vary and are discussed more fully below.
It should nevertheless be stressed at the outset that, as Geoffrey Kirk (1949, 140) observed, it is r­ easonable to as-
sume that vase painters depicted types of ships with which they were at least somewhat familiar. A segment of the
consumers who shaped demand likely also contributed to the establishment of such imagery, perhaps wishing
to associate their own self-perception with these scenes, either because they actually took part in a­ nalogous
activities or because these scenes were associated with the display of a particular status. Even if one accepts the
view advanced by some scholars that these scenes draw on mythological or epic tradition (see Kirk 1949, 146;
Moore 2000, 23), the selection of specific myths at this particular historical moment and for the ­relatively brief
period in which they appear points to an underlying relationship with contemporary social realities.

Expressions of warrior identity
Warrior burials furnished with weapons and grave goods imported from the east or the west attest to a sustained
concern with the display of martial status, a concern that continues into the later stages of the EIA and reflects
clear continuity with Mycenaean practices (Whitley 2002, 227; Lemos 2014, 178–79; Eder and Lemos 2020, 136;
Emanuel 2021, 301). The number of these burials, along with their broad spatial and chronological distribution,
points to a pervasive warrior ethos that occupied a central place in EIA society, where warfare and martial
prowess appear to have commanded considerable prestige (Eder and Lemos 2020, 136).
    This emphasis on the warrior’s identity is particularly significant because it resonates closely with the social
position of the raider, whether operating on land or at sea. The absence of a specific term for “pirate” during
this period (de Souza 1999, 9), together with the lack of a strict conceptual separation between terrestrial and
maritime raiding, effectively situates piracy within a broader spectrum of predatory behavior. For example,
Telemachus’ attitude toward the booty that his father had seized (Od. 1.397–398) and Odysseus’ explicit decla-
ration that he intended to recover the losses inflicted on his oikos by the suitors through acts of plunder (Od.
23.356–358) indicate that such actions were neither prohibited nor unusual for members of the upper social
stratum; if anything, they formed an accepted part of elite conduct (this issue is examined more fully in Samaras
and Gounelas forthcoming).
    When one also considers that these same groups were responsible for most long-distance contacts and trade
activities, and that the roles of trader and pirate often converged (see, for example, the contributions of A. Ladas,
V. Samaras and K. Tsonakas in this volume), it becomes plausible that individuals who embraced raiding on
land could apply similar practices at sea. Their participation in maritime predation may therefore be viewed not
as an aberration but as an extension of attitudes and behaviors embedded in the social and economic strategies
of the period.

Raiding and social norms in the Homeric epics
The reference above to the attitudes of Telemachus and Odysseus toward acts of plunder brings the Homeric
epics into the discussion of the elements that render the EIA Aegean an ideal context for the development of
intensive pirate activity. Although the epics cannot be treated as historical sources in a strict sense, it would be
unwise to disregard them, since they offer valuable insights both generally and, more specifically, regarding
piracy. In the Odyssey in particular, raiding is presented as a recognized practice within Homeric society and
one undertaken by nearly all social groups (Samaras and Gounelas forthcoming). Engagement in such activ-
ities does not attract moral condemnation; rather, it confers social esteem, admiration and material gain, as
clearly illustrated in Odysseus’ narrative to Eumaeus (Od. 14.235–239). The poems also introduce groups who
habitually incline toward piracy, such as the Taphians (Od. 15.425–429, 16.426–430) and the Phoenicians (Od.
15.415–484).
     The characters of the epics transcend simple moral binaries (good versus bad, sanctioned versus ­disapproved,
straightforwardness versus cunning) and are grounded in their society, while simultaneously shaping it through
exemplary models. Indeed, it is no exaggeration to suggest that the Odyssey, through Odysseus’ invented p     ­ ersona
as the son of Castor from Crete and through the figures of the Phoenician traders, offers one of the e­ arliest
­literary representations of the archetypal pirate, complete with the defining traits of mêtis [μῆτις], ­irregular and
 asymmetric action, courage, greed, deception and opportunism.

To conclude this discussion of the context of the EIA Aegean, the factors outlined above (trade, fortified
­settlements, iconography, warrior burials and the Homeric epics) and, importantly, their entanglement in a
 constellation with social, political and economic implications, constitute not merely a well-founded ­hypothesis,
 but a strong basis for accepting the presence of piracy. When the geography of the Aegean and the long-standing
 persistence of piracy until well into later periods are also considered, it becomes especially reasonable to ­consider

ARCHAEOLOGICAL EVIDENCE FOR PIRACY IN THE EARLY IRON AGE
AEGEAN

Settlements, fortifications and potential pirate bases
Recognizing pirate bases: Criteria and limitations
Alexandra Hartnett and Shannon Lee Dawdy (2013, 39) articulate a set of heuristic criteria intended to support
the archaeological identification of piracy, with the aim of stimulating the emergence of a more systematic
analytical field dedicated to the phenomenon. In recognition of the interpretive constraints inherent in such
inquiries, they propose a series of potential diagnostic markers for identifying a settlement as a pirate base
or haven. These markers include the presence of defensive architecture, evidence of destruction or abandon-
ment in settlements, pronounced heterogeneity in the provenance and economic value of artifacts, elevated fre-
quencies of luxury items, weaponry, drinking vessels, and other materially expressive categories (Hartnett and
Dawdy 2013, 41). A comparable logic underlies the criteria advanced by Samaras (2015, 191–92), which have
more recently been formalized by the research team of the A.P.Pir.A. project (see Samaras, this volume). Yet,
as stressed in the introduction to this volume, the construction and deployment of such heuristic frameworks
must be approached with methodological circumspection. Overreliance on these criteria or an inflated sense of
their diagnostic capacity, risks engendering premature or overstated interpretations, an epistemic hazard that
remains central to any attempt to delineate piracy archaeologically.

Vathy Limenari and other possible pirate bases
Vathy Limenari on Donousa is a small, fortified settlement of the MG period with a short lifespan, founded in
the third quarter of the 9th century BCE and abandoned in the early 8th century BCE (Fig. 2). Situated along
the maritime route that links Attica and Euboea with the Dodecanese, Cyprus and the Syro-Phoenician coast,
the site’s ceramic assemblage demonstrates its integration into local seafaring networks, indicating contacts
with both the Cyclades and the Dodecanese. These observations led the excavator, Photeini Zapheiropoulou
(1990, 52), to suggest that the settlement functioned as a trading post. Nevertheless, the limited duration of its
occupation and, above all, the choice of a location seemingly unsuitable for habitation and with a secure yet very
small harbor (rather than, for example, the larger and more convenient bays of the modern port or of Kedros;
Fig. 3) prompted Kåre Fagerström (1988, 72, 147–48) and Vangelis Samaras (2015, 199) to argue that the site
served as a pirate nest.
     The case of Vathy Limenari is particularly significant because dozens of Geometric-period sites exhibit
­similar characteristics, although they have not yet been excavated or studied in comparable depth, making
 secure conclusions difficult to draw. This situation may eventually change with studies emerging from projects
 such as “The Small Cycladic Island Project” (SCIP, see Knodell et al. 2020, Athanasoulis et al. 2021) or from
 more focused regional investigations. For the present, however, the only observation that can safely be made
 concerns their geographical distribution along nodal points of the maritime routes dictated largely by the Ae-
 gean currents (Papageorgiou 2008, 204–9). Some of these sites, being obligatory passages for travelers, are well
 placed to function as trading posts or ports of call, as has been proposed not only for Vathy Limenari but also for
 other settlements such as Zagora on Andros (Cambitoglou et al. 1988, 241), Kephala on Skiathos and additional
 sites situated along the western current linking northern Greece with Euboea (Mazarakis Ainian 2012a, 53–7).

Yet for precisely the same reasons, many of these locations are equally suitable as pirate bases or as points
from which occasional raiding could be launched, particularly those situated at narrow passages created by
islands, capes or strong currents (Hitchcock and Maeir 2016, 255). When favorable geographical conditions for
pirate activity coincide with several of the criteria discussed earlier, certain sites emerge as plausible candidates
for pirate bases.
    One example that might be considered is Kipoula, located on the notorious Cap Grosso at the southern tip
of the western coast of Mesa Mani, on the promontory known in antiquity as Thyrides (Strabo 8.2.2, 8.4.4, 8.5.1;
Pausanias 3.25.9). The site was possibly inhabited in the LBA and certainly from the end of the EIA onward
(Forster and Woodward 1906, 244–45; Waterhouse and Hope Simpson 1961, 123; Cavanagh et al. 1996, 304;
Cartledge 2002, 111, 165). Although Kipoula has not been systematically investigated, its strategic location, the
natural defensibility of the promontory and, above all, its position within a region with a long history of piracy
(Krantonelli 1991, 13–14, 276, 279, 306) might suggest such a function.
    Another compelling case is Choriza on Hydra, located on the island’s northern coast and controlling the
maritime corridor between the Saronic and Argolic Gulfs. Situated on a coastal hill and fortified, the site was oc-
cupied across several phases from the Mycenaean to the Hellenistic period (Xatzimixali 1965, 130; Lolos 2006).
Adonis Kyrou (1990, 137–41; 1996–1997) has in fact advanced strong arguments that Choriza functioned as a
pirate base during the Late Archaic period.

The case of Naoussa Bay on Paros
The bay of Naoussa on northern Paros was of strategic importance in the longue durée for Aegean seafarers and
pirates. Its large size, strategic centrality within the Cyclades and proximity to the routes linking the eastern and
western Aegean made it an especially attractive anchorage (Forsyth 2021, 510–11). Indicative of its suitability for

pirate activity is the marked presence of pirates in the bay during the 16th and 17th centuries ­(Koutzakiotis, this
volume), while it has also been proposed that during the Postpalatial period (ca. 1200–1050 BCE) ­Koukounaries
served, possibly as one among several roles, as a pirate base (Samaras 2015, 195–96).
    During the EIA, the bay exhibits intensive settlement activity, particularly in the Late Geometric (LG, ca.
760–700 BCE) and Early Archaic (7th century BCE) periods. Numerous small sites developed at this time,
many in sheltered or concealed and, in some cases, fortified positions. Among these are (arranged from west
to east) Diakofto, Livadera, ­Koukounaries, ­Sarakinika, the islets of Oikonomou and Filizi, and Kargadoura
(Samaras 2017, 115–30, with further b   ­ ibliography; Fig. 4). Of particular interest is the islet of Filizi, which
possesses a fortification system (Schilardi 1974, 186; 1975a, 209; 1975b, 95–6; 1980, 272) and occupies a nodal
location that links Paros and Naxos as well as the northern and southern Cyclades. Systematic survey under-
taken within the SCIP project confirms the islet’s participation in a network of contacts during the LG and
Archaic periods, involving regions of mainland Greece, the southeastern Aegean, and Cyprus (Knodell et al.
2020; Athanasoulis et al. 2021).
    The EIA sites around the bay of Naoussa share several recurring characteristics: small size, proximity to the
sea and natural defensibility and/or concealment, sometimes enhanced through fortification systems. Although
only Koukounaries has been systematically excavated and the others are known primarily from surface surveys,
initially by Demetrius Schilardi (e.g., 1973, 1975b) and more recently by SCIP (Knodell et al. 2020; Athanasoulis
et al. 2021), these sites are nonetheless of particular importance for the study of piracy in the EIA Aegean. The
combination of an apparent desire for proximity to the sea and a simultaneous concern for protection renders
equally plausible the possibilities of active involvement in piracy, fear of pirate attacks or, perhaps most likely, a
combination of both.

Naval encounters in Geometric iconography
Attic funerary vases and sea-combat scenes
In a period such as the EIA, it is difficult to imagine the absence of ship chases and confrontations occurring
either at sea or on vessels drawn up on the shore. Although this aspect of EIA maritime reality is extremely
challenging to approach archaeologically, the iconography provides several compelling testimonies. Scenes de-
picting clashes on board ships make their first appearance in the MG period and increase markedly in the LG
(Moore 2000, 20). Most of the examples currently available come from the Kerameikos cemetery in Athens and
are found on vessels used as grave markers or as grave goods.
    These ship-combat scenes constitute a particularly intriguing corpus which, in whole or in part, has been
included in studies now considered classic for their contribution to early Attic iconography (e.g., Kirk 1949;
Marwitz 1961; Ahlberg 1971; Grunwald 1983; Moore 2000). The interpretations traditionally proposed link
this iconographic theme either to episodes drawn from epic or mythological narratives, or to the Athenian
­naucraries (for the Athenian naucraries, see Schubert 2008; Figueira 2011), or to the possibility that the de-
 ceased met his death in a naval engagement, or even to the putative emergence of the Athenian navy (these
 views are summarized and discussed by Kirk (1949, 144–45), who supported the latter interpretation; see also
 Moore 2000, 23).
   More recent studies have sought to situate these scenes within the historical context of the Geometric ­period.
Barbara Bohen (2017, 90–5), drawing on Herodotus (5.85.1–87.2), argues that all related examples from the
Kerameikos were prompted by the Athenian defeat at the hands of the Aeginetans and Argives on the island of
Aegina. On the contrary, Samaras (2015, 196–98) maintains that the increasingly frequent appearance of naval
combat imagery in EIA ceramic iconography is connected to a parallel intensification of pirate activity.

Interpreting sea-raiding and maritime violence
The explicit association of these pictorial scenes with piracy is largely absent from scholarly discussions (with
Samaras 2015 appearing to be the sole exception, insofar as can be ascertained). Kirk (1949, 145), however,
briefly invokes the phenomenon when he considers the possibility that they depict “the activities of individual
­trader-privateers” or “the repelling of pirates from the Attic coasts.” He ultimately rejects this view, arguing
 that it is difficult to assume that the attackers (the crew of the ship) could be pirates. His reasoning rests on the
 idea that, since the outcome of the engagements in the relevant examples appears favorable for the attackers,
 they must be the protagonists of the depiction. In other words, he does not consider pirates worthy of being
 represented as victors or as central figures in a visual narrative. He further argues that pirate raids had disap-
 peared by the late 8th century BCE, since the Homeric references to such activities are, in his view, “presumably
 archaizing.”
      Regarding the claim that pirates cannot be the protagonists of pictorial representations, Kirk’s position
r­ eflects a negative attitude toward piracy that need not have applied during the period under discussion. As
 noted above, in the Odyssey raiding, whether on land or at sea, is not consistently construed in negative terms.
 In fact, the moral value attached to raiding varies considerably depending on the circumstances (Samaras and
 Gounelas forthcoming). More than once the heroes appear neutral or even receptive to the practice, as in the
 case of Nestor, who extends hospitality to Telemachus before asking whether he and his companions were
 traders or pirates (Od. 3.71–74; see also van Wees 1992, 214; Jackson 1995, 97; Luraghi 2006, 33). Even more
 strikingly, Odysseus’ self-presentation as the son of Castor from Crete vividly illustrates that a life grounded in
 raids and plunder could confer status, prestige and social acceptance (Od. 14.235–239; Emanuel 2017, 37–8).
    As for the claim that Homer’s references are archaizing, even if one accepts that Odysseus’ narrative or the
episodes involving the Phoenicians and the Taphians (for the Taphian pirates, see Vikatou and Staikou, this
volume) reflect earlier societies, such as those of the Postpalatial, Submycenaean or Protogeometric Aegean, it
remains unclear why those societies should be considered more receptive to piracy than that of the Geometric
period. As already noted, the archaeological evidence, and especially the warrior burials discussed below, in-
dicates that warfare maintained a central role during the EIA (Eder and Lemos 2020, 136). Signs of status and
social position continued to uphold broadly similar values and it is therefore plausible that practices associated
with raiding and theft did not disappear, even if their intensity and frequency may have changed.

The New York krater MMA 34.11.2
Many of the Attic Geometric depictions of warriors and shipboard confrontations are of considerable interest
in the discussion on piracy in the EIA Aegean, although a detailed examination of the entire corpus lies beyond
the scope of this study. The analysis, therefore, focuses primarily on a pedestaled krater in the Metropolitan Mu-
seum of Art (MMA) in New York (object number 34.11.2), which stands as one of the most important examples
for the present inquiry.
   The krater MMA 34.11.2 originates from Attica and undoubtedly comes from a funerary context (Fig. 5).
Although some scholars have proposed an early LG date (e.g., Bohen 2017, 90), the majority place it in the later
phase of MG II, probably toward the end of the first quarter of the 8th century BCE (ca. 780 BCE; see Moore
2000, 13, 18–20). The handle zone consists of a metope-triglyph band decorated with various geometric motifs,
while the central metope on each side portrays a prothesis scene and the handle spandrels contain mourners.
Below this zone runs a frieze in which two warships alternate with two processions of warriors (for detailed
descriptions, see Marwitz 1961, 40–4; Ahlberg 1971, 29–30; Moore 2000, 13–8).
    The frieze can be read as a true narrative showing two successive stages of a single episode (Fig. 6). On Side
A, the opening phase of the encounter is depicted: The fighting takes place on a ship that has been beached, as
indicated by the warrior attempting to board the enemy vessel while threatened by an archer standing on the
prow, where four spears are also shown ready for use. At the stern, a hand-to-hand clash between two warriors

is already underway. Side B illustrates the final moments of the conflict, as the ship appears poised to depart.
The helmsman, presumably having fought earlier alongside his companions, has now taken his position and
the sail has been raised. The spears at the prow have been used and a final skirmish seems to be unfolding on
board, near the stern.
    Two details on Side B are particularly significant for the interpretation of this krater within the context of
piracy. The first concerns the two Dipylon shields resting on the deck on either side of the sail. According to
Christiane Grunwald (1983, 181), these shields were placed there for use by the crew, much like the spears on
Side A. Yet if the frieze is read narratively, with Side A preceding Side B, this interpretation becomes difficult to
sustain, since the fighting is already concluding and the shields would almost certainly have been employed. A
more convincing view is that the shields represent part of the booty seized by the ship’s crew (Ahlberg 1971, 29;
Moore 2000, 24).
 P. G O U N E L A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                          · 167 ·

the crew as pirates is quite plausible: Having beached their vessel, they conducted a raid and were then counter-
attacked by their victims. Such an interpretation accounts coherently for both the sequential stages shown on
the two sides of the krater and the presence of the fettered woman, positioned between the two Dipylon shields,
which likewise appear to represent spoils.
    Interpreting the scene as a pirate raid strongly recalls the initially successful attack by Odysseus and his
companions in the land of the Cicones, after which the Cicones regrouped and launched a counterattack. This
resulted in a fierce battle at the Achaeans’ ships, during which the latter were defeated, many of their men died
and the survivors barely escaped (Od. 9.39–52). In that same episode, it is explicitly stated that the Achaeans
seized women as part of their booty (Od. 9.41) and in several other raiding narratives in the Homeric poems
women likewise appear among the spoils (e.g., Od. 14.264; 15.425–429). The seizure of women, which likely
occurs already in the Early Bronze Age (Giagkoudaki, this volume), was among the principal motives for pirate
raids across the Aegean; the EIA would hardly have been an exception.
    The New York krater is not the only vessel depicting combat on a ship grounded along the shore (see, for
example, the Copenhagen oinochoe 1628 (Kirk 1949, 111; Ahlberg 1971, 29–31; Coldstream 2008, 76–7, with
further bibliography)), yet it is perhaps one of the most instructive examples for the study of EIA piracy. While
the possibility cannot be excluded that shipborne attacks and ensuing clashes belonged to military operations
with political or strategic aims, it appears increasingly likely that the relevant Geometric iconography is more
closely connected with piracy than previous discussions have generally allowed.

Warrior burials and maritime identities
Warfare, status and the possibility of piracy
Warrior burials have been found across numerous regions throughout the EIA. Their defining feature is the
presence of weapons, although the wealth and range of grave goods, as well as the type and combination of
weapons, vary according to period and area. Scholars generally interpret weapons in funerary contexts as indi-
cators of prestige that affirm the elevated social status of the deceased (e.g., Whitley 2002, 227; Emanuel 2021,
301). At the same time, the practice is seen as a means of associating the dead with warfare, even when the pos-
sibility that the individual was not an active warrior remains under discussion (e.g., Whitley 2002, 219; Lloyd
2014, 2).
    Regarding piracy, Emanuel explicitly links this phenomenon to weapon-bearing burials of the LBA. His
assessment of the mortuary evidence for seafaring individuals of the time is particularly perceptive: “a role in
piracy and other violent, predatory naval activities may certainly be posited, both for these individuals and for
the societies they may have led” (Emanuel 2021, 304). The persistent difficulty of identifying archaeological
markers that can be unambiguously connected to piracy does not preclude a similar interpretation for some
EIA warrior burials.

Given the widespread acceptance that Tomb 79 at Lefkandi represents a figure whose activities included
warfare and long-distance mobility, it is striking that piracy has remained almost absent from the discussion.
Only Luraghi (2006, 34) has ventured to replace the term warrior with pirate and to draw an explicit connection
between such warrior-traders and the world of raiding and piracy. Indeed, if warfare is understood to coexist
with trade, as the warrior-trader category suggests, it becomes difficult to imagine circumstances in which such
an individual would not also have been involved in pirate activities. Even if such circumstances existed, there is
little reason to assume that they constituted the norm rather than the exception.
    It should be underscored that, as in any comparable case, the aim is not to identify an individual who was
exclusively a pirate. Yet, within a broader context characterized by the scarcity of direct indicators, Tomb 79
offers eloquent testimony that a person engaged in trade and long-distance travel may have undertaken pirate
raids, given that objects from other regions accompanied him in death alongside weighing equipment and, no-
tably, his weapons. Based on this burial, it does not seem unwarranted to propose that when, in the EIA Aegean,
evidence appears for individuals, who combined martial equipment with indications of extensive seafaring and
exchange, it is plausible that such persons may have participated in forms of violent acquisition that accompa-
nied or underpinned their trading operations.
   The bronze grater in Tomb 79, considered together with the rest of the assemblage, may also be relevant
here, as similar objects have been found in other 9th-century BCE burials at Lefkandi that likewise contained
weapons (Ridgway 1997, 325; Antonaccio 2002, 22–3). According to David Ridgway (1997), these items were
used in the preparation of a drink of the kind described in the Iliad, where Hekamede mixes goat’s cheese into
wine for Nestor and his companions using a bronze grater (κνήστι χαλκείῃ; Il. 11.639–640; see also Od. 10.234).
Despite the reservations expressed by Susan Sherratt (2004, 208, 213), the association of such objects with wine
consumption has been broadly accepted (e.g., West 1998, 191; Antonaccio 2002, 22).
    Considerable attention has been devoted to the role of wine-drinking and feasting as mechanisms for
strengthening bonds within Postpalatial and Homeric society (see, for example, Sherratt 2004, 188, 211; Maran
2012, 129). Hitchcock and Maeir (2016, 5; 2017, 150–53) have emphasized the significance of feasting as ritual
practice and of Mycenaean serving and drinking vessels as material symbols intended to reinforce collective
identity among Sea Peoples communities during the LBA III. Within this broader context, and in light of the
coexistence of the grater with weapons, it is worth considering whether this object may relate to feasting and
wine-drinking practices that served to consolidate and renew bonds not only within a settled social group, but
also within a smaller circle of individuals involved in maritime mobility, trade and warfare, even pirate raids.

Ship-shaped firedogs
Another noteworthy class of objects that may be situated within the same interpretive framework as the graters
comprises the iron spits and the ship-shaped firedogs, which likewise occur in Geometric warrior burials and
are associated with feasting practices, since they were intended for roasting meat. Examples of this type have
so far been recovered from Argos (Courbin 1957, 368–85; Coldstream 2003, 125–26), Crete (Boardman 1971;
Coldstream and Catling 1996, 575, 591–92, 720; Vonhoff 2011, 146–47; see also Kotsonas 2008, 284, 317, with
further bibliography) and Cyprus (Tandy 1997, 157–58), and all are approximately contemporary, dating to the
late 8th/early 7th century BCE (Fig. 10).
      Most scholars accept that these artifacts are indicators of status and that, by virtue of their form, they
­establish a symbolic association between themselves (and through them the deceased) and the sea (e.g.,
 Courbin 1957, 384–85; Buchholz 1991, 76–8; Tandy 1997, 161–65; Vonhoff 2011, 150; contra Déonna 1959).
 Moreover, their inclusion in burials furnished with weapons leaves little doubt as to their placement within a
 warrior-­identity context. In this light, their role within the funerary assemblage appears to extend beyond mere
 functionality, ­operating instead as visual statements about social position and modes of life. The interpretation
 that views these firedogs as symbols of a seafaring warrior, who forged essential bonds with his companions,
 not only through the communal consumption of wine but also through the sharing of roasted meat, is therefore
 ­compelling. As emerges from the foregoing discussion, this seafaring warrior can plausibly be understood, at
  least in the ­context of the EIA Aegean, to have engaged in activities that amount to piracy.

A consideration for the future: Calibrating grave assemblages
As discussed above, Tomb 79 at Lefkandi represents one of the few favorable cases available to the scholar of
­piracy in the EIA Aegean. Although artifacts or assemblages that clearly suggest identities or activities s­ urpassing
 a basic warrior attribution are exceptional, this scarcity should not discourage the search for possible traces of

piracy. Since in the EIA, as in any other period, the burial of an individual, whose activities included piracy,
did not differ in any essential way from the burials of other people inhabiting the same region and era, the
­archaeology of piracy should adopt innovative methodological approaches in order to overcome the persistent
 difficulties of linking specific archaeological finds to the phenomenon of piracy and to make effective use of the
 limited relevant evidence.
    Using Tomb 79 at Lefkandi as an illustrative case, it may be argued that it would be worthwhile attempting a
calibration of its entire grave-goods assemblage to assess the relative weight of each item, both individually and
in combination with the others, regarding its potential association with piracy. The systematic implementation
of this idea lies beyond the scope of the present study, although certain preliminary observations may be offered
here. In such a calibration, the presence of weapons would understandably serve as a fundamental criterion,
while imported items would further enhance the evaluative index. The weighing equipment, however, would be
of greatest significance in this instance (see Kroll 2008, 38, on the importance of balance weights not only for the
interpretation of piracy but also for other activities), since it points most clearly to the deceased’s involvement
in trade. A similar line of reasoning has prompted scholars such as Jung (2009, 73–5), Hitchcock and Maeir
(2017, 257) and Emanuel (2021, 301) to propose that the mixture of Aegean and central Mediterranean grave
goods, including a substantial number of weapons, in LBA IIIB/C Tomb 21 at Langada on Kos may indicate a
possible “pirate identity” for the deceased. It is not unlikely that a systematic calibration of grave assemblages
from regions and periods conducive to pirate activity will in future reveal additional potential pirate burials.
PIRACY IN THE EARLY IRON AGE AEGEAN

Occasionality, opportunism and fluid maritime roles
The attempt to identify the exclusively pirate individual, the purely pirate settlement or the strictly pirate artifact
tends to hinder rather than facilitate the examination of piracy, particularly in the EIA. If the interpretive focus
shifts from fixed social roles (such as pirate or trader, aggressor or victim) to more fluid forms of maritime iden-
tity, a clearer interpretive space opens for recognizing the situational nature of pirate behavior. Opportunism
and occasionality emerge as key concepts for understanding and detecting the phenomenon of piracy. These
concepts are shaped by, and at the same time arise from, objective conditions, including for example the periods
in which seafaring in the Aegean was possible, since maritime activity occurred only then and thus opportuni-
ties for pirate action could materialize only within that temporal window. At the same time, and more impor-
tantly, they are closely connected to the contingencies of maritime life and to a mindset oriented towards the
exploitation of opportunity. This is why, in the Odyssey, rulers, household leaders, traders and many others raid
whenever conditions allow, acting opportunistically and when the likelihood of minimal cost is in their favor.
Similar behavior may be expected from groups not explicitly mentioned in the epics, such as humble fishermen
or others regularly engaged with the maritime sphere.
     On this basis, no restrictions seem to arise regarding the social position of a potential pirate. Such an
i­ndividual could come from any part of the social spectrum and could hold multiple, context-dependent roles
 and occupations (see, for example, Tsonakas, this volume, for the LBA seafarers). Those who possessed martial
 skill, nautical knowledge and leadership ability were, however, better equipped to confront the difficulties in-
 herent in such a way of life (Hitchcock and Maeir 2016, 252–54, for a discussion of the skills required of pirates).
 Yet individuals of this sort appear across all social strata and perhaps especially among the more elevated ones,
 such as those buried in graves comparable to Tomb 79 at Lefkandi or those who made use of vessels like the New
 York krater. These groups also possessed the resources necessary for building and maintaining ships.
    It should nevertheless be noted that the concepts of occasionality and opportunism do not pertain ­exclusively
to individuals, but may also apply to settlements. Even if many island and coastal sites functioned as trade posts
or ports of call, they could at the same time engage in pirate activities, particularly during periods of ­intensified

The tactics and timing of Early Iron Age piracy
Regarding pirate tactics, the passages from the Odyssey mentioned above highlight a particular mode of action:
bringing the ships ashore and subsequently launching a raid inland. It is worth asking whether it is a coinci-
dence that certain 8th-century BCE images depict precisely this mode of operation. If the view that coastal
raiding constituted the predominant, if not exclusive, form of maritime attack at least until this century is
correct (Raaflaub 1999, 129, 131), then the practice defined here as piracy may in fact have been more typical
than exceptional. In any case, the similarities between the practices described in the epics and those depicted in
the iconography should not be attributed to the direct illustration of specific epic episodes, as was commonly
proposed in earlier scholarship. A more convincing explanation is that poets and vase painters were responding
to, and refracting through their media, the lived realities of their time.
    As for the intensity of the phenomenon during the EIA, the available evidence does not yet permit firm
conclusions. Even so, it has been aptly suggested that, after the LBA IIIC period, piracy may have re-emerged
in the 9th century BCE and reached a peak in the following century, in parallel with the expansion in maritime
activity and the rising number of depictions of sea battles on pottery, which begin in MG and increase during
LG times (Samaras 2015, 199–200). The early part of this chronological frame, namely the second quarter and
the middle of the 9th century BCE, includes Tomb 79 at Lefkandi and other burials from the same cemetery that
also combine graters and weapons, while the majority of ship-shaped firedogs belong to the subsequent period
of intensification, appearing primarily in funerary assemblages of the late 8th century BCE (Tandy 1997, 156;
though examples from Crete appear already in the 9th century BCE, see Kotsonas 2008, 317).

A closing note
None of the categories of material evidence discussed above can, on its own, decisively advance the i­ nvestigation
of piracy in the EIA Aegean. Considered in isolation, each is more likely to lead to analytical dead ends. Yet it
is their examination in conjunction and their integration within both the historical context of the EIA and the
long-term trajectory of piracy in the Aegean that render the phenomenon a matter of genuine significance for
understanding the period’s maritime realities. Piracy emerges not as a marginal curiosity but as a ­structurally
embedded feature of EIA seafaring, one that becomes visible only when disparate strands of evidence are
brought into concert. However challenging its study may be, it remains incumbent upon the scholar not only
to explore every opportunity to examine this phenomenon, but, above all, to avoid consigning it to invisibility
through silence.

 From Homer’s Taphians to the Pirates of Ayia Mavra
Exploring the Legacy of Piracy in the Central Ionian Sea

The geomorphology of Lefkada and the Inner Ionian Archipelago, with their rugged coastlines, intricate network of
­islands, and strategic location along important trade routes, have significantly impacted the region’s maritime history. The
 ­prevalence of piracy has also left some traces on these islands. The recent discovery of Late Helladic t­ umuli, a ­fortification
  wall and a prehistoric settlement at Meganisi has shed new light on the Taphians mentioned by Homer. According to
  legend, the Taphians were renowned for their seafaring skills and piracy. The discovery of these a­ rchaeological sites
  ­provides important new insights into the Taphians’ way of life and the extent of their influence in the region.
Written sources suggest the constant presence of pirates in the Ionian Sea, which posed a serious threat to trade. The
ancient ports played an essential role in the region’s maritime history, and there must have been numerous hideouts for
pirates in the broader network of the small islands like Atokos, Arkoudi, Echinades, Kythros, Kastos and Kalamos. The
long-standing presence of pirates in the restless waters of the central Ionian Sea is well-documented since the castle of Ayia
Mavra in Lefkada became an infamous pirate’s nest during early modern times.

Piracy, which can be defined as armed robbery involving the use of ships (de Souza 1999, 1), has been a ­pervasive
issue throughout history, and the ancient world was no exception. Greece and the Eastern Mediterranean Sea
were hotspots of piracy in antiquity, and it is a topic that has captivated scholars and historians for centuries
(e.g., Gabbert 1986; Ormerod 1924; de Souza 1999; Beek 2006; Konstam 2008; Emilio-Ioannidou 2017).
     This paper seeks to explore the evolution of piracy in the broader region of Lefkada, the Inner Ionian
­Archipelago, Echinades islands and the opposite Akarnanian coast, with an emphasis on the prehistoric times.
 Our finds strongly support the research regarding piracy in the Mediterranean Sea and more specifically in
 the Aegean during prehistory (see for example Hitchcock and Maeir 2018). The strategic position of Lefkada
 along crucial maritime trade routes, the geomorphology of Meganisi with its lace-like shores, and the com-
 plex network of small islands in the Inner Ionian Archipelago have significantly influenced the maritime his-
 tory of the broader region. Given the potential impact of piracy on these islands, there is a possibility that

a­ rchaeological remnants associated with piracy may be present. Therefore, a comprehensive exploration of the
 available ­archaeological and historical records from this intricate landscape has the potential to enhance our
 understanding of piracy as a nuanced phenomenon substantially.
ΤAPHOS – THE LAND OF HOMERIC PIRATES

The Homeric poems constitute the earliest extant literary works depicting individuals and groups as pirates
(Od. 16.424–430). While the poems express a measure of disapproval for piracy, they simultaneously illustrate
the potential for a pirate to attain a higher social status through successful marauding. In essence, piracy was
not regarded as intrinsically ignominious or objectionable in the Homeric world, reflecting the socio-cultural
milieu of Homer’s Greece. Furthermore, piracy and warfare were so inextricably intertwined in the Homeric
universe that they were virtually indistinguishable.
    Meganisi, situated east of Lefkada, occupies a maritime area amidst the western coast of Akarnania and
the islands of Lefkada, Ithaca and Kephalonia. Within this region, numerous small islands and islets form the
Teleboides and Echinades island groups. Meganisi, belonging to the Teleboides group, is commonly identified
by scholars as the island referred to as Taphos in ancient texts (Od. 1.105, 1.181, 1.417–419, 14.453, 15.427,
16.426; Strabo 10.2.14, 10.2.20, 10.2.24). According to the Homeric tradition, this island served as a homeland
for pirates and traders. The name itself suggests that it may have been associated with tombs. In the epic poems,
capes and small islands positioned along sea passages were often linked to hero worship due to the proximity of
heroic deaths (for example, Ajax Lokros in Mykonos, Leukos in Lefkada, and according to Homer, the tomb of
Achilles in the Black Sea was visible to seafarers).
    The Taphians are considered Leleges or Phoenicians, who arrived in the region with Cadmus from the East.
Their main occupation seems to have been piracy in the southern Ionian region, as was the case with most tribes
of the Leleges, who were settled in other coastal areas and were usually mentioned in tradition as formidable
pirates (Vikatou 2019, 76–7).
    Although only the Taphians are mentioned in the Homeric epics, in later writers they are associated with the
Teleboans, another Lelegian tribe. According to Strabo (10.2.14, 10.2.20, 10.2.24), the Teleboans preceded the
Taphians. Both tribes inhabited the coastal cities of Akarnania and, after being displaced by the K
                                                                                                  ­ ephalenians,
settled on the neighboring islands of Akarnania, primarily Taphos, which is located between Ithaca and Lefkada.
However, it is possible that they represent the same tribe, initially known as the Teleboans and later as the
­Taphians (Vikatou 2019).
    The first references to the Taphians can be found in the Homeric epics. In the Odyssey, they are portrayed as
neighboring people of Odysseus’ kingdom, who, apart from being pirates, were also skilled traders, traversing
the Mediterranean Sea and competing even with the Phoenicians. In Book 1 (180–184), the king of the Taphians
Mentes, the son of wise Anchialos and a friend of Odysseus, is mentioned. He travels to the city of Temese to
exchange iron for copper. The epithet φιλήρετμοι, used by Mentes himself to describe his people, demonstrates
that they were renowned rowers, indicating furthermore that they were a seafaring nation. Additionally, the
term ὰλλόθροοι, meaning “speaking a different language”, implies their commercial activities with other people
of the Mediterranean. In other parts of the Odyssey, the Taphians are referred to as ληΐστορες (15.427, 16.426;
see also 14.452), indicating their piratical and plundering nature, as well as their involvement in the slave trade.
Specifically mentioned is their abduction of a slave woman from the city of Sidon in Phoenicia (15.425–429).
    In short, ancient sources offer indefinite testimonies regarding the Taphians-Teleboans and the islands they
inhabited (see Vikatou 2019, 79). Among other information, we learn that the island of Taphos derived its name
from the heroic first king of the seafaring Taphians, Taphios, brother of Teleboas. Later, Pterelaos, Taphios’ son,
extended his power to the surrounding islands and Kephalonia came under his rule. Its first inhabitants were
named Taphians or Teleboans. The small islands of Kastos, Sparti, Skorpios, Meganisi, Kalamos, etc., located

between Lefkada and the Akarnanian coast, took their names from the two brothers and were called Taphian
or Teleboan Islands.
    The mystery surrounding the people of Taphians and the exact location of the island is not easy to clarify, as
the ambiguity observed in Homer and the limited amount of information regarding their origin and ancestry
led to confusion and the formulation of many different opinions by later writers, including ancient ones (such
as Strabo, Pliny the Elder, etc.). As a result, the search for Ithaca naturally prompted efforts to identify Taphos.
Current research on the Homeric Taphos remains uncertain, with some scholars suggesting its placement in
Kephalonia, where a region named Taphios exists, while others propose Meganisi or Kalamos as potential loca-
tions (see Vikatou 2019, 83–4). However, from the entirety of the testimonies, it is inferred that the Taphians,
a piratical and trading people, dominated the Ionian Sea during the Mycenaean period, before the rise of the
Kephalenians, when they constituted a powerful naval kingdom. According to myths, they did not hesitate to
campaign against the Mycenaeans themselves, and they not only faced the powerful forces of that time but also
required trickery to be defeated (see Vikatou 2019, 76).

Utilizing the existing archaeological evidence, one could formulate the perspective that the Taphians,
­ perating as both a piratical and mercantile community along the Ionian and Akarnanian coasts, extensively
o
sailed across the entire archipelagic region. They erected enduring stations and bases at strategically significant
locations, with one such outpost situated in the Meganisi region.

PIRACY IN THE CENTRAL IONIAN SEA FROM CLASSICAL ANTIQUITY TO
THE EARLY MODERN ERA

The activity of pirates continued unabated, even after prehistoric times, in the broader area of the Ionian and
Adriatic Seas, where Greeks, Etruscans, Liburnians and other pirates ravaged the islands and coastal regions
(especially for the Liburnian pirates see Budić, this volume). Thucydides (1.5.3) mentions the Ozolian Locrians,
the Aitolians and the Akarnanians as peoples engaged in maritime piracy. He provides insights into the various
factions and activities during the war. One aspect he highlights is the prevalence of piracy in the region.
    Establishing colonies along the coasts of the Ionian Sea, which provided safe harbors, was an essential step
in combating the phenomenon of piracy that flourished from the shores of Zakynthos to Illyria. In the colony
of Lefkada, the Corinthians built the canal, which, especially during times of war, offered an alternative route
for a peaceful journey away from the dangerous promontory of Lefkatas in the southern part of the island
­(Rontogiannis 1988, 92–3; Zachos and Douzougli 2003; Bonelou 2020, esp. 82–6).
     In the present coastal zone of the settlement of Lygia, the large harbor of the island was constructed,

 in the Ionian Sea, the excavations in this area bring to light “exotic” products that arrived on the island from all

     On the northeastern side of the island, close to the harbor, the sanctuary of Aphrodite Limenida (or
­Limenarchis) is noted (Melfi 2016, 90–3), the precise location of which archaeologists have not yet been able
 to ascertain. Facing the goddess of the sea, the mariners would pray for safe journeys without storms and,
 ­evidently, without any encounters with pirates!
     The Messenian sculptor Damophon was called to Lefkada to repair the statue of Aphrodite Limenida (Melfi
2016, 90–8). An honorary decree inscribed on a monumental Doric column found in the Asklepieion of a­ ncient
Messene states that the people of Lefkada provided a rowing ship and many men for the protection of the
­Messenian sculptor during his return from Lefkada to the port of Kyparissia (IG IX.12 iv 1475). We can assume
 that the waters of the southern Ionian were not particularly safe during the 2nd century BCE, but as gradually
 over the next centuries the Romans imposed their forces in the Eastern Mediterranean basin (Etruria, Sicily,
 Illyria, Ionian Sea), and thus the pirates might have begun to lose their bases (Semple 1916, 143–44).
    Later on, from the early 16th to the late 17th century, the castle of Ayia Mavra, on the northeast edge of
Lefkada (Fig. 5), became one of the most famous pirate dens in the Adriatic Sea, as noted in the travel book
of Evliya Çelebi (Sarigiannis 2011, 50–1; Vikatou and Staikou 2023a, 22–3). The crews, consisting of renegade
Christians and Muslim sailors of Anatolian or even North African origin, were conscripted by the Ottoman ad-
ministration of the castle to assist the Ottoman fleet in maintaining control over the wider maritime area under
the rule of the Ottoman Empire. The pirate ship’s captain, who held the title of hâssa reis, was designated as the
legitimate leader of the other pirates of Ayia Mavra (Sarigiannis 2011, 57). Their targets were passing Venetian
merchant ships and the neighboring Venetian territories of Kephalonia and Zakynthos.

The provocative actions of the pirates led to a counterattack by Maltese knights in May 1625 (Krantonelli
1991, 325). The corsairs arrived outside the fortress of Ayia Mavra with nine ships, blew up the eastern gate with
explosives, and climbed the walls using ladders. A prolonged confrontation followed, with casualties on both
sides.
     Considering the resurgence of piracy, on August 15, 1658, the Venetians attempted to capture the
­Turkish-held castle with Admiral Biki leading the operation (Vikatou and Staikou 2023a, 23). Pope Alexander
 VII supported the endeavor by sending three warships, while the Knights of Malta also participated. A general
 attack commenced after troops were disembarked in the neighborhoods surrounding the castle. However, the
 allies lost the element of surprise as they arrived in front of the castle walls during daylight due to bad weather.
 Furthermore, their coordination was inadequate, and they did not act swiftly. Thus, when they tried to climb
 the walls with the ladders they had brought, they discovered they were too short. Despite their attempts to
 blow up the fortress gate with explosives, they ultimately failed. After these mishaps, Admiral Biki was forced
 to order a retreat just a few hours after the operation began. Following the collapse of the Venetian Republic
 in 1797 and the presence of the French, Russian, and British on the island of Lefkada, Greeks and foreigners
 intermittently engaged in piracy or attacked ships of opposing naval forces (Çoruh 2018). The western coasts of
 Lefkada, particularly around Gria Langada, were a hotspot for renowned pirates until the early 19th century. In
 fact, their descendants have erected a –still standing– monument by the Pefkoulia beach to immortalize their
 legacy (Fig. 6).

Throughout time, pirates in the central Ionian Sea would seek hideouts to avoid detection and launch s­ urprise
attacks on passing ships. The small natural harbors and bays along the islands’ rocky shores provided con-
cealment points suitable for ambush. At the same time, the intricate network of maritime passages offered
­alternative escape routes in case of pursuit.
    According to Dörpfeld’s theory (Dörpfeld 1927, 117–19) that Homeric Ithaca is identified with Lefkada and
considering the significant prehistoric settlement he found in the Nydri plain, he identified the sheltered bay
of Vlycho, near Nydri, as the primary harbor of Odysseus’ kingdom (see also Vikatou 2014, 10–1). The Vlycho
harbor is characterized by its depth, substantial horizontal expanse, and effective protection provided by the
cape of Ayia Kyriaki. Employing the same rationale, Dörpfeld (1927, 123–24) identified a small harbor at the
base of Mount Skaros, where the Dimosari stream meets the sea, as the location of Rheithron harbor (Od. 1.186).
From there, a commanding view towards the Pringiponisia is secured (meaning the cluster of small islands,
including Cheloni, Sparti, Skorpidi, Skorpios, Tsokari and Madouri). Finally, the harbor of Phorcys –where the
Phaeacians disembarked the sleeping Odysseus (Od. 13.116–124)– corresponds, according to the German ex-
cavator (Dörpfeld 1927, 109–13), to the present-day Syvota. The topographical details described in the Odyssey
(13.96–125, 13.345–351) are consistent: a small, enclosed, deep bay with sources of brackish water, large and
small caves around, at a remote location on the island.

In the northern part of Meganisi, there is a noticeable fragmentation of the coastline, leading to the creation
of five large bays (Spilia, Vathy, Bali, Ambelaki and Atherinou), as well as numerous small ones resembling
fjords. Coves and natural moorages form in this area and in other parts of the island, providing ideal settings for
pirate activities. Today, only a limited amount of ancient construction material is preserved in Vathy, which can
be associated with the remains of the ancient harbor (Palmos 1992).
     The marine Papanikolis cave, located in the southwestern part of Meganisi, was undoubtedly used for
­thousands of years by ancient sailors who sought refuge in this shelter to protect themselves from storms or to
 hide. Its length is 120 m, the width varies from 60 m near the entrance to 23 m inside the cave, and its depth
 is approximately 30 m. It is large enough for ships, even those with relatively tall masts. It was named after the
 submarine Papanikolis, as it is said to have used the cave as a base during World War II, although this is more
 of a myth than a reality.
     The islets of Kythros and Atokos, characterized by their rocky coastlines, coupled with their relatively
­secluded locations, could have served as optimal natural hideouts for pirate vessels. Of particular interest is
 the islet of Arkoudi, situated south of Lefkada. Dörpfeld (1927, 98–101) associated this islet with the Homeric
 islet Asteris, where Telemachus sought refuge while being pursued by the suitors. Noteworthy are the islet’s two
 similarly configured harbors, as described in the Homeric narrative (Od. 4.844–847, trans. J.E. Huddleston,
 https://topostext.org/work/3):

Closer to the coasts of Akarnania are the islets of Kastos and Kalamos, which feature secluded bays and
anchorages that would be attractive to pirates. In the central-western part of Kastos, there is a natural harbor
called Sarakiniko, facing north. Today, this name can be found in many coastal areas in Greece, where, as it is
said, Saracen pirates passed by and left their mark. In the Ionian Sea, the toponym Sarakiniko is also found in
Kephalonia, Ithaca and Preveza.
    Kalamos is the second-largest island in the Teleboan complex after Meganisi, resembling a lush mountain
in the heart of the Inner Ionian Archipelago (Μοutzali 2003, 71–6). Dörpfeld (1927, 134–35) believed that Ka-
lamos was the ancient Taphos, as the iron traded by the Taphian king Mentes (Od. 1.184) was not found on Me-
ganisi, but was abundant on Kalamos. The Porto Leone Bay, as named by the Venetians, who mapped the area,
could have been an ideal refuge for pirate ships throughout antiquity due to its adequate horizontal expanse.
Nowadays, at the bay’s entrance architectural material of the Venetian period is still visible (Fig. 7).
   Further south, the labyrinthine sea passages and small hidden coves among the islands of the Echinades
could have served as excellent locations for pirates attempting raids in Akarnania. In Platygiali, on the western
coast of Akarnania, facing the Echinades complex, an Early Bronze Age cluster of buildings has been excavated
underwater in the past. The tidally washed settlement inside the deep bay probably had a maritime character
(Delaporta and Spondylis 1991, 45).
    It is essential to delve into the profound significance of caves concerning pirate activity, particularly within
the karstic region of the Ionian islands and the shores of Akarnania. These areas boast a plethora of expan-
sive caves (Chirotrypa at Apolpaina, Chirospilia at Evgiros, the Cyclops’ cave in Meganisi, Chirospilia at Nea
Plaghia, to name a few) that probably could offer refuge to local inhabitants when confronted with the immi-
nent threat of marauding pirates prowling the coastal waters.
     The island’s northeast side is unlikely to have served as a refuge for pirates during the period when the for-
tified ancient city thrived. The narrow channel would have functioned as a trap for hostile ships. Additionally,
as already mentioned, it is probable that there were military maritime installations alongside the commercial
harbor. Regular patrols by the city’s naval forces, which also possessed a second smaller harbor near Kamini
Beach on the northern side of the island (Vikatou and Staikou 2015, 627), would have been common. However,

the southern and western shores of Lefkada, with their steep cliffs and hidden coves, could potentially have
provided pirates with a temporary hideaway.

The Ephorate of Antiquities of Aitoloakarnania and Lefkada is actively sharing archaeological knowledge,
­creating a new educational brochure designed for secondary education students (Vikatou and Staikou 2023b).
 This comprehensive brochure delves into the intriguing topic of piracy in the central Ionian region, tracing its
 roots from the prehistoric period to the era of the pirates associated with the Ayia Mavra fortress. Furthermore,
 an interactive info-kiosk has been installed within the newly constructed museum, situated in the two-room
 casemate of the Ayia Mavra castle. The multi-touch screen table, equipped with a rich array of visual materials,
 provides visitors with detailed information on the historical evolution of piracy on the island of Lefkada.
     The unearthing of the prehistoric tombs on Meganisi and the continuous exploration of Lefkada’s maritime
history, spanning from excavations at the ancient harbor in Lygia to the documentation of the adventurous
­episodes in the pirate haven of Ayia Mavra, shed light on the intriguing but elusive world of pirates.

 “Savage” Liburnians, Notorious for Piracy
Reconsidering the Liburnian Thalassocracy and the Role of Seaborne Raids

The Liburnians, native people who lived along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, are in ancient written sources
­frequently associated with piracy. Based on Strabo’s (6.2.4) and Appian’s (B Civ. 2.6.39) accounts of their presence on
 Korkyra and Epidamnos, scholars have developed the concept of the Early Iron Age Liburnian thalassocracy (ca. 800–
 500/400 BCE). Numerous historical interpretations have tried to strengthen or dispute the extent, scale, frequency and
 chronological scope of Liburnian influence and piracy. Through the analysis of regional geographical, economic and social
 circumstances, this paper aims to reconsider the concept of thalassocracy and give the explanatory tool for understanding
 Liburnian inclination to piracy.

THE LIBURNIANS – THE EARLY IRON AGE TERRITORIAL SPAN AND ITS
CONNECTION TO THALASSOCRACY AND PIRACY

­ ppian (B Civ. 2.6.39) added that Liburnians had taken Epidamnos from Taulantii before being expelled by the
A
Korkyreans in 627 BCE. Furthermore, the Liburnian presence on the western Adriatic coast was also directly
or indirectly mentioned by Polybius (3.100.2), Florus (1.21.1) and Pliny the Elder (HN 3.110, 3.112). All afore-
mentioned accounts led scholars to conclude that Liburnians dominated much of the Adriatic maritime space
during the EIA. The concept is frequently repeated in the literature under the term the Liburnian thalassocracy
(e.g., Suić 1953; 1981, 90; Wilkes 1969, 4; Stipčević 1989, 31–2; Katičić 1995, 108–9; Zaninović 1996, 292–301;
Malkin 1998, 77–8; Šašel Kos 2015, 6–13).
    Unsurprisingly, the Liburnian thalassocracy concept is closely intertwined with widespread and far-flung
piracy. In addition to the narratives that imply Liburnian control of maritime hubs, such as Epidamnos and
Korkyra, the more peculiar elaboration is based on two Roman literary sources – Livy and Appian.
    Describing the military venture of the Spartan exile Cleonymus, Livy (10.2.4) mentioned that the Spartan
fleet was carried up the Adriatic, where on the left (west) side were the harborless shores of Italy and on the right
(east) side the Illyrians, the Liburnians and the Histrians, all characterized as savage tribes chiefly notorious
for their acts of piracy. The supplement to Livy’s account of the eastern Adriatic piracy is some verses from the

conduct piratical expeditions against their neighbors.
    Florus (1.21.1–3), who compiled his history in the first half of the 1st century CE, equated the Liburnians
and the Illyrians, while describing the savagery Romans experienced in the Adriatic Sea during the reign
of Queen Teuta (late 3rd century BCE). The Liburnian maritime raids were once again directly highlighted
in ­Appian’s ­account (Ill. 4.16), who wrote that Octavian deprived the Liburnians of their ships because they
­practiced ­piracy. Since the Liburnians are often identified with the Illyrians in historical sources, the accounts
 should be supplemented with Strabo’s general remark on the Illyrian habits:

But although the Illyrian seaboard is such, people in earlier times made but small account of it [the
              land] – perhaps in part owing to their ignorance of its fertility, though mostly because of the wildness

ADDITIONAL INGREDIENTS TO THE LIBURNIAN PIRACY NARRATIVE
AND THEIR CRITICISM – IN THE TURMOIL OF THE TRANS-ADRIATIC
NETWORK OF EXCHANGE

In the scholarly literature, historical accounts are frequently reinforced with archaeological details in an attempt
to support the Liburnian piracy narrative. For the authors who claim that intercepting and engaging with enemy
ships had been an integral part of Liburnian routine, rare and valuable objects, such as the helmet from the Cape
Jablanac on the island of Cres dated between 550 and 400 BCE, serve as a tempting proof for crimes on the sea
(Boršić et al. 2021, 21–2). In the light of Strabo’s (6.2.4) and Appian’s (B Civ. 2.6.39) accounts of the Liburnian
maritime dominance during the EIA in the south Adriatic and north Ionian Seas, scholars observe some for-
eign objects, particularly ones of Greek origin, as a possible outcome of sea raids. No wonder, piracy has been
highlighted as the probable way of acquiring Middle and Late Corinthian or Italo-Corinthian vases found on
the eastern Adriatic coast (Zaninović 2015, 86, 147). Nevertheless, this hypothesis deserves to be observed more
closely, due to many social and economic factors regarding the current state of archaeological research and the
knowledge about the EIA exchange networks in the Adriatic Sea.
    Firstly, the number of Liburnian sites containing Archaic or Early Classical Greek material is not abundant
(Šešelj 2009, 412–39; Čelhar and Borzić 2016, 78; Budić 2022, 62–4). Since many locations have not yet been
properly explored or excavated, it would be overambitious to conclude that valuable Greek objects scarcely
reached the Liburnian communities, and hence could be defined as potential spoils of occasional piratical raids
as Marin Zaninović (2015, 86, 147) suggested. The recent excavations in Zadar (ancient Iader) have exposed a
different pattern. Judged primarily on the size, location and political role of the site in later history (Čondić and
Vuković 2017, 32–3), Iader should be designated as the leading Liburnian hillfort and a strategic maritime hub.
The excavations in the Zadar old city, i.e., the former core of the Liburnian settlement, revealed a significant
number of imports, mostly of Daunian and Greek origin (Čondić and Vuković 2017, 74–99).
    Secondly, a discussion about the way foreign goods arrived among the Liburnians should not be observed
without insight into the trans-Adriatic prehistoric network, an often-overlooked phenomenon in the literature.
The circulation of the indigenous material shows a well-established pattern of exchange between the eastern and
the western Adriatic coast. During the EIA, Liburnian exchange with the opposite Italian coast is attested by
numerous imports, particularly from the region of Picenum and Daunia (Batović 1976; Majnarić-Pandžić 1998,
