Roman counter offensives remained desultory until 67 BCE, when the Roman popular assembly
c­ ommissioned a proven young general, Cnaeus Pompeius Magnus, with an extraordinary command to eradicate
 the pirates once and for all. With some twenty-four legates, 270 ships and the authority to draw upon a potential
 complement of 120,000 infantry, 4000 cavalry and 8000 talents of revenue, Pompeius swept the Mediterranean
 from west to east in a three-month campaign, cornering the last holdouts in their bases in Cilicia and defeating
 them, ultimately, in the waters off Coracesium (Broughton 1952, 146; de Souza 1999, 166–72). Through lenient
 terms, Pompeius was able to persuade the majority of the pirates to surrender, and after dismantling the walls
 of the dreaded pirate bases, he resettled his former adversaries as colonists in Cilicia Pedia and elsewhere (Plut.
 Pomp. 28.1–4). With that, Mediterranean piracy subsided for at least a generation, or until Pompeius’ son,
 Sextus Pompeius, renewed the pirate wars in his rivalry with the triumvirs, Antony, Octavian and Lepidus. But
 that is another story. With Pompeius’ settlement of the Cilician pirates in 67 BCE, their menace largely subsided.
     The above summary is compiled from ancient literary testimony, much of which tends to address the
­Cilician pirate menace with a considerable degree of hyperbole. It is worth noting, however, that surviving
 public records likewise acknowledge the gravity of the pirate menace. For example, the SC de piratiis of 102
 BCE, the preserved texts for which survived at Delphi and Knidos, records the Roman Senate’s decision to
 declare the waters of Cilicia a provincia, that is a sphere of military influence where Roman forces intended
to engage the pirates, as well as the expectation that neighboring states would cooperate fully (Hassall et al.
1974; de Souza 1999, 108–15). Votive offerings, oracular responses and civic decrees recorded at Delos, Klaros,
Epidaurus and Megara similarly attest to the menace of piracy (IG IV.22 750; Sokolowski 1968; Rauh 2003,
64). The French excavations at Delos have demonstrated that this once affluent trading community underwent
irreversible decline through repeated pirate assaults, including a devastating raid in 69 BCE (Rauh 1993, 68).
Publius Servilius V ­ atia’s victory over the pirates is not only preserved in the Fasti Triumphales at Rome, but his
sack of Isaura Vetus is confirmed by the discovery of his ritual evocatio of the city’s patron deity, inscribed in
Latin on a block found in Bozkır, Turkey (Strabo 12.6.2; Hall 1973). Several sources, meanwhile, claim to quote
directly from preserved records of Pompeius’ triumph in 61 BCE. According to Pliny the Elder, in the “senatus
consultum” that officially sanctioned Pompeius’ triumph, the Senate proclaimed that he had “rescued the sea-
coast from pirates and restored to the Roman People the command of the sea” (HN 7.98, trans. H. Rackham,
Cambridge, Mass., 1942; cf. 37.6.12–13; Palmer 1990, 3). As stated by Plutarch, bronze tablets borne at the head
of Pompeius’ triumphal procession displayed a list of the adversaries he conquered, including “all the power of
the pirates by sea and land which had been overthrown” (Plut. Pomp. 45.1–3, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass.,
1917; cf. Diod. Sic. 40.4.1; Vogel-Wiedemann 1985). Referring to the same tablets, Appian adds Pompeius’
claim to have captured some 800 warships with brazen beaks (Mith. 17.117). These records lend considerable
credence to the argument that the Roman hierarchy viewed the Cilician pirate threat and the events culminating
in its defeat as significant milestones.
     The significance, the breadth and the scale of the pirate wars remains contradicted, nonetheless, by the
seeming absence of an archaeological footprint in Rough Cilicia. Participants in the Rough Cilicia ­Archaeological
Survey Project (RCSP), conducted between 1996 and 2011 in the region of the pirate bases of Coracesium and
the Cragus, have addressed this matter in several publications (e.g., Rauh 1997; 2003, 169–202; 2019, 45–50;
Rauh et al. 2000; 2013). As we will demonstrate below, the evidence for piracy in this region is meager and all
but indistinguishable from an otherwise nondescript pattern of Hellenistic settlement along this coast. Scholars
legitimately question the existence of pirate enclaves along this shore (de Souza 1999, 128–30, 136–41; 2013;
Tomaschitz 2013, 57–8). Philip de Souza (2013, esp. 46-53) challenges the categorization of indigenous navies
as pirates altogether, arguing that dominant maritime powers, such as Rhodes or Rome, were all too inclined
to brand as pirates any lesser polity that attempted to control its neighboring sea lanes. De Souza’s argument
has the advantage of associating the pirate enclaves on the coast with local populations, including those of
the Taurus interior. As we noted above, not only did Publius Servilius Isauricus extend his campaign to the
­Isaurian interior, but Plutarch and Appian recount that the “mountain Cilicians” (ὄρειοι Κίλικες) likewise op-
 posed ­Pompeius, only to see their tyrants paraded in his triumph (Plut. Pomp. 45.2–4; App. Mith. 14.96; cf.

Strabo 14.5.10). More recently, Rauh (2019, 49) has conceded that piracy of this magnitude could only have
occurred through collaboration between indigenous Cilician populations and renegade maritime elements. In
many respects, the Cilician pirate menace represented a Mediterranean-wide response to rising political insta-
bility provoked by the severity of Roman imperialism. Especially during the wars against Mithridates VI, the
harshness of Roman exactions and reprisals reportedly drove provincial elites into the fold of the pirates (Plut.
Pomp. 24.2; App. Mith. 14.92; Cass. Dio 36.20.2–4). In essence, disturbances catalyzed by Roman expansion
created both a power vacuum for piracy to thrive in and a recruiting ground for disaffected warriors, sailors,
profiteers and sympathizers.
      These musings return us to the question of ancient historical hyperbole. Conceivably, the ancient sources
i­ nterpreted as a sustained menace something resembling a series of sporadic, geographically shifting outbreaks
 of piracy over a seventy-year interval. We have attempted to argue, for example, that the original core region
 of the Cilician pirate phenomenon was possibly Pamphylia and eastern Lycia (Rauh et al. 2000, 152). Several
 sources draw attention to the fact that urban centers, like Phaselis, Attaleia, Side and Aspendos, openly col-
 luded with pirates, such as Zenicetes, prior to their suppression by Publius Servilius Isauricus (CIL I2 2662;
Cic. Leg. agr. 1.5; Verr. 2.1.53). With the suppression of this Lycian-Pamphylian-Isaurian network in 75 BCE,
retreating pirate elements conceivably relocated eastward to bases at Coracesium and the Cragus. Christoph
Konrad (1994, 217) has proposed a similar pattern of relocation in the western Mediterranean, where, following
the ­demise of Quintus Sertorius in 72 BCE, renegade supporters coalesced at Sertorius’ pirate base in Dianium
before abandoning the Spanish peninsula altogether for Sicily. As Konrad notes, these holdouts would have
included warriors, merchants, pirates and citizens that were, for whatever reason, incapable of making peace
with Rome. As such, the pirate menace may have posed not so much a through line of violence, as it did an un-
dulating series of crises, with contingents repeatedly coalescing, relocating, and recombining, only to reemerge
with renewed vigor. A better perspective requires, accordingly, a balance between what is recorded with what
seems geographically feasible, chronologically coherent, and archaeologically demonstrable. In this respect, our
summary highlights several issues that return us to the relationship between maritime topography and social
dissidence.

What the evidence of the RCSP survey has revealed is that a Hellenistic horizon of ceramic remains is ­consistent
throughout the region, but the numbers are minimal in quantity and indicate a shallow pattern of small, d ­ ispersed
settlements. As the published context ceramics of the survey indicate (Autret et al. 2019), counts of H  ­ ellenistic
ceramics in the survey region were limited (6%, or 339 out of some 5418 dated sherds). It is not so much their
numbers as it is their distribution that seems significant. Hellenistic ceramics were encountered in every region
that has been investigated, including the coastal sites and ridges investigated in 1996–1999, the Adanda Canyon
in the mesogeia investigated in 2000–2003 and the highland sites in the upper Bickici river basin investigated in
2003–2011. One highland site, Sugözü Yayla (RC 1102), seems particularly noteworthy, because it sits at 1600 m
elevation, overlooking the pass that connects the Bickici River on the coast to the southern branch of the Göksu
or Calycadnus River on the interior. Moreover, Hellenistic ceramics were encountered at every categorized
locus, regardless of scale, from the large urban sites such as Iotape and Selinus, to village scale settlements, to
isolated farmsteads, kiln sites and press complexes, to random rural survey units. As we have noted previously,
the presence of pre-Roman ceramics at Iotape and Antiochia ad Cragum (Fig. 3) seems particularly important,
because both communities were established in the mid-1st century CE by the Roman client king Antiochus
IV of Commagene. What the pre-Roman pottery indicates, therefore, is that local settlements preceded these
foundations, settlements that may possibly have served as pirate bases.

ad Cragum in 2003 and fragments of the same form were found at a fortified rural site in the Adanda Canyon,

itself to demonstrate the presence of pirates, particularly when it is offset by the rising numbers of Lamboglia 2
and other Italian forms of the Republican era that are emerging throughout the wider eastern Mediterranean,
including examples published at the nearby Alanya, Anamur and Taşucu Archaeological Museums (Sibella

widely distributed in the eastern Mediterranean that previously understood. It is fair to ask, therefore, whether
the presence of these forms indicates the transactions of pirates, or whether they are merely indicative of an
eastern Mediterranean distribution pattern for Roman trading commodities?
    Turning to the evidence for economic activity, the pottery recovered at the Bickici kiln site indicate that
this site was utilized during the Hellenistic era. The Koan type amphora that was manufactured at this site
conceivably came into production in the 1st century BCE. The freshwater caves with rich clay deposits that
loom directly above the site, and timber brought down from the mountains via the river, undoubtedly attracted
artisans and passing maritime shippers at that time. In the same coastal plain the RCSP survey identified an ex-
tensive press complex at nearby Kale Tepe (RC 0201), a fortified village (RC 2201) and another nearby site (RC

9605), all of which yielded Hellenistic ceramics. In other words, a cluster of small Hellenistic sites were situated
at the mouths of two perennial rivers (the Delice and the Bickici) that descend precipitously from the Taurus

    From an architectural standpoint, the evidence for Hellenistic settlement in Rough Cilicia is equally meager,
the one exception being the presence of numerous Hellenistic fortification systems. Fortifications exhibiting
unbonded courses of large limestone blocks (ashlar, polygonal, pseudo-isodomic) represent the earliest stone
monuments of any significance throughout the region. Surviving remains range from the impressive fortresses
at Hamaxia, Alanya (Coracesium), Meydancık Kale (Kiršu) and the Ovacık peninsula (Aphrodisias), to small
acropolis citadels at Selinus, Kahyalar (RC 2201), Anemurium and Kelenderis, to the isolated towers at Lamos
and Antiochia ad Cragum, and the roughly hewn vernacular defenses recorded at Iotape, Guda Tepe (RC 9712),
Güzelce Harman Tepe (RC 9716) and Tomak Asarı (RC 0019) (Rauh et al. 2013, 66–78; Kaye and Rauh 2020,
156–62). Memorializing as they do the scarred landscape of the Macedonian Wars of Succession, these defensive
remains mark the incipient phase of monumental architecture throughout Rough Cilicia. Livy (33.20.4–5) re-
fers, for example, to the existence of “fortified places” (castella) at several coastal settlements that were seized by
Antiochus III in 197 BCE, including Aphrodisias, Anemurium, Selinus and Coracesium. As such, the remnant
fortifications at these sites predate the rise of Cilician piracy. Fortifications constructed with a “­ vernacular” ma-
sonry technique are more difficult to date and could be indicative of pirate activity, were it not for the possibility
that they were indigenous constructions. None of this eliminates the possibility, moreover, that pirate e­ lements
simply seized and utilized preexisting defenses as they infiltrated the region. From a practical standpoint, it
needs to be added that, apart from Alanya-Coracesium, none of these sites (including A          ­ ntiochia ad Cragum;
Figs. 1 and 3) exhibit harbor remains or topographical features capable of accommodating large, decked war-
ships; whereas, several of the sites could easily have accommodated smaller, open hulled pirate ships that were
more typically employed by pirates. In this respect, the emphasis placed on Coracesium as the center of the
pirate menace in 67 BCE grows in importance, as does our awareness of the capacity of the region to harbor
small clusters of pirate war craft along its intimidating coast.
COVERT SPACES OF THE PIRATE BASES

Although the material evidence for the Cilician pirates may be scant, it can be contextualized to gain a firmer
understanding of the archaeology of piracy. By contemplating the affordances of the Cilicians, we can evaluate
the use of settlements during the “pirate period” and how they differ from other sites. Devised by the ecological
psychologist James J. Gibson (1977, 1979), affordance theory states that our perception to the world is not only
built on the physical characteristics of a space, but that a large amount of an actor’s perception derives from the
possibilities an actor can conceive for that space. In short, affordance is determined by an actor’s relation to the
environment as opposed to the environment alone. For example, a tree may have a high affordance for climbing
(climb-able) for a monkey, whereas it would have a low affordance for a dog. Or a knife may be “cut-with-able”
for a person, but impossible to use for a creature without fingers or thumbs. By identifying what is pirate-able, it
is possible to use geo-spatial analysis to reconsider the archaeological material in Rough Cilicia and understand
how pirates would have made use of the landscape at the time.
      Much can be gleaned of the affordances of Cilician pirates, both from ancient history and maritime
 e­ thnography. Appian (Mith. 14.92) mentions that Cilicians favored light swift craft, naming specifically the
  myoparo and hemoilia (a one-half decked ship). To this list could logically be added the lembos, an older Illyrian
pirate vessel, which later became a mainstay of the Hellenistic navies the Cilicians would associate with. These
­navies would use lemboi for reconnaissance and small raids, which are operationally very similar to piracy. In
  practical terms, it appears it was common for pirates of this era to lurk behind juts in the landscape, hidden
  ­

ndscapes. Cilicia, Crete and the Balearic Islands all
contain rocky jagged coastlines, ideal for hiding small fast ships.
    Cilicia in particular had the ideal environment for piracy to prosper. The impoverished land was, c­ ompared
to the rest of Anatolia, devoid of natural resources apart from cedar timber ideal for ship building. In addi-
tion, recent studies by Gal et al. (2023, 424), which focus on modeling sailing mobility in antiquity, suggest
the straight between Cilicia and Cyprus was one of the most challenging sections of the Mediterranean to sail,
making it more likely that ships would be driven off course and into the hands of pirates. Plutarch states that
the main Cilician stronghold was Coracesium (Pomp. 28.1), whilst Appian suggests it was Cragus (Mith. 14.92).
They further say that pirates did not wholly contain themselves to the coastline. Plutarch mentions that during
Pompeius’ campaign the pirates placed their families and treasures in “strong citadels near the Taurus Moun-
tains” (Pomp. 28.1, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass., 1917). Similarly, Appian mentions Cilicia was a useful
region to the pirates because of its high mountains (Mith. 14.92). Wandsnider and Nelson’s (2015, 55–69) work
demonstrates how cities in Asia Minor signaled group identity through monumental architecture broadcast
throughout the landscape. This could be expanded to suggest that settlements communicated via signals to pass
messages from the coast up to the mountains, and vice versa.
    This grants a blueprint of how pirates in Cilicia could have operated at this time. Small swift ships hiding in
inlets and behind promontories would attack unsuspected vessels struggling in difficult waters. Raiders were
likely aided by agents at inland sites observing passing ships and signaling to those on the coast. They would
therefore have required locations to harbor their ships, protect their goods and areas offering expansive views
to survey potential targets. Despite offering expansive views, the sites would still need to be hidden from the
sea. In this manner, signaling could occur undetected by passing sailors, otherwise alerting them to an attack.
Therefore, we have our required affordances for Cilician piracy. Just because Coracesium and the Cragus are
the only sites with sufficient harbors to store ships, does not automatically make them suitable for piracy. What
seems required are sites that simultaneously offer expansive views of the sea whilst also being hidden. The best
way of measuring this is through a form of visibility analysis known as covert spaces.
    Covert spaces is a form of visibility analysis that not only maps invisibility, but also areas “that are hard to
see but afford expansive views” (covert spaces) and in particular areas that “see little but are overseen” (ambush
zones) (Gillings 2015, 5). This is doubly beneficial for piracy, as covert spaces would indicate the optimum
location for pirate settlements, whereas ambush zones would indicate areas where ships are most likely to be
attacked by pirates. A basic viewshed analysis works as a simple binary; you have a single point and a pixelized
map known as a raster. Viewshed analysis shows whether a pixel is visible from your stated point (1) or not
visible (0). Multiple points on the same map can be combined to show the most visible areas on that map. Here,
the scores of individual pixels in every viewshed are totaled and displayed on a new raster. The pixels most com-
monly visible have the highest scores, whilst the least visible have the lowest. Covert spaces analysis works by
creating two separate cumulative visibility rasters of the same region, one which shows how many views can be
seen from a given location, views-from (Vf ), and another which shows how many times a viewpoint was visible
from the surrounding landscape, views-to (Vt) (Gillings 2015, 3–5). Vf and Vt rasters are then normalized to
scale values, after which Vf are subtracted from Vt to create an index for covert

For the purposes of this study, Vf are points in the sea surrounding western Rough Cilicia, in this instance
representing what ships could see as they sail past the coast. Vt come from sites identified in the Rough Cilicia
survey projects, which could be used to survey the coast for potential targets. There were 2058 evenly spaced
points that made up Vf and 1200 evenly spaced points between the Cilican coast and Taurus ridge that made up
Vt. The results of this process are shown in the map in Figure 4, with RCSP sites and pottery finds also included.

­Alternatively, the Cragus does not offer the same level of covertness as Coracesium. However, it is strategi-

To understand the likely connection between the pirates of coastal Rough Cilicia and the unruly tribal e­ lements
of the Taurus interior, we need to contextualize the latter. Rauh has previously referred to the Taurus ridge
as an ancient “Green Line” that separated the semi-periphery of the Cilician coast from the periphery of the
­Isaurian hinterland (Rauh et al. 2009, 296, 299). In some respects, this serves as a useful line of demarcation. The
 ­hinterland was inhabited by dispersed populations of rural agro-pastoralists identified according to four tribal
  entities: the Isaurians to the northwest (directly south of Konya), the Homonadenses to the southwest (bor-
  dering Pisidia and Lycaonia), the Lalasseis directly north of western Rough Cilicia and the Cennetae slightly
  east (Fig. 5). The matter is confused somewhat by references to an additional tribal element known as the
  Ceitae. However, this term appears to apply generally to highlanders throughout eastern Rough Cilicia, in the
  same manner that Isaurians referred to those in the west (Hild and Hellenkemper 1990, 301; Casabonne 2004,
  85; ­etymologically, Qedi, Kitti, Ketis, Ceitae). Two things need to be stressed at the outset: social organization
  among these tribes was segmentary, lineage based and dominated by tribal chieftains, and their cultural heritage
  was Luwian (Hopwood 1983; 1989; 1991; Shaw 1990; Lenski 1999a; 1999b; Casabonne 2004, 22–5; Grünewald
  2004, 105, 119–23). One characteristic of segmentary societies is their tendency toward r­ ecombination over
  time. By late antiquity, the inhabitants of the interior were known generally as Isaurians, which entitles us to
  refer to them collectively as such. Each tribal element consisted of separate chiefdoms, which were o  ­ ccasionally
  galvanized by particularly powerful warlords into larger realms. These chieftains are referred to by several
  terms, such as tyrannoi or basileis in Greek and dux in Latin (Strabo 14.5.10; App. Mith. 17.117; Tac. Ann.
12.55). Rarely are they named as individuals; more typically, they are bunched together as warlords. Pliny the
Elder (HN 5.94) comments that, in 52 CE, some 44 castella existed in the Isaurian hinterland, from which one

hreatened Neo-Babylonian territories on the opposite Syrian coast, prompting a mili-
tary response from king Neriglissar in 557 BCE. Despite his defeat, Appuašu’s family remained influential, with
a likely descendant being Epyaxa, the wife of the Persian satrap Syennesis of Tarsus, in 401 BCE (Casabonne
2004, 148). Another dynasty, the Teucrid priest kings of Olba, dominated eastern Rough Cilicia as client kings
to the Seleucids, at one point claiming authority over the koinon of the Lalasseis and Cennetae (Syme 1986, 16;
Durugönül 1998, 85–9). However, according to Strabo, their ascendancy was overturned by unruly tyrants at
the time of the pirates (Strabo 14.5.10; Trampedach 1999). A pattern of violent competition among highland
warlords generally prevailed (Strabo 12.6.2; Syme 1939; 1986; Grünewald 2004, 119–23). On occasion, leader-
ship was wrested from the hands of the hereditary elite by charismatic leaders who emerged from the impover-
ished herders of the highlands; for example, the 3rd century CE warlord Lydius, who “had been brought up in
the brigandage customary to his nation, and surrounding himself with a band of similar men, pillaged the whole
of Pamphylia and Lycia” (Zos. 1.69, trans. R.T. Ridley, Canberra, 1982).
    In other words, even among the tribal elements, sharp cleavages existed between dynasts and renegades,
landowners and pastoralists, rich men and poor. These potential sources of conflict were offset by a collective
sense of cultural identity. This is demonstrated by the Luwian names of regional cults and deities, by the icono-
graphic displays of fune

, who was referred to as an archipirata, assumed the title of emperor, struck
coins and established an imperial palace at an Isaurian stronghold (SHA Tyr. Trig. 26.2; Grünewald 2004, 115).
Although many assume Trebellianus to be fictitious, his behavior conforms to a pattern. In the 490s CE another
Isaurian noble, Longinus of Selinus, mounted a rebellion against his brother, the emperor Anastasius, from for-
tified bases at Selinus and Antiochia ad Cragum. When defeated by Anastasius, Longinus and his allies retreated
into the Taurus, yet were able to hold out for five years by importing foodstuffs through Antiochia, all the
while conducting piratical raids as far removed as Lycia, Cyprus, Rhodes and Syria (Theophanes Chronographia
139–40; Lenski 1999a, 428–29). Despite the obvious separation in time and context, in other words, examples
of Isaurian warlords who dominated the highlands, yet engaged in seaborne piracy do present themselves. One
scenario might posit, therefore, that when offshore authority was weak, warlords such as Appuašu, Trebellianus
and Longinus filled the void along the coast. What is less clear are the mechanisms by which this was achieved.
    Comparative cultural anthropology furnishes one likely scenario for a pattern of communication, namely,
the mobile lifeways of the transhumant pastoralists themselves. Modern studies of transhumant herders in the
Pindos range in Greece (Wace and Thompson 1972, 19, 77, 177; Chang 1993) reveal a similar settlement pattern
of lowland farming, mixed agro-pastoral activities in the midlands and transhumant pastoralism in the

that erupted against the Roman
client king Archelaus II of Cappadocia in 36 CE. Archelaus had attempted to conduct a census in the Taurus
hinterlands and, as Rudi Lindner (1983, 53) demonstrates for medieval Turkey, censuses were long abhorrent to
transhumant populations, who correctly interpreted them as preliminaries to taxation. Dwelling on the margins
of settled agricultural society, living off the land and expropriating resources by force when required, pasto-
ralists invariably view taxation as an illegitimate interference to their traditional way of life, particularly when
authorities furnished little in return. During the era of the pirates, “mountain Cilicians” conceivably exploited
the resentment of pastoralists dwelling to either side of the Taurus “Green line” to plunder the coast and to
promote piratical activities.
     The question remains, whether the transhumant economy and cultural affinities of the pastoralists who
dwelled in the midlands of western Rough Cilicia were sufficient linkages to facilitate Isaurian domination
of communities on the shore. This is where sites such as the Hellenistic site at Sugözü Yayla (RC 1102), the
Isaurian necropolis at Yunt (RC 0702) and the fortified Isaurian settlement at Çokele Kale above Coracesium
become important (Bean and Mitford 1970, 105, 126; Rauh 2003, 183; Rauh et al. 2019, 12; Fig. 2). These sites
­conceivably straddled pathways across the Taurus “Green Line” and enabled warriors from the interior to de-
 scend into the Cilician mesogeia. Such a threat is demonstrated by the presence of a Ptolemaic bastion at Lamos
 (800 masl), as well as by the Isaurian-styled narrative relief that was discovered by the survey at the Isaurian
 necropolis cluster at Kenetepe (RC 0304) (Fig. 6). This 5

proved unreadable, these two remains, one Hellenistic, the other Early Roman, demonstrate that the Rough
Cilician mesogeia remained contested territory (Rauh et al. 2009, 296–305).
     Highland pathways appear to have furnished the necessary lines of communication between the maritime
settlements along the coast and the inhabitants of the interior. During periods when security along the coast
was enforced by offshore naval powers, the economic equilibrium of the transhumant society was possibly
disrupted, provoking reprisals in the form of banditry and the highland rebellions described by our sources.
However, during periods of political vacuum at sea, the tyrannoi of the “mountain Cilicians” conceivably ex-
ploited their influence over the highland populations on both sides of the Taurus to impose their will on coastal
settlements. To explore this last point, we will employ least cost path analysis to consider the direction of likely
thrusts from the interior to the shore based on the chronological sequence of piracy as presented in the sources;
first by means of a least cost path between the Isaurian settlements of Isaura Vetus and Nova and the coast, then
one between the hinterland castella of the Lalasseis and the maritime settlements in western Rough Cilicia.

Least-cost-pathways (LCPs) are a useful means to analyze the evolving interconnection between the Cilician
coast and Isaurian highlands. This form of geographical analysis is designed to show the easiest route through
a given landscape. Relying on a list of 70 sites in Rough Cilicia and 16 in Isauria furnished by the RCSP (Rauh
and Pejša 2021a, 2021b), we employ an iterative model to reconstruct all potential routes from any given site
in Rough Cilicia to one in Isauria. To accurately simulate the cost of traveling, Tobler’s hiking function (THF)
was used. Devised in 1993 by avid hiker and geographer Waldo Tobler, it estimates walking velocity relative to
slope (Tobler 1993). The equation, as described by Goodchild (2020, 558), is as follows, v=6e-3.5|g+0.05|, “where v
is walking velocity in Km/h, and g is the gradient of the slope expressed as tangent of the slope angle and e the
constant 2.71818” (Goodchild 2020, 559).
      If Isaurian warlords supported piracy as a seasonal activity, it would be worthwhile investigating the coastal
bases from which they could undertake these activities. Early Roman campaigns focused on regions west of
Cilicia. Marcus Antonius Orator’s much derided campaign involved him capturing Side in Pamphylia. Philip
de Souza (1999, 137–40) characterizes Servilius Vatia’s campaign against Lycian pirates as pacifying the pro-­
Mithridatic eastern Lycians to the benefit of the pro-Roman western Lycians. After the expulsion of anti-Lycian
League forces from the region, Vatia continued his campaign into Isaurian territory, suppressing the fortified
communities of Isaura Vetus and Isaura Nova. The fact that Vatia earned the agnomen Isauricus indicates that,
together with Lycia and Pamphylia, Isauria enjoyed an important place in the pirate hegemony. The suppression
of Pamphylia and Isauria may have quieted things for a while, as resistance coalesced to new centers of gravity.
In 67 BCE, the pirate bases at Coracesium and the Cragus were perceived as the largest pirate threat and across
the Taurus directly north of them resided neighboring tribes of the Ceitae, including the Lalasseis and the
­Cennetae. Still turbulent in 6, 36 and 52 CE, these elements were clearly unaffected by the suppression of Isauria
 in the previous century (Syme 1934, 1986). To what degree were these the “mountain Cilicians” who opposed
 Pompeius and who, according to Tacitus, “had already broken the peace on many occasions” (Ann. 12.55, trans.
 J. Jackson, Cambridge. Mass., 1937)?
      LCPs can be used to evaluate the links between the Isaurians based in Nova and Vetus and the coastal
r­ egions of Pamphylia. These LCPs show not only the shortest distance between the locations, but also the total
 pathcost, or the difficulty of a given path. If warlords from these regions were dominating the coast, this analysis
 would be useful for identifying the ideal naval centers for these groups, as well as suggesting how they may have
 traveled to them. The major coastal centers in this region are Attaleia, Aspendos, Coracesium, Perga and Side.
 Table 2 includes distance and pathcost between these coastal sites and Isaurian strongholds, while the map in
 Figure 7 shows the LCPs between them.

LCPs suggest that the two coastal settlements closest to the Isaurian strongholds were Coracesium and Side.
Coracesium has the shortest route in terms of distance. However, the steep journey which skirts around some
of the higher parts of the Taurus, means the pathcost is high. The northeasterly journey from Side has a lower
pathcost and would have been more efficient. Both Coracesium and Side are mentioned as important centers for
early Cilician pirates. Coracesium’s value has already been discussed. As far as Side is concerned, according to
Strabo (14.3.2), pirates were permitted to trade in its harbor, giving them a convenient market center to fence
their goods. These two ports nearest to the Isaurian strongholds provided ideal centers to connect Isaurians
to the coast. This may explain why Marcus Antonius Orator captured Side and why Servilius Vatia used it as
a staging ground to assault Isaura Vetus. Initial Roman intelligence possibly indicated that an elimination of
the Isaurian hinterland threat would cause Cilician piracy to wither. Instead, it appears that a coalescence and
relocation of forces in the highlands led to a resurgence elsewhere.
     Following the suppression of the Isaurians, tribal disturbances appear to have shifted to the region of the
Lalasseis, or more specifically to a cluster of settlements in the interior mesogeia near the modern Ermenek
reservoir along the southern branch of the Göksu (Calycadnus) River. In the Roman era, this area would
emerge as the seat of the Decapolis of the Lalasseis and the Cennetae. As the names of several settlements (e.g.,
­Germanicopolis, Domitiopolis, Eirenopolis, Titiopolis and Philadelphia) indicate, Roman veteran’s colonies
 were installed throughout this region to secure the peace following decades of military intervention. Since the
 Ermenek mesogeia emerged as a hotbed of resistance in the Early Roman period, for purposes of LCP analysis
 we will utilize Germanicopolis as the symbolic location of the “mountain Cilicians” who opposed Pompeius
 (Fig. 8).
   From the settlements near Ermenek, the “mountain Cilicians” had excellent accesses to Rough Cilicia, being
uniquely situated at the confluence of the two major routes between the coast and highlands. One of these runs

northward from Anamur (the location of a Hellenistic castellum in 197 BCE), the other runs eastward from the
Bickici. Relying on these pathways, we will consider four major coastal settlements in Rough Cilicia that were
inhabited at the time of the pirates: Coracesium, the Bickici basin (between Iotape and Selinus), Antiochia ad

When comparing the routes between Ermenek and Cilicia to those from between Isaura Vetus and
­ amphylia, we can see that routes are shorter and more cost effective for an Isaurian-Cilicia connection. This

would suggest that the Lalasseis were indeed in a better position to exert influence over coastal pirate enclaves
following the suppression of the Isaurians. Of the four routes, the one from Coracesium appears to be some-
thing of an outlier. The easterly route follows the modern Dim Çay, then crosses a valley below Çokele Kale,
before following the ridge eastwards past Fariske and then to Ermenek. Despite Coracesium being a prime

site and the terminus of Pompeius’ campaign, it is the longest route to the heart of the Ermenek mesogeia by
both cost and distance. However, it is important to contextualize these results. The distance is still shorter than
the journey to Isaura Vetus and only somewhat higher in cost, making it still a convenient base for hinterland
groups. Furthermore, with the loss of major harbors in Lycia and Pamphylia, Coracesium would be one of the
remaining few maritime centers available to the pirates as base. The fact that the LCP passes the fortress of
Çokele Kale and the ­necropolis of Fariske would seem to suggest that the “mountain Cilicians” of the Ermenek
mesogeia were interested in controlling traffic along this route and were indeed influencing Coracesium.
      The relative distance from Ermenek to Coracesium may explain the Hellenistic presence in coastal r­ egions
closer to the Lalasseis-Cennetae federation, namely, the areas best suited for pirate visibility, Bickici and
Cragus. The route from the Bickici region follows the river northeast before passing through Günnercik Yayla,
then ­follows the Göksu River to Ermenek. This is shorter and easier than traveling from Coracesium, which
is perhaps why the Bickici route frequently intersects with sites related to the Lalasseis-Cennetae federation.
­Günnercik Yayla was a seasonal site for grazing livestock. Whilst following the Bickici river, the route is also
 littered with Hellenistic material in Sarıağac Mahalle (RC 9908), Kenetepe (RC 0304), Karaçukur (RC 0303),
 Sivaste (RC 0301) and Sugözü Yayla (RC1102), all of which also demonstrate hinterland cultural attributes. In
 terms of visibility, the settlement of Kenetepe and Sivaste are both covert and ideal for monitoring traffic going
 up and down the Bickici. Despite being ideally located for piracy and displaying a strong Isaurian presence, the
 Bickici basin lacks the harborages for large ships (though Iotape and Selinus are nearby). This might in turn ex-
 plain the prominence of the Cragus. The route from Antiochia ad Cragum to Ermenek again passes useful sites
 related to piracy. These include an ideal pirate monitoring station in Gocuk Asarı, a lumber camp and accompa-
 nying village in Gürçam Karatepe (RC 0305) and Taslı Seki (RC 0306). All three settlements contain clusters of
 Hellenistic material. The harborages at Antiochia ad Cragum with closer proximity to Ermenek may have made
 it an ideal alternate to Coracesium for “mountain Cilicians” based in Ermenek. This may help explain why it is
 mentioned as a capital of the pirates by Appian (Mith. 14.92), but otherwise goes unmentioned by other sources.
     Finally, Anemurium, which while not suited for piracy appears to be the most easily accessible site from
Ermenek. The path largely follows the modern 33–62 highway, before passing through Eirenopolis (Irenbol), a
second Roman-era settlement of the Decapolis, and then heading north to Ermenek. Along with ­Philadelphia
and Germanicopolis, Eirenopolis are believed to have been established as veterans’ colonies following the
­suppression of the general revolt of the Ceitae led by Troxobor in 52 CE. Though perhaps not a prime location
 for piracy, given its relative ease of access to these highland settlements, it is possible that the Ceitae gener-
 ally viewed Anemurium as their territorial heritage. In this context, Troxobor’s uprising could be seen as a
 ­continuation of the Isaurian push eastwards, having been suppressed by the Romans further west.

but never assimilated. The
various military campaigns, spanning from 100 BCE to 54 CE, suggest a cat-and-mouse dynamic, where Roman
armies destroy one Isaurian connection to the coast, only to see another one emerge elsewhere. At times, when
a particular Isaurian tribal element appears to be in ascendancy, the nearest maritime centers on the coast also
appear to be prominent. Initially, this appears to be Side and Coracesium, under the influence of Isaura Nova
and Vetus. Following the deterioration of relations with Romans and the sack of Isaura Vetus, a new axis was
possibly forged between the tribal elements in the Ermenek mesogeia and the pirate enclaves at Coracesium,
the Bickici Basin and the Cragus. In this context, it is perhaps possible to see the benefits of Pompeius’ cam-
paign to the renegade sailors who had flocked to the coast of Rough Cilicia. Initially forced into the region due
to conflict with Rome, these sailors possibly came to find themselves dominated by surrogates of hinterland
warlords. In these circumstances, many may have found Pompeius’ proposals of land and franchise in 67 BCE
more appealing. In short, merchants and sailors at that juncture may have had more to gain by choosing the
side of Rome over that of the Isaurian warlords, since peace with Rome and protection from the Isaurians
would only have proven preferable to war. This perhaps explains the speed at which the pirate settlements in
western Rough Cilicia capitulated. However, even with their coastal influence diminished, there was still no

If, as suggested, piracy in Cilicia was catalyzed by a diaspora of Hellenistic maritime actors into the region,
then connections between the Isaurian hinterlands and coastal Cilicia would have been mutually beneficial. As
already discussed, the Isaurians had a penchant for raiding. Where wealth is measured in terms of livestock,
rustling can become a prominent practice. This form of raid mentality lends itself well to a transition into
piracy. Mohamed Ingiriis (2013, 241) states his belief that the origins of contemporary Somali piracy tran-
scend the more obvious explanations of poverty and illegal fishing that results from local political instability.
Instead, he posits that Somali piracy has its origin in camel rustling practices employed by Somali pastoralists.
In this way, Somali piracy was not simply a new phenomenon brought on by changing conditions, but instead
a long-standing Somali cultural tradition that pivoted to the seas. As maritime activity began to increase on the
Cilician coast, Isaurian pastoralists conceivably acquired additional means of employment alongside herding,
muleteering, timbering, mining and itinerant farm laboring. This complements Appian’s comment that “having
lost both livelihood and country by reason of the war and fallen into extreme destitution, [the pirates] harvested
the sea instead of the land” (Mith. 14.92, trans. H. White, New York, 1899), not to mention Plutarch’s comment
that the pirates drew their recruits from “men whose wealth gave them power, and those whose lineage was
illustrious” (Pomp. 24.2, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass., 1917). Not only would sailors and merchants new
to the region have acquired local recruits and collaborators for their maritime ventures, but Cilicians and Isau-
rians would have benefitted from the process of settling sailors in opportune locations and furnishing them with
foodstuffs, supplies and the knowledge of local pathways.
     At times when collaboration between pirates operating on the coast and Isaurian highlanders was great,
 the shorter, less costly routes to the coast demonstrate an overlay of Hellenistic activity and Isaurian cultural
 attributes. For example, a LCPs analysis would suggest that from the Ermenek mesogeia of the Lalasseis, the
 easiest coastal region of Cilicia would have been the Bickici river basin from its headwaters at Sugözü Yayla
 to its settlements, press complexes and kiln site on the shore. The hypothesis that Isaurians used this route to
 exert control over Cilicia is supported by the fact that these routes pass by sites that existed at the time of the
 pirates, were rich in Isaurian material culture and were ideal for surveying the wider region. Later, Roman set-
 tlements that remained hostile towards Isaurian tribes appear further removed and devoid of intersecting routes
 with hinterland Isaurian settlements. What this discussion has demonstrated is that the combined historical
 and ­archaeological evidence for the Cilician pirates conforms very well to empirical analyses of the chosen
­landscape.

A Comparative and Diachronic Approach of the Ships Used by the Pirates of the
Aegean during the Classical and Hellenistic Period

The ship has always been the primary weapon and asset of every form of piracy. The ability of pirates to build, maintain
and man their ships would condition the success of any piratical endeavor, while the size and the type of these ships was,
in turn, determined by their owners’ needs and abilities. In the Aegean Sea, from the beginning of the history of piracy,
lighter and faster oared vessels were preferred, which were able to take advantage of their speed, as well as the r­ egion’s
geomorphology, moving swiftly between friendly and hostile coasts and islands, and offering the possibility of efficient
maneuvering and stealth. At the same time, their size was dependent on the ability of the piratical ­communities to support
their construction and manning. This paper explores the typology of the Classical and Hellenistic-era piratical ships in
the Aegean, as these are known through written sources and iconography, giving a comparative image of these ships and
connecting their use with practical issues, such as cost, manning and seaworthiness.

Piracy has been one of the main features of the maritime cultural landscape in the Aegean Sea already since
Prehistory, as iconography, textual evidence and verbal tradition has documented, and has remained one of the
most important (and quite troublesome for many) occupations of the locals until the 19th century (Ormerod
1924, 13–4; Krantonelli 1985, 1991, 1998). The ramifications of piratical activity were numerous (political, fi-
nancial, social, symbolic), affecting nearly all aspects of life on the islands and coasts of the archipelago. Never-
theless, the practice of piracy required one essential tool and/or weapon, and that was the ship. The availability
of ships, their numbers, sizes, crews and seaworthiness dictated to a great extent the possibility of practicing
piracy in a successful way, as well as its impact on the communities that employed it (or suffered by it). It is
thus essential to have a clear view of the types of ships used by pirates throughout the ages, in order to fully
­understand and study the extent, form and impact of piracy both to perpetrators and victims.

Piracy in the ancient world is a rather elusive subject of study (de Souza 1999, 2). The reason is simple: it was
predominantly (as has remained until today) an activity practiced in the margins of organized society and usu-
ally by small maritime communities, who had little interest or means in leaving proper documentation of their
activities. Piracy was, also, often interweaved with other, legal, activities, such as trade and warfare, r­ esulting in
the limits between the predatory/piratical economies and domination spaces or thalassocracies being obscure
and difficult to establish with precision in historiography (Bresson 2008, 214–19; for a discussion on the various
approaches on the issue, see Deramaix 2013, 359–87). Things become worse by the fact that the oared vessels
commonly employed for piratical activities in antiquity do not survive as shipwrecks in the region, due to their
light construction and lack of cargo to protect their wooden hulls (Wilson 2011, 33–9; Boetto 2012), and by the
fact that when galley images survive, there is no evidence to connect them to any piratical activity whatsoever.
And this is true also in the Aegean Sea, despite the richness in finds, both in the sea and on land, and iconog-
raphy.
    The only direct (to a certain degree) source of information concerning the ships used by the pirates of the
Classical and Hellenistic Aegean is, therefore, written evidence. The period studied here is, most probably, the
richest in terms of written documentation of nearly all aspects of contemporary life, with sources ranging from
historical texts to inscriptions and from poetry to graffiti. The methodology employed by this study is based
on the thorough examination of all written evidence available and their correlation with archaeological data,
iconography and historical parallels, in order not only to merely document the types of ships used by pirates,
but also to explore the practicalities and logistics of their employment and the ramifications these could have in
the practice of contemporary piracy. The basic questions this paper tries to answer concern the types of ships
used by pirates of the period studied, whether these were specially-built vessels or whether they were the same
as ships used in other types of maritime conflicts, whether these ships had a dual use for trade too, and, finally,
why did pirates choose specific types of vessels.

The Classical period
Despite the establishment of strong state naval fleets, such as the famous Athenian one, during the Classical
­period, piracy remained a constant threat to ship traffic and coastal communities (Ormerod 1924, 108–9;
 de Souza 1999, 43–96). The earliest references to piratical ships in the period come from two passages from
 ­Thucydides. In the first one, the historian describes how some Megarians, who conspired with the Athenians in
  431 BCE, would pretend to be pirates, using a small boat or akation, which they carried on a cart in and out of
  the city walls every night:

In the second passage, Thucydides describes the events in Sphakteria (425 BCE). He documents how
the Athenian general Demosthenes, preparing the defense of the islet, took weaponry “from a thirty-oared
[τριακοντόρου/triaconter] Messenian privateer [λῃστρικῆς] and a boat [κέλητος/keles] belonging to some
­Messenians who happened to have come to them” (Thuc. 4.9.1, trans. J.M. Dent, London and New York, 1910).
    The use of triaconters as raiding and plundering ships is also attested by Polyaenus, who reports that around
378 BCE Iphicrates raided the coasts of Phoenicia with one hundred such ships with great success (Strat. 3.9.63).
Although the reference does not describe Iphicrates’ actions as piratical, the use of these ships for a successful
raid implies that it was ideal for piratical use too (Casson 1971, 125). Around 350 BCE, Aeschines refers to the
ship epaktrokeles as a proverbial pirate ship, in which men with great lust and desire board as pirates to seek
their fortune: “these it is that fill the robbers’ bands [τὰ λῃστήρια], that send men on board the pirates’ boats [τὸν
ἐπακτροκέλητα]” (Aeschin. In Tim. 191, trans. C.D. Adams, London and New York, 1919).
     A new type of piratical ship, the hemiolia, which was a light galley that included a second file of oarsmen at
its center, appears in the 4th century BCE and a series of references in written sources underlines its importance.
It is first reported in the Etymologicum Magnum, at a reference roughly dated in the 4th century BCE, where
a Carian hemiolia, most likely belonging to pirates, is mentioned (450.38). Also, Arrian (Anab. 3.2.4) reports
that in 331 BCE Aristonikos, the tyrant of Methymna in Lesvos, sailed into the harbor of Chios with five pirate
hemioliai (ξὺν ἡμιολίαις λῃστρικαῖς πέντε) before being apprehended by Alexander’s troops and put to death
(Morrison and Coates 1996, 262).

The Hellenistic period
The conquest of the Aegean and Ionia by Alexander brought a short period of peace and safety in the seas,
which was, however, soon to finish, with the series of wars of the Successors, in which pirates took advantage
of the instability and were also employed by the rulers of the period as corsairs (de Souza 1999, 43–96). The
hemiolia continues to be firmly associated with piracy. Theophrastus, around 300 BCE, mentions the term as
the ­proverbial symbol of piratical threat, seen by cowards lurking behind each cape: “The coward, when he is at
sea, claims that p­ romontories are pirate ships [ἡμιολίας] (Char. 25.2, trans. J. Diggle, Cambridge, Mass., 2004).
Even in the 2nd century CE, Longus reports Carian pirates raiding the coast with a hemiolia (Daphnis and Chloe
1.28.1). In the early 3rd century BCE, the Rhodians counteract the piratical hemiolia by developing an improved
and larger version of it, the trihemiolia, one of the most successful warships of the period (Casson 1971, 130–31;
Gabrielsen 2001, 224; Pacheco 2020, 101). The trihemiolia was heavier and faster than the hemiolia by being a
full bireme along its whole length, but with a third file of oarsmen added at its center and, interestingly enough,
is never cited as a vessel used by pirates, but solely by official state fleets.
    About 200 BCE, another type of ship is reported as a pirate vessel. The lembos (λέμβος) is first mentioned
as the main vessel of the Liburnian pirates in the Adriatic, along with the later liburnae (Polyb. 2.9.1–2; Livy
45.30.12–15; see also Boršić et al. 2021), but is soon introduced in the Aegean too. In 197 BCE, Philip V sailed
to a parley at the Maliac Gulf in central Greece on a pristis (πρίστις, i.e., saw-fish), accompanied by five lemboi
(Polyb. 18.1.1). It is very likely that the lemboi and pristis (possibly a heavier version of the former) were
­similar to the liburna and were used for similar purposes, i.e., for piracy, raids etc. (Casson 1971, 25–6, 126–27;
 ­Morrison and Coates 1996, 263–64).
     The last heyday of piracy in the Aegean during the Hellenistic period was the Mithridatic wars (88–63 BCE),
during which the region became the main theater of a series of conflicts, both on land and in the sea ­(Morrison
and Coates 1996, 115–19). Mithridates employed and supported the Cilician pirates, who thus became p      ­ owerful
and numerous, greatly improving their military power and organization (App. Mith. 14.96; Ormerod 1924, 190–
247; de Souza 1999, 97–148). Initially, they employed relatively small ships, such as h­ emioliai and m
                                                                                                      ­ yoparones,
but they soon managed to build or acquire larger vessels, such as biremes (δίκροτοι), triremes and even, for the
first time, heavier cataphract vessels (Plut. Pomp. 24.4–5). The final defeat of Mithridates and his allies and the

Typology of the pirate ships
The Classical and Hellenistic period saw the creation and development of multitude of galley types, each with
different size, crew and purpose (Morrison 1995, 68–77; Morrison and Coates 1996, 255–78). As it has become
clear, however, from the presentation of the evidence, the ships used by the pirates belonged to relatively small
types, fitted best for their uses within piratical activities. In this section, each ship type is presented and dis-
cussed according to its size and size of crew, from the smallest to the largest one.
      The akation (ἀκάτιον) and the lembos (λέμβος) appear to have been the smallest piratical ships used during
the period studied, since both terms mean boat or skiff in ancient Greek. The akation appears only once in
written sources in relation to piracy and in the peculiar circumstances of the Megarians using a skiff that can
be easily carried on a cart (see above), so it is very likely that it was not a term employed regularly for piratical
­vessels. It is also possible that the vessel was too small to accommodate any important attacking force to be
 useful in piratical activities. Lembos, on the other hand, appears much more often as a piratical ship in written
 sources. According to these references (as well as to others, which are not related to piracy), the term de-
 scribed various undecked small galleys with 16 to 50 oarsmen and was quite similar to the liburna, with which
 it ­operated side-by-side in Hellenistic Illyria (Ormerod 1924, 29; Morrison and Coates 1996, 264; Boršić et al.
 2021) and probably appears on the Illyrian coins of the 2nd century BCE (Höckman 1997, fig. 1.2–3, 5–6). It is
 possible that the liburna was introduced in the Aegean by the so-called Tyrrhenian pirates, who had expanded
 their operations there in the 2nd century BCE (Ormerod 1924, 127). A unique example of a lembos most likely
 survives in Pisa (Boat C): the well-preserved vessel was a small undecked galley with six pairs of oars, a single
 mast and a cutwater, that could have been used for various activities, such as espionage, raids or simply for
 ­ferrying passengers within harbors and estuaries (Bonino 2010; Olaberria et al. 2023).
     The triakonter (τριακόντορος) was one of the simplest and lightest types of galleys employed in the Aegean
and known already from the Geometric period (Ormerod 1924, 29; Casson 1971, 44–5). It was a light, undecked
monoreme galley with 15 benches of oarsmen, arranged in single files on the sides of the ship. It was most
­probably equipped, like almost all oared vessels of the period, with a cutwater at the bow. It is unknown whether
 such a small vessel could also employ a ram in battle, being probably too light to withstand the tensions created
 by ramming. It had limited space both for provisions or loot, as well as for extra marines and, as described by
 Polyaenus for Iphicrates’ raid in Phoenicia (see above), oarsmen doubled as fighters. Thanks to its small size and
 corresponding draft, a triakonter was not only swift, but it could also approach shallow waters and estuaries and
 be hauled on beaches and required a smaller crew. There are no known depictions of this type of ship during
 the period studied.
    The myoparo (μυοπάρων), which means mouse in ancient Greek, is known as one of the ships used by the
Cilician pirates in the early 1st century BCE, but little is known about its size and form. A unique image of it
survives in the 3rd-century CE ship mosaic of Althiburus in Tunisia, where a series of ships are depicted, along
with their names (Gauckler 1905, 134–35, fig. 16; Duval 1949; Redaelli 2014). It appears to have been similar
to the lembos described above: a small, undecked oared vessel (Ormerod 1924, 30; Casson 1971, 132, fig. 137).
     As its name suggests (κέλης, i.e., racehorse), the keles (celes in Latin) and its diminutives (κελήτιον) or
­variations (ἐπακτροκέλης) were swift oared ships, ideal for piratical use. Very little is known about this ship,
 which appears in the Althiburus mosaic as a small, simple galley. It was most likely very similar to the lembos
 and the myoparo, whereas the epaktrokeles must have been a larger version of it (Ormerod 1924, 30; Casson
 1971, 161–62, fig. 137).
    Probably the pirates’ favorite ship, the hemiolia (ἡμιολία) was a two-banked, undecked variation of a

 it could reach a speed of 7½ knots, less than a trihemiolia or a trireme but more than a liburna (Morrison and
Coates 1996, Appendix D). It is possible that the hemiolia was developed as a pirate ship in Caria, since it is
related by written sources with Carian pirates (Morrison 1995, 73).
    The bireme, the trireme and the cataphract appear only once in relation to piratical fleets, and that is in the
fleets of the Cilician pirates that allied with Mithridates in the early 1st century BCE. All three types were widely
employed by contemporary and earlier naval fleets, and they were relatively heavy vessels, with crews of 100
to 200 people, whereas the cataphracts were even heavier (usually tetreres’/fours or penteres’/fives; Casson 1971,
123, n. 94), with closed superstructures in order to protect their rowing crews (Morrison and Coates 1996,
255–57). Nevertheless, these cannot be considered common pirate ships, since they only appear within this his-
torical framework, when the Cilician pirate cities developed, thanks to the wealth accumulated through raiding
and the support by Mithridates, proper naval fleet.

Evolution of the pirate ships
According to the written sources discussed above, in the Classical and Hellenistic Aegean there seems to have
been an evolution from simpler and lighter to more elaborate and heavier piratical ships. The earliest ships em-
ployed in piracy were the small triakonters and keletes, which were relatively small vessels. The operation of great
naval fleets during the 5th and the early 4th centuries BCE in the Aegean most likely prevented pirates from
building, capturing or buying larger ships and limited them to the simplest galleys they could afford, which also
fitted their purposes better. The rising of piracy within the endemic warfare of the Successors after Alexander
boosted the size of piratical ships and that is when the hemiolia appeared, a larger and heavier ship, which was
no match for the much larger Hellenistic galleys in terms of fighting power, but was much faster and easier to
handle and hide. Smaller vessels, such as myoparones and lemboi, continued to be used, although the hemiolia
became the “trademark” of the pirates of the period. Finally, as Cilician piracy reached its peak –with the organi-
zation of a proper “pirate state”, the acquisition of enough resources, but also the need to deploy stronger vessels
to fight the naval fleets of the Romans– we witness a surge both in the number and in the size of vessels em-
ployed, and for the first time triremes and cataphracts appear (Morrison 1995, 73; Morrison and Coates 1996,
115–19). This period, however, is unique in the history of ancient piracy and most probably no ship heavier
than a hemiolia was ever properly used for any piratical operations in the area during the ­Graeco-Roman an-
tiquity. It is not surprising that also in much more recent periods, like the 16th–19th centuries, ships of similar
dimensions, such as the fusta, the galliota, the felouka or the mistico, were used in the Aegean by the local pirates
(Ormerod 1924, 26–8; Krantonelli 1985, 341–49; 1991, 425; 1998, 286–88).

Fighting techniques and employment
There is little to no evidence in written sources about the techniques used by the piratical vessels during the
­period studied and ancient authors hardly ever describe how pirates employed their vessels in battle. Pirate
 ships always belong to oared types, as would be naturally expected, since the ability to move without the help
 of wind and to achieve great speed was an essential part of ambushing, raiding and evading pursuing ships.
 ­Ramming could have also been employed in battle, but it is quite likely that this would have been possible only
  by relatively large and sturdier vessels, such as hemioliai or triremes (Coates 1995, 133–34). It should also be

There is no reference to the existence of marines (ἐπιβάται) on pirate vessels. In smaller vessels, where there was
also little space for extra troops, the rowing crew could easily double as marines too, but larger ones should have
had a number of marines (hoplites, archers etc.) onboard in order to tackle enemy ships in sea battles, as well as
hostile forces on land. A useful weapon would have also been catapults, which were a common feature of Hel-
lenistic warships, but there is no reference to their use by pirates. The large piratical fleets of the Cilician pirates
were, most likely, organized in the models of other contemporary naval powers, with larger vessels manned by
large numbers of well-armed and trained marines, were equipped with rams and catapults, and were employed
like every other proper naval fleet of the period, particularly when joining forces with rulers like Mithridates,
but there is no direct information about how these fleets were organized and used.
LOGISTICS OF THE PIRATE SHIPS

A vital element of the operation of piratical fleets or single vessels that often eludes the attention of scholars is the
logistics related with it. Every ship requires certain resources to be constructed, equipped, manned, provisioned
and maintained, especially the oared vessels, which not only needed much larger crews (oarsmen, ­marines
etc.), but also constant maintenance, in order to remain in fighting condition (Coates 1995, 132; Dotson 1995,
217). The ability of a community or state to maintain a fleet (or in the cases of small islands even a single ship)
depended on the availability of resources, monetary or not.
    A major issue must have been the provisioning of timber, which was often scarce in the arid Aegean islands
and would have had to be imported or ships to be constructed in areas, where there were natural forests, such
as the coasts of Asia Minor (Morrison and Coates 1996, 354). Although these practices were common in the
naval fleets of the period (e.g., the Athenians would construct triremes in Macedonia; Borza 1987, 39), it is
doubtful whether pirates had the abilities to fund such endeavors, keeping in mind that local timber would also
have to be used for the rest of the regional fleets, consisting of merchant ships, ferries or fishing boats. It is not
surprising that the largest piratical fleets were the ones employed by the Cilicians, who had direct access to an
extended mountainous hinterland that would easily provide material for galley building.
    The same logistic problems would have existed for the rest of the shipbuilding material. Metal was employed
for the nails (bronze or copper), although the extent of their use in galley hulls remains unknown (Coates 1995,
131), as well as for anchors (iron, lead or bronze; Kapitän 1984, 36–43; Votruba 2014, 78) and possibly for
seathing (lead; Kahanov and Ashkenazi 2011). Rigging equipment (ropes, sails, pulleys etc.) was also essential
for navigation, since all ancient galleys would regularly hoist sails and avoid rowing when wind was favorable
(Casson 1971, 229–38; Dotson 1995, 220). Finally, special protective primers or other types of paint were im-
portant to protect the wooden hull from rotting and from shipworms, but also to decorate them (Galinier and
Nantet 2020, 60–8), whereas in one case it is reported by Philostratus that scout and pirate ships would be
painted blue for camouflage (Imag. 1.19; cf. Casson 1971, 212, n. 48).
    The light, undecked galleys of the period, required regular maintenance, especially during the winter months,
to remain seaworthy, as well as specialized personnel to undertake such tasks. It is thus not surprising that pi-
rates preferred relatively small ships, which were easier to build and maintain. Piratical communities, being,
most probably, small and functioning in the margins of society and in remote and poor regions like some of
the small Aegean islands or Cilicia, were unable and unwilling to maintain proper galley fleets (Ormerod 1924,
14–5, 142–43). Furthermore, for communities, where piracy was a “part-time” occupation of poor farmers or
mariners who had turned to it out of necessity, as Aristotle describes (Pol. 1256b; Gabrielsen 2013, 141; Pacheco
2020, 99), the maintenance of oared vessels was an extra burden, since, due to their lack of space that could be
used to transport cargos, these ships could have no dual use as warships and merchantmen and any income
supplied by them would be strictly related to warfare, raids or piracy (merchant galleys were not ­unknown, but
they are not reported in relation to any piratical activity; Casson 1995, 117–23).

in sight. Nevertheless, there has been no firm evidence connecting any of these naval installations with piracy
and these could as well have been outpost for squadrons of small, swift coastguard vessels (φυλακίδες νῆες or
navis speculatoria) that are known to have operated along the coasts in antiquity.
    Another important issue related with the logistics of piratical ships was provisioning. A hemiolia, with a
crew of 50 oarsmen, plus five other crewmembers, would require considerable daily provisions of water and
food to be able to operate. Each oarsman would consume 2.1 to 6.6 liters of water per day (­ depending on the
temperature and the amount of rowing involved) and 4,000 to 5,000 kilocalories (Dotson 1995, 219–20). It is
doubtful that such a vessel could carry water for more than a couple of days in the sea due to the limited hold
underneath the rowing benches, and thus would require regular stops for provisioning. ­Furthermore, it would
not spend nights in the open sea, seeking instead shelter in protected bays and beaches (Tarn 1930, 124; Casson
1971, 89–90). Piratical ships, therefore, had a rather limited operational radius, unless they were supported by
allies or managed to control their illegal activities and act as regular vessels.
   One final, logistical and human resource deficiency of piratical fleets was their manning. Not only they
required an experienced and trained rowing crew, which would also double as fighters, but it was a task that
had to be undertaken by the fittest members of the community and, at the same time, was a rather dangerous
occupation. The loss of a piratical galley at sea would mean the loss of many of the youngest and most dynamic
members of the community. Taking into consideration that the coastal communities of the Aegean (at least the
ones from the smaller islands and coastal settlements that were most likely to harbor piracy) were relatively
small (Reger 1994, 51–5), the operation of piratical ships would have been an activity done with great caution
and care, especially towards the precious tools of piracy, i.e., the ships.

This brief examination of the sources concerning piracy in the Classical and Hellenistic Aegean shows that
the ­pirates of these periods tended to use small, light and swift ships for their endeavors. Their favorite ships
appear to have been the triakonter and the hemiolia, which they preferred for their small size, speed and
­maneuverability. Smaller ships, such as the lembos or the keles, were also employed. Larger units, such as tri-
remes or cataphracts, were only used in the occasion of the heyday of Cilician piracy in the early 1st century
BCE, when pirates expanded their sphere of operations, along with their resources and funding, but this was a
unique event. The choice of smaller vessels was not only due to their qualities concerning speed, small draft and
stealthiness (Ormerod 1924, 26–8), but was also imposed by the nature of piracy, which operated in the fringes
of society and states of the period, and considered relatively small communities of limited means, for which
ships were precious as tools and weapons but also difficult to obtain, man and maintain. Finally, there seems to
have been no type of vessel specially designed and built for or by pirates, who would adopt and use the vessels
most ­suitable for their activities and deploy them in accordance with their needs.

  Tyrrhenian Pirates and Dionysus
The Iconography of an Ancient Story of Piracy

The present study examines, through selected monuments from the Archaic to the Roman era, the iconography of the
myth of the abduction of Dionysus by Tyrrhenian pirates. The Homeric Hymn to Dionysus refers to the abduction of
the god by the pirates and their punishment for this lawless act because they tried by force to keep him as their captive.
Tyrrhenian pirates, identified by modern researchers with the Etruscans who lived in Italy or the inhabitants of Lemnos,
considered him the son of a king and captured him to demand a ransom from his parents. Through a series of miracles
based on symbols of his religion, Dionysus completed the circle of his revenge by transforming the impious pirates into
dolphins. The story of the Tyrrhenian pirates allowed Greek and Roman writers and artists to present their version of
this episode. The pirate ship at sea and its crew play a central role in the pictorial renderings of the subject. By studying
this mythological episode, the plausible elements and historical ramifications are sought in relation to the phenomenon
of piracy, as it exerted a timeless effect on ancient art and religion, each time allowing imagination and faith to provide
distinct approaches to oral or visual narratives.

The Mediterranean Sea was the first broad geographic area, where piracy took on the features of a mass
­phenomenon. As a means to acquiring material wealth and slaves, it was utilized by almost all the peoples
 that settled on its shores during antiquity: the Sea Peoples, the Tyrrhenian marauders, but also the Greeks,
 who, along with classical civilization, produced some of the most fearsome pirates in the known world. An
 ­interesting composition of reality and fiction may be observed in the myth of Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian
  pirates, which is commonly found both in ancient literature and in the pictorial arts.
    The story of Dionysus is full of journeys and peregrinations to spread his cult, and cruel treatment meted
out in irrational fury to those who opposed it, as was the case with Lycurgus, king of Thrace, Pentheus, king
of Thebes, as well as the Tyrrhenian pirates. Notwithstanding the diversity of the modern theories governing
research into myths, there is often a historical reality that triggers each myth, however abstract and fanciful its
plot may be. Therefore, it is often possible to look for chronological limits and geographical boundaries within
the evolution of the myth.

The name Tyrrhenian Sea is attributed to that part of the Mediterranean, which is off the southwestern coast of
Italy and all the way to Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily. The ethnic name Tyrrhenoi (Tyrrhenians) was used by the
ancient Greeks to denote non-Greeks in general and pirate people in particular (LIMC 8:154–5, s.v. Tyrsenoi).
In ancient written sources, the term “Tyrrhenian” is found for the first time in the end of Hesiod’s Theogony:

According to the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, which is discussed in more detail below, Tyrrhenians pirates
wanted to take Dionysus away from the Greek world and sell him to barbarians who lived either in the west or
northwest (Hyperboreans), the south (Egypt) or the east (Cyprus). In Euripides’ Cyclops (10–22), Sicily is men-
tioned as the area of operations of these marauders from Tyrrhenia (γένος Τυρσηνικὸν / λῃστῶν). The presence
of Tyrrhenians in the Aegean is also attested to by several written sources. Thucydides (4.109.4) reports that
in the old days the Tyrrhenians lived in both Athens and Lemnos. Myrsilus of Methymna, a 3rd-century BCE
author, states that the Tyrrhenians were originally from Italy, but they had migrated to the Aegean region, and
ever since that time they became known as Pelasgians (FGrHist 477 F8–9). In the 1st century CE, Dionysius
Halicarnassensis (Ant. Rom. 1.28.1–4) claimed that the Tyrrhenians were not of Pelasgian origin, but lived in
Italy instead (Kobakhidze 2008, 74–7).
     The island of Lemnos has become the focus of numerous debates and arguments ever since the discovery
of the famous inscribed stele of Kaminia in 1884, which depicts a warrior holding a spear. The stele has two
long texts incised on the front face (around the figure of the warrior) and on one of its narrower sides, written
in Greek letters but in a non-Greek language, most probably closely related to Etruscan (Lehr 1942–1945;
Di ­Cesare 2024). Herodotus considered the inhabitants of Lemnos to be Pelasgians (e.g., 4.415.2–5, 5.26.1).
The same author informs us that the Pelasgians of Mountain Hymettos, who, driven away by the Achaeans,
­settled on Lemnos, other islands of the Aegean and the shores of Asia Minor (Hdt. 6.136.2–140.2), were called
 ­Tyrrhenians (Hdt. 1.57.1–3).
    The Tyrrhenians of Lemnos, who were directly related to the Pelasgian Tyrrhenians, must have migrated to
the north Aegean region at the beginning of the 1st millennium BCE (De Simone 1996, 39–84). They rapidly
evolved into a great maritime power and are rightly credited with being the first to use the naval ram. Sources
after the 5th century BCE refer to the inhabitants of Lemnos as “Tyrrhenians”. Numerous pieces of evidence,

Homeric Hymn may also include the inhabitants of Lemnos (see Greco 2010, 3–180). One cannot, however,

­century BCE onwards, Lemnos was considered to be a possession of Athens; this might explain the Athenian in-

TYRRHENIAN PIRACY

Despite the great civilization of the Tyrrhenians, the ancient Greek written sources refer mainly to their intense
 pirate activity (e.g., IG II2 1629, line 223; IG XI.2 148, line 73; Syll.3 1225, line 8; Diod. Sic. 15.14.3; Strabo 5.2.2,
10.4.9; Aristid. Or. 44.570). One of the better-known Tyrrhenian pirates was Postumius, who went raiding at
the head of a flotilla of twelve pirate ships in the 4th century BCE and was captured in Sicily. Timoleon, the
­Corinthian general and politician who was sent to Sicily to rid the local Greeks of tyrants and Carthaginians,
 executed Postumius, whose raids had been playing havoc with the local sea lanes of communication:

Timoleon himself seized and put to death Postumius the Etruscan, who had been raiding sea traffic
               with twelve corsairs, and had put in at Syracuse as a friendly city (Diod. Sic. 16.82.3, trans. C.H.
               ­Oldfather, Cambridge, Mass., 1954).

However, the Tyrrhenian pirates are mainly associated with the well-known myth of Dionysus, both in ancient
written sources and in the arts (e.g., James 1975; Paleothodoros 2012).

ΤHE MYTH OF DIONYSUS AND THE TYRRHENIAN PIRATES IN THE
­A NCIENT WRITTEN SOURCES

The myth of the abduction of Dionysus by the Tyrrhenian pirates is mainly known from three ancient written
sources: the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, the Metamorphoses of Ovid (3.564–691) and the Dionysiaca of Nonnus
(31.86–91, 44.231–252, 45.105–168). Brief references to the myth may also be found in Euripides (Cyc. 10–22),
Apollodorus (Bibl. 3.5.3), Hyginus (Fab. 134), Seneca (Οed. 449–466) and Philostratus the Elder (Imag. 1.19).
Oppian also mentions the transformation of men into dolphins by Dionysus (Halieutica 1.650).
   The earliest hint of the Dionysiac myth with the Tyrrhenian pirates may be traced to the Late Archaic pe-
riod. The first reference to the appearance of the Tyrrhenian pirates is in the seventh dithyramb of the Homeric
Hymns, which is dedicated to Dionysus, probably dating from the late 6th or early 5th century BCE:

Presently there came swiftly over the sparkling sea Tyrsenian pirates on a well-decked ship — a m
                                                                                                               ­ iserable
               doom led them on. When they saw him, they made signs to one another and sprang out quickly, and
               seizing him straightway, put him on board their ship exultingly (Hymn. Hom. Bacch. 6–10, trans. H.G.
               Evely-White, Cambridge, Mass., 1914).

According to Apollodorus, mythographer of the 2nd century BCE, when Dionysus decided to sail from
Ikaria to Naxos, with the aim of initiating the local inhabitants into his cult, he chartered a Tyrrhenian pirate
ship (Τυρρηνῶν λῃστρικὴν τριήρη) to ferry him to the island (Apollod. Bibl. 3.5.3). The Tyrrhenians accepted,
but their ulterior motive was to sell him into slavery in Asia (Romizzi 2003, 352 n. 1; Emilio-Ioannidou 2017,

­A NCIENT ARTS

The most significant depiction of the myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates in south Italian vase-painting appears on
a Late Archaic black-figure Etruscan kalpis, formerly in the Toledo Museum of Art, Ohio (inv. no. 82.134) and
now repatriated to Italy (Fig. 1). It is attributed to The Painter of Vatican 238, a follower of the Μicali Painter
